title: Leases Used for Animal Fighting Are Void
bodyText: North Carolina makes a lease of property void if the property is used or intended to be used for an exhibition of cock fighting, dog fighting or baiting, or the fighting or baiting of any other animal, and a landlord who knows of that use or intended use is under a statutory duty to evict the tenant immediately. Allowing property you own or control to be used for such an exhibition is itself a crime (a felony for cock or dog fighting, a misdemeanor for other animals on a first offense). Evict only through the court process (edu-eviction-process-nc, edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-nc); the library's criminal-activity clause (criminal-activity-nc) already makes such activity a breach.

title: Security Deposit Rules
bodyText:
North Carolina's Tenant Security Deposit Act applies to anyone in the business of renting or managing residential units, other than single rooms. The deposit must be kept in a trust account at a licensed, federally insured bank or authorized trust institution (an out-of-state account needs a bond), or the landlord may instead buy a bond from a licensed insurer, and the tenant must be notified, within 30 days after the lease term begins, of the name and address of the bank or institution where the deposit is held (or the name of the insurance company providing the bond); the statute does not say how, so give the notice in writing.

The deposit may not exceed two weeks' rent for a week-to-week tenancy, one and one-half months' rent for month-to-month, or two months' rent for longer terms; a reasonable nonrefundable pet fee is allowed on top.

The deposit may be used only for unpaid rent and landlord-billed water, sewer or electric charges, damage (including to smoke and CO alarms), damages for not finishing the term (not after a military or domestic-violence termination, an unlawful lockout or a constructive eviction), liens caused by the tenant, re-renting costs including a broker's fee, removal and storage costs after an eviction, court costs, and fees the law allows.

Within 30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant gives back possession, the landlord must mail or deliver an itemized list with the balance; if the damage cannot be figured in time, an interim accounting within 30 days and a final one within 60. No deductions for normal wear and tear or above actual damages.

If the tenant's address is unknown, the landlord must, after 30 days, apply the deposit to the permitted charges and hold the balance for the tenant to collect for at least six months.

On a sale or other end of the landlord's interest, the deposit must be transferred to the new owner (with notice to the tenant) or returned within 30 days.

A landlord who willfully fails to follow the deposit, bond or notice rules loses the right to keep any of the deposit and can be ordered to pay the tenant's attorney's fees.

The Act says nothing about interest (none is owed) or about prepaid last-month rent; the library treats prepaid last-month rent as part of the deposit, counted toward the cap, unless the lease makes it Rent for a named calendar month, because a court could treat it as security.

title: Landlord's Repair and Fitness Duties
bodyText:
A North Carolina landlord must comply with applicable building and housing codes (and elevator safety rules), make all repairs and do whatever is needed to keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas safe, and maintain and promptly repair electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances the landlord supplies once the tenant gives written notice (no written notice is needed in an emergency).

The landlord must also repair any 'imminently dangerous condition' within a reasonable time after learning of it: unsafe wiring, flooring, steps, ceilings, roofs, chimneys or flues; no potable water; no operable locks on exterior doors or ground-floor windows, or broken windows; no heat able to keep living areas at 65 degrees when it is 20 degrees outside (November 1 to March 31); no operable toilet or bathtub or shower; rat infestation from structural defects; and standing water, sewage or flooding from leaks or poor drainage that contributes to mosquitoes or mold. The landlord may recover the reasonable cost of repairs the tenant caused.

These duties cannot be waived: a tenant's acceptance of a defective unit, before, at or after the signing of the lease, does not release the landlord (except while a government body blocks a repair, for no more than six months). After the lease is made, the parties may make a later written contract for the tenant to do specified work, but only if it is supported by adequate consideration other than the letting of the home and is not made with the purpose or effect of evading the landlord's duties.

The tenant's rent obligation and the landlord's fitness duty depend on each other, but the tenant may not withhold rent on their own before a court decides they may. A violation is not negligence per se.

The tenant must keep the unit clean and safe, dispose of waste, not damage the property or disable alarms, and pay for damage in the tenant's control beyond wear and tear; the landlord must tell the tenant in writing of breaches of those duties except in emergencies.

Cities and counties with 200,000 or more people in their planning and development jurisdiction must also require by ordinance a heat source able to heat at least one habitable room other than the kitchen to 68 degrees (measured 3 feet above the floor when it is 20 degrees outside), which the owner must keep in good and safe working order.

The landlord puts new batteries in battery-operated smoke and carbon monoxide alarms at the start of a tenancy and the tenant replaces them during the tenancy, unless the two agree otherwise in writing (a tamper-resistant 10-year lithium smoke alarm needs no new batteries); this library's alarm clause keeps that split, because the landlord must check every alarm at the start of each tenancy anyway. A landlord who wants a different split may agree it in writing.

title: Late Fees and Eviction Fees
bodyText:
North Carolina tightly limits what a landlord can charge. A late fee is allowed only if rent is five or more calendar days late (counting from the day after it was due), is capped at the greater of $15 or 5% of the monthly rent ($4 or 5% for weekly rent), may be charged only once per late payment, cannot be deducted from a later payment to make it late, cannot be charged for unpaid landlord-billed water or sewer, and is figured on the tenant's share only if rent is subsidized.

When a landlord files an eviction or money-owed case, a written lease may provide for ONE administrative fee: a complaint-filing fee (up to $15 or 5% of monthly rent, if the tenant cures and the case is dismissed before judgment), a court-appearance fee (10% of monthly rent, if the landlord wins in small claims) or a second-trial fee (up to 12%, if the landlord wins after an appeal).

The landlord may also recover court filing fees, service costs and, under a written lease, attorneys' fees up to 15% of what the tenant owes (15% of monthly rent for a non-rent eviction), plus all actual reasonable attorneys' fees if the tenant's appeal to district court is found frivolous and the landlord prevails.

These amounts can be included in the cure amount but an administrative fee cannot be deducted from later rent or used as the ground for a later eviction. Any other administrative fee or litigation cost for filing an eviction is against public policy, and a lease term contrary to these rules is void.

Separately, a lease that requires renter's insurance cannot require a particular insurer or agent.

title: Summary Ejectment (Eviction) Process
bodyText: North Carolina evictions are 'summary ejectment' cases heard by a magistrate in small claims court. The landlord may sue when the term has ended and the tenant holds over, when the tenant breaches a lease term that the lease says ends the tenancy, or (for nonpayment where the lease has no forfeiture clause) when rent stays unpaid 10 days after the landlord demands it. The clerk issues a summons setting a hearing within seven days (excluding weekends and holidays); the officer mails the papers and must try to serve them in person or at the home, or posts them on the premises. If the tenant pays or tenders the rent due plus court costs before judgment in a nonpayment case, the case ends. The tenant may appeal within 10 days; to stay the eviction during an appeal the tenant pays undisputed back rent to the clerk (indigent tenants excepted) and signs an undertaking to pay rent into court as it comes due, and missing a payment by five business days dissolves the stay. The sheriff must execute a writ of possession within five days of receiving it and gives the tenant notice of when; if the judgment is more than 30 days old, the landlord must first sign an affidavit that it has not made a new lease with or accepted rent from the tenant since judgment. Eviction and default notices under a lease for a primary residence are outside North Carolina's electronic-records law, so they should be given on paper. A separate expedited procedure (Article 7) lets a landlord evict for drug and other criminal activity, including partial eviction of household members and guests; collecting rent with knowledge of the activity is not a waiver. Unpaid landlord-billed water, sewer or electric charges are never a ground for eviction.

title: No Lockouts, Utility Cutoffs or Seizing Belongings
bodyText: North Carolina public policy allows a residential tenant to be evicted, dispossessed or 'otherwise constructively or actually removed' only through a court eviction (summary ejectment or the Article 7 criminal-activity procedure). Changing the locks, removing doors, cutting off utilities to force a tenant out, or removing the tenant's belongings is unlawful self-help. Distress and distraint (seizing a tenant's property for rent) are prohibited, and a landlord may deal with a tenant's personal property only under the specific abandonment, post-eviction and tenant-death procedures in the statutes. Any lease term to the contrary is void. A tenant removed or threatened with removal unlawfully may recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages (not punitive, treble or emotional-distress damages); the same applies to seizing or blocking access to belongings. A landlord that bills tenants for water, sewer, electricity or gas may not disconnect those services for nonpayment.

title: Retaliatory Eviction
bodyText: A tenant (or a household member the landlord knows of) may defend an eviction as retaliatory if it is substantially in response to, within the 12 months before the filing: a good-faith complaint or repair request to the landlord about conditions the landlord must repair; a good-faith complaint to a government agency about a health or safety law or housing code; a government's formal complaint to the landlord; a good-faith attempt to enforce rights under the lease or law; or involvement with a tenants' rights organization. The landlord still wins if the tenant breached the rent covenant or another substantial covenant and that breach is the reason; if a fixed-term tenant with no renewal option is holding over; if the tenant's household or guests caused the condition; if code compliance requires demolition or major work that displaces the household; if the notice to quit was given before the protected activity; or if the landlord in good faith wants possession at the end of the term to live there, to demolish or remodel, or to stop renting the unit for at least six months. If the court finds retaliation it denies possession, but the landlord may still recover rent due. The tenant's rights cannot be waived.

title: Property Left Behind
bodyText: North Carolina allows only a few ways to deal with a tenant's belongings. After a voluntary move-out: property is abandoned only if clear evidence shows the tenant voluntarily left after the paid rental period ended and the landlord has no notice of a disability causing the absence; a presumption arises 10 or more days after the landlord posts a notice of suspected abandonment inside and outside the unit without response. If the abandoned property is worth $750 or less, the landlord may give it to a nonprofit that provides free or low-cost clothing and furnishings, which must store it separately for 30 days and release it free to the tenant; the landlord must post and mail a notice naming the recipient. After an eviction: the sheriff notifies the tenant of the writ; for seven days after being put in possession the landlord may move the property for storage but may not throw it away or sell it, and must release it to the tenant on request during business hours; after seven days the landlord may dispose of it or sell it (with seven days' written notice of any sale by first-class mail, applying proceeds to rent, damages, storage and sale costs, and paying any surplus to the tenant on request within seven days or then to the county). If everything left is worth less than $500, it is abandoned five days after the writ is executed. Special rules: if the landlord knows the tenant is an attorney, the landlord must notify the North Carolina State Bar at least 15 days before destroying client files or trust account records left behind, and may then destroy or discard any the State Bar does not take as the lease provides; and when a sole occupant dies, the landlord may use the clerk's affidavit procedure instead of an eviction. North Carolina has no separate rule for animals left behind after an eviction; they are handled with the tenant's other belongings under these procedures, subject to animal welfare laws.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute that ends a residential lease when the tenant dies (the only statutory termination tied to death is for military technicians who die on active duty). If a lease ends because of a death partway through a rent period, rent is apportioned to the date of death.

When the tenant was the sole occupant and left belongings, the landlord may, instead of filing an eviction, file an affidavit with the clerk of court once at least 10 days have passed since the paid rental period expired and no estate representative or small-estate affidavit exists in the county; the affidavit must attach the death certificate and an inventory, name the authorized emergency contact from the application or lease, and describe the landlord's attempts to reach that person.

The landlord may then remove and store the belongings and re-rent the unit, and after 90 days (with no estate opened) sell them under notice or give them to a charity; belongings worth $500 or less may go straight to a charity that holds them for 30 days. A landlord acting at the direction of a proper small-estate affiant is discharged.

title: Ending a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: North Carolina's notice periods are short. A month-to-month tenancy ends on seven days' notice, a week-to-week tenancy on two days' notice, and a year-to-year tenancy on one month's notice before the end of the year; a space rented for a manufactured home needs at least 60 days' notice before the end of the rental period. The statute does not require the notice to be in writing, but a written notice is the only practical proof. A tenant who stays after proper notice (or after a fixed term ends) can be removed by summary ejectment. The lease may set a longer period by agreement (periodic-tenancy-notice-nc). There is no statewide just-cause or renewal requirement.

title: Servicemember Rights
bodyText: Two layers of North Carolina law protect servicemember tenants, alongside the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. First, the North Carolina Servicemembers Civil Relief Act applies the federal Act's rights (to the extent military service materially affects the servicemember's ability to meet obligations), including the federal right to terminate a residential lease on entering military service or receiving qualifying orders, to servicemembers who live in North Carolina and to members of the North Carolina National Guard, and extends them to Guard members on State active duty for more than 30 consecutive days (who must give the landlord a copy of the orders within 30 days after the duty ends). A Guard member whose lease expires during State active duty and who is current on rent may extend the lease until 10 days after the duty ends, on the same terms, by written or electronic notice. These rights cannot be waived; a knowing violation is an unfair or deceptive trade practice, and the Attorney General or the servicemember may sue. Second, a military technician (10 U.S.C. § 10216) may end a lease on 30 days' written notice with orders or a commanding officer's verification after permanent change-of-station orders to move 50 miles or more or an early discharge, or on deployment of 90 days or more (effective the earlier of 30 days after the next rent due date or 45 days after notice); family or the estate may terminate if the technician dies on active duty. The technician owes prorated rent plus, if fewer than nine months have been completed and the landlord has actual damages, liquidated damages of no more than one month's rent (under six months) or half a month's rent (six to nine months), and nothing if notice comes 14 or more days before occupancy. The deposit cannot be applied to the early termination.

title: Fair Housing
bodyText: North Carolina's State Fair Housing Act protects the same classes as federal law: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, handicapping condition (disability) and familial status (including pregnancy). It bars refusing to rent, discriminating in terms or services, discriminatory statements, ads, forms or inquiries, misrepresenting availability, and interference or retaliation; it requires reasonable accommodations in rules and policies and allowing reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (with a possible restoration agreement). Exemptions (which do not cover discriminatory advertising): renting in an owner-occupied building of up to four units, renting rooms in an owner-occupied house, certain religious organizations and private clubs, and single-sex dormitories. A landlord need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or cause substantial physical damage, reasonable occupancy limits still apply, and housing for older persons is exempt from the familial-status rules. Complaints go to the North Carolina Human Relations Commission within one year; penalties reach $10,000, $25,000 or $50,000 for repeat violations, plus damages. It is also a crime for a residential landlord or agent to demand sexual acts as a condition of a lease or of lease rights, and a landlord may not discriminate against a tenant or applicant because they are a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. North Carolina has no statewide source-of-income, immigration-status, or firearms rule for private rentals. A landlord may use criminal background checks and has no duty to screen.

title: Service Animals: North Carolina Rules and Penalties
bodyText: Under North Carolina law a person with a disability has the right to keep a service animal on any premises the person leases or rents, on showing either the animal's Department of Health and Human Services registration tag ('North Carolina Service Animal Permanent Registration') or that the animal is being trained or has been trained as a service animal. The law does not limit service animals to dogs. No extra compensation (deposit, fee or pet rent) may be charged for a service animal, but the person is liable for any damage the animal does. Depriving a person of these rights, or charging a fee for the service animal, is a Class 3 misdemeanor; so is disguising an animal as a service animal or service animal in training. Emotional support and other assistance animals are handled as reasonable accommodations under fair housing law, which allows denial for a direct threat or substantial damage.

title: State Limits on Local Rental Rules
bodyText: North Carolina counties and cities may not regulate the amount of rent for private residential or commercial rental property, and since 2024 may not require landlords to accept tenants who pay with federal housing assistance (such as Housing Choice Vouchers). Local governments may still regulate their own property, make rent agreements for subsidized properties, restrict rents on properties assisted with Community Development Block Grant funds, and regulate owners that take local funding or incentives. State law also sharply limits local rental registration and inspection programs: a local government generally may not require a permit or registration to rent, may inspect only with reasonable cause (or in a small designated blight area), and may require registration or a permit only for individual properties with repeated verified code violations or in the worst 10% for crime or disorder. Local housing codes, heat ordinances and inspections otherwise still apply.

title: Bounced Checks
bodyText: North Carolina lets a person who accepts a check 'in payment for goods or services' charge a processing fee of up to $35 if the bank refuses it for insufficient funds or because the account does not exist; whether rent counts is not settled by the statute's words, so treat $35 as the most a landlord may charge for a returned check. If the tenant knowingly wrote the bad check and does not pay the check amount, any bank service charges and the processing fee in cash within 30 days after a written demand sent by certified mail in the statutory form, the landlord may sue for those amounts plus damages of three times the check amount (at least $100, at most $500), after a second statutory-form demand if the landlord chooses to send one; a court may reduce the extra damages for economic hardship. No statute sets a fee for a failed electronic payment.

title: Billing Tenants for Utilities
bodyText:
A North Carolina landlord may bill tenants for water and sewer, electricity, natural gas or a central heating or cooling system only under a written rental agreement and with authority from the North Carolina Utilities Commission, following the Commission's rules on how charges are calculated and billed (for water, generally metered use at no more than the supplier's rate, plus a Commission-capped administrative fee).

The landlord may not disconnect these services for nonpayment, may not charge a statutory late fee for unpaid water or sewer, may not end the lease because of unpaid water, sewer, electric or natural gas charges, and must apply payments to rent first unless the tenant says otherwise; the security deposit may be used for unpaid water, sewer and electric charges. A landlord that bills for water and learns the water exceeds a contaminant limit must tell tenants.

Multi-unit buildings permitted since September 1, 1977 must have individual electric and gas meters in tenants' names unless the Commission approves otherwise or the lease includes the utility in the rent with the account in the landlord's name.

title: What a Landlord Need Not Disclose
bodyText: When offering property for rent, it is not a material fact that a previous occupant died or had a serious illness in the property, or that a registered sex offender lives or lived there or nearby. A landlord need not volunteer these facts, but may not knowingly make a false statement about them if asked.

title: Removing Squatters
bodyText: Since December 1, 2025, a North Carolina property owner (or a broker or other person with written authority) can use an expedited court procedure to remove an 'unauthorized person' from residential property: someone with no legal claim, no valid rental agreement or contract for deed, who has never paid rent or any other payment to the owner, and who is not otherwise authorized. It does not apply to a tenant, to a tenant holding over after the lease ends, or to anyone who ever paid rent; those cases go through summary ejectment. The owner files a complaint (with a magistrate if the clerk's office is closed) alleging the statutory facts; the sheriff serves it within 24 hours, a magistrate hears it within 48 hours of service, and if the owner wins the order requires the occupant to leave within four hours of service. The occupant must post at least a $10,000 bond to appeal. Staying after the order is second-degree trespass, and the owner may move belongings left behind to the property line. The owner is liable only for actual damages if the removal was wrongful.

title: Lead Poisoning Hazards: North Carolina Duties
bodyText: Besides the federal lead disclosure, North Carolina's health law gives the state duties that reach rental owners. When a child under six or a pregnant woman has confirmed lead poisoning, the Department of Health and Human Services investigates the home and notifies the owner or managing agent of any lead poisoning hazards; the owner must submit a written remediation plan within 14 days, give occupants three days' notice before work starts, finish within 60 days of approval, and may not use prohibited methods such as dry scraping, torch burning or uncontrolled sanding. Owners and tenants must give the Department information about children in the unit within 10 days of a request. An owner of pre-1978 housing who follows the state lead maintenance standard (and, where young children live, repeats it yearly and obtains a $10 annual certificate of compliance) is shielded from liability to occupants for lead injuries. Tenants of leased units are advised to report deteriorated paint to the owner within 72 hours of discovery.

title: Former Meth Labs: Cleanup, Not Disclosure
bodyText: An owner or lessee of a residence who knows it was used to manufacture methamphetamine must comply with the state's decontamination rules before it is lived in. North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose a former drug lab to a tenant.

title: Towing Vehicles from Rental Property
bodyText: North Carolina's statewide private-lot towing statute applies only in listed counties and cities (Craven, Cumberland, Dare, Forsyth, Gaston, Guilford, Mecklenburg, New Hanover, Orange, Richmond, Robeson, Wake and Wilson counties and the municipalities in them, and Durham, Jacksonville, Charlotte and Fayetteville). There, an owner or lessee may have an unauthorized vehicle towed on written request only if signs at least 24 by 24 inches at every entrance name the towing company and its phone number (and individually assigned spaces are marked), and only 72 hours after the signs go up; the vehicle may not be taken more than 15 miles (25 if no storage within 15) and the owner may contest the towing lien. Elsewhere, and in addition, city and county towing ordinances apply.

title: When the Landlord's Property Is Foreclosed
bodyText: If a residential property with fewer than 15 rental units is being sold in a North Carolina power-of-sale foreclosure, the notice of sale must also be mailed to the tenants (by name or to 'occupant'), and must tell them that a tenant whose lease was made or renewed on or after October 1, 2007 may end the lease by written notice effective 10 to 90 days after the sale date, owing only prorated rent, unless the owner cures the default first. The termination right itself has no date limit, and a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy renews every period, so treat every tenant of a covered property as having it. After the sale, the buyer can get an order for possession only after giving occupants 10 days' notice (30 days in buildings with 15 or more rental units), and the order is carried out like an eviction writ. Federal law (the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act) can give bona fide tenants more time.

title: Electronic Notices: Not for Default or Eviction
bodyText: North Carolina's electronic transactions law, which lets parties sign and send records electronically, expressly does not apply to any notice of default or eviction, or of the right to cure, under a rental agreement for an individual's primary residence. A lease can be signed electronically, but default, cure and eviction notices to a residential tenant should be delivered on paper by hand or mail as the lease and law provide, even if the lease or the parties otherwise use e-mail or text.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: A developer converting a building to condominiums must give each residential tenant and subtenant notice of the conversion and an offering statement at least 90 days before they must leave, by hand delivery or first-class mail. No tenant may be required to vacate on less than 90 days' notice (except for nonpayment, waste, disturbing other tenants or another breach giving a right of repossession), and the tenancy terms cannot change during that period. For 30 days after the notice the tenant has the first right to buy the unit. Failure to give the notice is a defense to an eviction.

title: Vacation Rentals and Hotel-Type Stays Are Different
bodyText: Rentals of a residence for vacation, leisure or recreation for fewer than 90 days, to someone with a permanent home elsewhere, are 'vacation rentals' governed by North Carolina's Vacation Rental Act (Chapter 42A), with its own rules on written agreements, advance payments, deposits, habitability and expedited eviction; the Residential Rental Agreements Act does not apply to them. Rentals by hotels, motels, campgrounds and similar lodging to the same guest for fewer than 90 consecutive days are 'transient occupancies' outside Chapter 42 entirely and create no tenancy unless the agreement says so. Since July 1, 2026, the innkeeper statute also covers an 'emergency or disaster declared occupancy', which can include an apartment's rental to a disaster-recovery grant recipient while the occupant's own home is repaired; the Chapter 42 exclusion still names only transient occupancies, so whether such an apartment stay is a tenancy is unsettled, and the cautious course is to treat it as one. Steinoak's lease library is for longer-term residential tenancies and does not cover either.

title: Expedited Eviction for Drug and Other Criminal Activity
bodyText:
Article 7 of North Carolina's landlord-tenant chapter applies to every residential rental agreement and gives landlords a faster court action against criminal activity: any violation of the controlled substances law other than simple possession, or other criminal activity that threatens the health, safety or peaceful enjoyment of other residents or the landlord's employees.

The court must order complete eviction of the tenant and household if the activity occurred in the unit, the unit was used to further it, or the tenant, a household member or a guest engaged in it on or near the premises, unless the tenant proves they were not involved and did not know or could not reasonably prevent it; the court can instead order partial eviction of the person involved and bar them from the property, with a conditional order against the tenant.

A criminal conviction is not required, an isolated incident is no defense, cases are heard on an expedited basis, witnesses can be protected, and police may share reports with the landlord. Collecting rent with knowledge of the activity is not a waiver, and a person who in good faith brings or helps with such a case is immune from civil liability.

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a landlord to pay interest on a security deposit or to hold it in an interest-bearing account.

title: No Statutory Entry-Notice Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute setting when or with how much notice a landlord may enter a rented home. The lease controls (this library's Access & Entry terms give 24 hours' notice except in emergencies); a court may still treat unreasonable entry as a breach of the tenant's right to possession.

title: No Statutory Rent-Increase Notice
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring advance notice of a rent increase or limiting how much rent may rise. During a fixed term rent can change only as the lease allows; a month-to-month tenancy can be ended on seven days' notice and re-let at a new rent. Local governments cannot regulate rent amounts.

title: No Application-Fee Cap
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute capping or regulating rental application or screening fees charged by landlords. (Late fees and eviction fees are strictly capped; see the late-fee and eviction-fee rules.) A separate statute regulates rental referral agencies that charge prospective tenants a fee to find housing.

title: No Immigration-Status Rule for Landlords
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute that requires, or forbids, a landlord asking about a tenant's immigration or citizenship status. Fair housing law's national-origin protection still applies.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to test for or disclose radon.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose bed bugs or setting a treatment timeline. The general repair duty still applies.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose mold or setting a treatment timeline. The general repair duty still applies, and plumbing leaks or drainage problems that cause standing water contributing to mold are an 'imminently dangerous condition' the landlord must fix within a reasonable time.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule for Leases
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose past flooding or flood-zone status to a tenant. (The residential property disclosure form for sales does not apply to leases.)

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: North Carolina gives tenants no statutory right to install an electric vehicle charger.

title: No Receipt Duty for Rent
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to give a receipt for rent, including cash rent, or regulating how rent may be paid. A licensed real estate broker who manages rentals must keep copies of receipts for cash payments in leasing transactions among its trust-account records, so a broker-managed property should give a receipt for every cash payment.

title: No Statutory Holdover Damages
bodyText: North Carolina sets no double-rent or other multiplier for a tenant who stays after the lease ends. The landlord may bring summary ejectment and claim rent and damages for the tenant's occupation since the lease ended.

title: No Statutory Right-to-Call-Police Protection
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute protecting a tenant's right to call police or emergency services or barring lease penalties for such calls. (State law does limit local crime-and-disorder rental programs and requires local governments to help landlords evict tenants charged with crimes if a property is targeted.)

title: No Owner or Manager Disclosure Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose the owner's or manager's name and address to the tenant. A licensed broker managing a property is not personally liable in a landlord-tenant suit merely because the lease does not identify the landlord.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute or court rule allowing summary ejectment records to be sealed or expunged. Court records are open to public inspection unless a law closes them, and the court system licenses remote and bulk access to civil case data, which includes eviction cases. A party may ask the court to seal a particular document under the general court rules, but nothing provides for sealing an eviction case as a whole.

title: No Statutory Move-In Inspection
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a move-in or move-out inspection, checklist or condition report. A written, signed condition report is still the best evidence for deposit deductions.

title: Selling a Rented Property
bodyText: When a North Carolina landlord sells or otherwise transfers a rented property, the lease goes with it: the transfer is complete without the tenant's consent or 'attornment', the new owner has the same rights and remedies against the tenant (for rent and for breach of other lease terms) that the old landlord had, and the tenant has the same rights and remedies against the new owner. A tenant who, without notice of the transfer, keeps paying the old landlord is protected. Within 30 days after the landlord's interest ends, the old landlord must either transfer the remaining security deposit to the new owner and notify the tenant by mail of the transfer and the new owner's name and address, or return the deposit to the tenant. Rent that is growing due when ownership changes because of a death or other uncertain event is apportioned between the successive owners. Converting a rental building to condominiums has its own 90-day notice and purchase-option rules.

title: Tenant Crimes Against the Landlord's Property
bodyText: Two North Carolina statutes make tenant misconduct a crime. A tenant who, during or after the term, willfully and unlawfully demolishes, destroys, defaces, burns or otherwise damages the landlord's house, outbuildings, fences or trees commits a Class 1 misdemeanor. A tenant who, willfully and with intent to defraud the landlord, gives up possession of the rented premises to someone other than the landlord also commits a Class 1 misdemeanor. These are in addition to the tenant's civil liability for damage beyond wear and tear. A tenant is not liable for damage that happens accidentally despite reasonable diligence, unless the tenant agreed otherwise.

title: No Statewide Source-of-Income Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring landlords to accept Housing Choice Vouchers or other rent assistance, or barring refusal based on source of income. Since September 9, 2024, counties and cities may not adopt or enforce such a rule where the income includes a federal housing assistance program, except for property they own, properties they subsidize, and owners that take local funding or incentives.

title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Assault or Stalking: Termination and Lock Changes
bodyText: A protected tenant (a tenant or household member who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking) may end the lease by written notice effective at least 30 days after you receive it, with a copy of a non-ex-parte Chapter 50B or 50C protective order, a criminal no-contact order, or an Address Confidentiality Program card; a domestic violence or sexual assault victim must also include a safety plan from a qualifying program, dated during the tenancy, recommending relocation (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-45.1). The tenant owes rent prorated to the termination date and nothing else for the early termination (nothing at all if they end it 14 or more days before occupancy), and you may not apply the deposit to early-termination damages. Remaining tenants stay bound, and a perpetrator excluded by court order stays liable. Any tenant may ask, orally or in writing, for the locks to be changed: within 48 hours with no documentation if the perpetrator isn't a tenant, or within 72 hours of the request if they are, and only after the tenant gives you a copy of a court order telling the perpetrator to stay away from the unit (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-42.3); the protected tenant pays, and if you don't act in time may change them and must give you a key within 48 hours. You may not terminate, refuse to renew, refuse to rent or otherwise retaliate based substantially on victim status or on a tenant's having ended a lease under this termination right (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-42.2). The termination right can't be waived or modified by agreement (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-45.1(d)); the lock-change and nondiscrimination sections have no anti-waiver sentence of their own, and whether a lease waiver of them is enforceable is case law.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule for private houses and apartments. A fixed-term lease ends on its last day, and a periodic tenancy ends on the notice North Carolina law sets (seven days for month-to-month, two days for week-to-week, one month before the end of the year for year-to-year), with no reason required. The limits are situational. A tenant may defend an eviction as retaliatory if it is substantially in response to protected activity in the 12 months before filing, such as a good-faith repair request or code complaint, an attempt to enforce lease or legal rights, or involvement with a tenants' rights organization; the landlord still wins in listed cases, including a breach of the rent covenant or another substantial covenant, a holdover after a fixed term with no option to renew, a good-faith notice to quit given before the protected activity, and a good-faith recovery at the end of the term to live in the unit, to demolish it or make major alterations that require the household to move out completely, or to stop renting it for at least six months. A landlord may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy based substantially on a tenant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. When a building is converted to condominiums, tenants cannot be required to leave on less than 90 days' notice except for nonpayment, waste, disturbing other tenants or another breach giving a right to repossess, and the tenancy terms cannot change during that period. Public housing authorities and manufactured home communities have their own rules, which this library does not cover. North Carolina has no rent-escrow procedure that bars eviction: rent paid to the clerk during an appeal only stays the eviction while the appeal is pending. Fair housing law applies.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or on landlords sharing rent data. North Carolina also bars counties and cities from regulating the amount of rent on private rental property. Federal and state antitrust and unfair-trade-practice law may still apply.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: No North Carolina statute says whether late fees, utility charges or other fees count as rent; that depends on the lease. Several statutes keep fees apart from rent. Unpaid landlord-billed water, sewer or electric charges can never be a ground to end the lease, and payments go to rent first unless the tenant directs otherwise. An eviction administrative fee cannot be deducted from a later rent payment or made a ground for a later eviction, and a late fee for one payment cannot be deducted from a later payment to put it in default. The eviction filing costs and fees the law allows may be included in the amount needed to cure a default. This library's clauses do not label fees as rent, and its default clause does not let an unpaid late fee alone end the lease.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Some states let a landlord give notice, do work the tenant failed to do, and add the cost to the rent. North Carolina has no such statute. Two narrower rules exist: after repairing an imminently dangerous condition that is the tenant's fault, the landlord may recover the actual and reasonable cost of the repair from the tenant; and a tenant who disables or damages a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm must reimburse the reasonable and actual cost of repairing or replacing it within 30 days of the landlord's written notice. Otherwise the landlord recovers the cost of tenant-caused damage as damages or from the security deposit. The landlord must give the tenant written notice of breaches of the tenant's maintenance duties, except in emergencies.

title: No Blank-Space or Lease-Copy Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be completed, treating a blank as a breach, or requiring the landlord to give the tenant a signed copy. Several North Carolina rules still turn on what the lease says: where the security deposit is held (the landlord must tell the tenant within 30 days after the term begins, and naming the bank or bond company in the lease is the simplest way), the late fee and the eviction fees and attorneys' fees (allowed only if the lease provides for them), and the emergency contact a landlord names in a tenant-death affidavit. A blank in one of those leaves a right lost or a duty unclear. Fill in every blank before signing and give the tenant a copy, as good practice rather than a statutory duty.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: No North Carolina statute states a landlord's covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession for residential leases. The closest statute is the policy statement behind the expedited criminal-activity eviction procedure, which recognizes residents' right to the peaceful, safe and quiet enjoyment of their homes and applies that procedure to every residential rental agreement. Possession is otherwise protected by the ban on self-help eviction: a residential tenant can be removed only through a court eviction. Whether a lease carries an implied covenant of quiet enjoyment is a question of case law.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: North Carolina prescribes no form for a residential lease or for a landlord's demand for rent or notice to quit. The statutes do supply a few forms a landlord may meet. The small claims statute sets out a sufficient form of complaint in summary ejectment. A court form published by the Administrative Office of the Courts may not be modified in a way that keeps its official appearance, and anyone who modifies one must clearly note that it was modified and say what changed. A tenant who appeals an eviction may stay it with a bond and undertaking substantially in a statutory form. A landlord who sues on a knowingly bad check must first send demand letters substantially in the statutory forms. The notice to the State Bar about an attorney tenant's files has statutory contents but no set form.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: North Carolina statutes do not address whether a tenant may install security cameras, video doorbells or similar devices. The lease's alteration terms govern; in this library that is the Alterations section, which requires the landlord's written consent before a tenant adds or changes a fixture. North Carolina's eavesdropping, electronic surveillance and privacy laws may limit what a camera records rather than its installation.

title: Unfair Trade Practices Act and Rentals
bodyText: North Carolina's Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act declares unlawful unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce, and defines commerce to include all business activities. How far it reaches residential leasing is settled by court decisions this library has not reviewed, but several landlord-tenant statutes assume it can apply (for example, the statute allowing a partial-payment non-waiver clause says using one is not a violation of the Act). The Act has no list of unfair practices for leases, and nothing on blank spaces filled in after signing or on giving the tenant a copy. A person injured by a violation may recover three times their damages, and a court may award attorney's fees where the violation was willful and there was an unwarranted refusal to resolve the matter. Separately, the Act's debt-collection article bars anyone collecting a consumer debt from collecting any fee, charge or expense incidental to the debt unless legally entitled to it, or from falsely representing that the debt may be increased by attorney's fees or other fees; a violation carries actual damages plus a civil penalty of $500 to $4,000 for each violation. So collecting a fee that a void lease term provides for, such as a late fee above North Carolina's cap or an eviction cost the law does not allow, can create liability, not just an unenforceable term. A knowing violation of the North Carolina Servicemembers Civil Relief Act is also an unfair trade practice.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no plain-language or readability statute for residential leases, no type-size or bold-print rule for the lease as a whole, and no statute requiring a lease to list the rights a tenant gives up. (An option to purchase combined with or signed with the lease has its own 14-point boldface cancellation statement, and an automatic-renewal notice, if that statute reaches a lease, has a 12-point bold rule; see edu-lease-type-size-nc.) Its unconscionability statutes cover leases of goods and other transactions, not leases of homes; a court may still refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term under case law.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText:
North Carolina law leaves much of the cost of tenant-caused damage with the tenant. A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly let anyone else do so, and is responsible for damage inside the unit under the tenant's exclusive control except ordinary wear and tear, acts of the landlord, defective products or repairs the landlord authorized, acts of third parties who are not the tenant's invitees, and natural forces.

The landlord must still make the repairs needed to keep the home fit and habitable, and must fix an imminently dangerous condition within a reasonable time even when the tenant caused it, but may then recover the actual and reasonable repair cost from the tenant; the security deposit may also be applied to damage.

The statutory right to surrender the lease after a fire or other casualty does not apply if the tenant's (or the tenant's agents' or servants') negligence caused the damage, or if the lease provides for repairs or casualty; the library's optional casualty clause excludes damage caused by the tenant, household members, guests or invitees.

No North Carolina statute addresses rent during repairs or the landlord's lost rent if the lease ends because of tenant-caused damage; the library offers an optional clause for that.

A tenant is not liable for damage that happens accidentally despite reasonable diligence unless the tenant agreed to be. That agreement is lawful, but the library does not offer it, because it would sit uneasily with the landlord's repair duty, which cannot be waived, and with the statute's list of damage the tenant is not responsible for; a landlord who wants one can add their own clause after taking legal advice. Willfully damaging the rented house is also a misdemeanor.

title: Arbitration Clauses in North Carolina Leases
bodyText:
North Carolina's Revised Uniform Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, except on a ground that would allow any contract to be revoked, and it has no exception for consumer or residential leases. A party to an arbitration may always be represented by a lawyer, and that right cannot be given up in advance. A lease term that waives a jury trial is unenforceable, but the same statute says it does not stop the parties from agreeing to arbitrate. An arbitration clause that requires the dispute to be heard in another state is void, so the library's clause holds any arbitration in the county where the property is.

The library offers its optional arbitration clause in North Carolina: it covers money claims only, leaves possession cases, small claims and deposit claims in court, and lets the tenant opt out within 30 days. Whether a court would find a particular lease term unfair or deceptive under the state's unfair trade practices law is case law.

title: Fitness Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: North Carolina does not let a lease, or any agreement, take away the landlord's fitness duties: meeting building and housing codes, keeping the home fit and habitable, keeping common areas safe, keeping supplied facilities and appliances in repair, providing smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and fixing imminently dangerous conditions. A tenant who accepts a defective unit, whether before the lease, at signing or later, does not release the landlord; the only release is while a government body blocks the repair, for no more than six months. After the lease is made, landlord and tenant may sign a later written contract in which the tenant agrees to do specified work on the property, but only if the tenant receives adequate consideration other than the right to rent the home, and only if the contract is not made with the purpose or effect of getting around the landlord's duties. North Carolina has no procedure for a tenant to accept listed defects in return for a lower rent and no separate-document rule for heat; whether a rent reduction could count as that other consideration is for the courts, so this library offers no accepted-conditions clause. The only fitness terms the statute lets a written agreement change are who puts new batteries in battery-operated smoke and carbon monoxide alarms at move-in and during the tenancy. Vacation rentals fall under the separate Vacation Rental Act, which also says its fitness duties may not be waived.

title: What a Lease May Change in the Fitness Duties
bodyText:
A North Carolina lease cannot shift or excuse the landlord's fitness duties, and a tenant's acceptance of a defect does not release the landlord from any of them. The statute lets a written agreement change one thing only: who puts new batteries in battery-operated smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Without such an agreement the landlord installs new batteries at the start of the tenancy and the tenant replaces them during it (a tamper-resistant 10-year lithium smoke alarm needs none), and whatever is agreed, the landlord must make sure every alarm works at the start of each tenancy and repair or replace one within 15 days of the tenant's written notice.

There is no water exception: the lease cannot excuse the landlord from providing water where the home has no well or utility water, and a lack of potable water is an imminently dangerous condition the landlord must fix within a reasonable time, based on its severity, after learning of it or being notified.

The repair duty for facilities and appliances covers those the landlord supplies or is required to supply, so the lease may list which appliances come with the home, but it cannot leave out anything the building and housing codes require. After the lease is made, the tenant may also agree in a later written contract to do specified work, for adequate consideration other than the tenancy itself.

title: No Material-Defect Threshold; Urgent Conditions Listed
bodyText: North Carolina's statute does not divide fitness defects into material and minor ones: every fitness duty applies in full, and the tenant's duty to pay rent and the landlord's fitness duty depend on each other. It leaves to a court what a particular failure is worth, and the tenant may not withhold rent on their own before a court has ruled. The statute ranks urgency in one way: it lists imminently dangerous conditions (unsafe wiring, floors, steps, ceilings, roofs, chimneys or flues; no potable water; no working locks on outside doors or ground-floor windows, or broken windows; no heat able to keep living areas at 65 degrees when it is 20 degrees outside from November 1 to March 31; no working toilet, tub or shower; rat infestation from structural defects; and standing water, sewage or flooding from leaks or poor drainage that contributes to mosquitoes or mold), which the landlord must fix within a reasonable time based on the severity once the landlord knows of them or is told. Repairs to other supplied facilities and appliances follow the tenant's written notice, except in an emergency. Whether a small defect reduces the rent owed is case law; cautious course: treat every listed condition and every code violation as urgent, and repair other defects promptly after notice.

title: Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: North Carolina's Residential Rental Agreements Act has no general rule making every tenant right non-waivable; instead, particular statutes say what a lease cannot change. (1) The landlord's fitness and repair duties: a tenant's acceptance of defects does not release the landlord, except while a government body blocks the repair for a set period of no more than six months; separately, the parties may make a later written contract for the tenant to do specified work, supported by adequate consideration other than the tenancy itself and not made with the purpose or effect of evading the landlord's duties. (2) The early-termination right North Carolina's own statute gives a federal military technician (and, after the technician's death on active duty, an immediate family member or the estate) may not be waived or modified under any circumstances (other servicemembers' lease-termination rights come from the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act as applied by state law; see the servicemember row), and (3) a domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking victim's right to end the lease early may not be waived or modified. (4) The limits on late fees, eviction fees and litigation costs: a lease term contrary to them is void. (5) A residential tenant may be removed only through the court eviction process, and the landlord may not seize the tenant's belongings except as the statutes allow; a contrary lease term is void. (6) Any waiver by the tenant or a household member of the protection against retaliatory eviction is void. Two general contract statutes add that a term requiring a party to waive a jury trial is unenforceable and that a term requiring a lawsuit or arbitration to be brought in another state is void. For the Act's other rules that carry no non-waiver sentence of their own (such as the bans on discriminating against or retaliating against victims and the lock-change rules), the statute neither allows nor forbids a waiver; whether a lease waiving one is enforceable is case law, so the library offers no waiver clause. Deposit rules are covered separately.

title: Eviction Notices Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: No North Carolina statute lets a lease waive or shorten the notices that come before an eviction, and none of them says the parties may agree otherwise. (1) Ending a periodic tenancy takes notice at least seven days before the end of a month-to-month period, two days for week to week and one month before the end of the year for year to year, and at least 60 days before the end of the rental period for a space rented for a manufactured home; this library's month-to-month clause lets the landlord set a longer period but never a shorter one, because whether a shorter or waived notice is enforceable is case law. (2) For unpaid rent where the lease fixes a definite time for paying rent and has no forfeiture term, the law implies a forfeiture if the rent stays unpaid 10 days after the landlord demands all past-due rent; a lease may instead say that a breach ends the tenancy, and this library's default clause still gives the tenant 10 days after a written demand. (3) Every summary ejectment needs a demand that the tenant give up possession before the case is brought, and because a residential tenant may be removed only through the court process, with any contrary lease term void, the library treats that demand as one the lease cannot waive. Federal rules can add a longer notice for some properties.

title: Deposit Rules a Lease Cannot Loosen
bodyText: North Carolina's Tenant Security Deposit Act has no sentence saying its protections cannot be waived, but every rule in it is written as a command, not as a default the parties may change. A deposit may be used only for the purposes the Act lists; it may not exceed two weeks' rent for a week-to-week tenancy, one and one-half months' rent for month to month, or two months' rent for longer terms; it must be held in a trust account at a licensed, federally insured institution or covered by a bond, and the tenant must be told within 30 days where it is; and within 30 days after the tenancy ends and possession is returned, the landlord must mail or deliver a written itemization with the balance (or an interim accounting then and a final one within 60 days). The landlord may not keep any part of it for normal wear and tear or keep more than actual damages. A landlord who willfully fails to meet the deposit, bond or notice requirements loses the right to keep any of the deposit, and a court may award attorney's fees for willful noncompliance. Whether a lease term waiving any of these rights is enforceable is case law; the library offers no waiver clause. The Act covers anyone in the business of renting or managing residential units weekly, monthly or yearly, except single rooms; vacation rentals have their own rules.

title: Smoke Drift and Smoking Bans
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute on tobacco smoke drifting between rental units, and none on a tenant giving up claims about it. State law bans smoking in the enclosed areas of restaurants and bars and inside State government buildings and vehicles, but it has no general workplace ban, so it does not reach the enclosed common hallways of a private apartment building just because building staff work there.

A city or county may adopt stricter rules for its own buildings, grounds and vehicles and for public places (enclosed areas the public is invited into or permitted in), but it may not restrict smoking in a private residence; whether a local rule reaches an apartment building's common areas depends on the local ordinance.

A landlord may set its own smoking policy in the lease (this library's smoking-policy clause). Whether a lease term in which the tenant gives up claims about drifting smoke is enforceable is case law; the library offers no waiver clause.

title: Jury Waivers Are Unenforceable
bodyText: In North Carolina a contract term requiring a party to waive a jury trial is unconscionable as a matter of law and unenforceable, so a lease jury waiver cannot be enforced; the same statute still allows agreements to arbitrate or use other forms of alternative dispute resolution. A jury is not the default in an eviction anyway: a summary ejectment case assigned to a magistrate in small claims court is tried without a jury. After the magistrate rules, a party may appeal for a new trial in district court before a judge or a jury, but an appealing party who does not demand a jury before the time to perfect the appeal runs out has waived it, and in district court a party must otherwise demand a jury in writing within 10 days after the last pleading on the issue. If the tenant's written answer denies the landlord's title, the case moves to district court, where the landlord may request a jury within five days after notice and the tenant in the answer. No North Carolina statute addresses class-action waivers in consumer contracts or makes form-contract jury or class waivers presumptively unconscionable beyond this rule, and none requires a signed writing for a waiver of a constitutional right in a lease; whether a lease class-action waiver is enforceable is case law, which this library has not reviewed, and the library offers no jury or class-action waiver clause.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: North Carolina allows a judgment by confession without a lawsuit, but only on a written statement signed and verified or sworn to by the person confessing and filed with the clerk of superior court, stating the amount, both parties and their counties of residence, and concisely why that person is or may become liable; it may be for money due or money that may become due, and may be entered only in the county where the debtor lives or owns real property or where the creditor lives. A lease clause is not that statement, and the rule makes no provision for confessing to possession: a residential tenant may be removed only through the court eviction process. No North Carolina statute bars a confession-of-judgment clause in a residential lease (the express bans cover consumer credit sales, consumer finance loans and insurance premium finance agreements), and none authorizes one; whether a lease clause letting the landlord or an attorney confess judgment for the tenant is enforceable is case law, which this library has not reviewed, so the library offers no such clause. The eviction statute headed judgment by confession covers a tenant who admits the complaint's allegations in court; it is a judgment in the eviction case, not a confession clause. What a tenant must pay into court to stay an eviction during an appeal is set by statute, not by court rule (see the rent-into-court row).

title: Liability Waivers and Indemnity Clauses
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute that voids, or expressly allows, a lease clause releasing the landlord from liability for its own negligence or making the tenant indemnify the landlord for it; the state's anti-indemnity statute is written for construction and design-professional agreements. A lease still cannot remove the landlord's fitness and repair duties, since a tenant's acceptance of defects does not release the landlord, although a violation of those duties is not by itself negligence.

Some limits on landlord liability come from statute without any clause: a tenant's, occupant's or guest's criminal record does not make a later injury foreseeable and the landlord has no duty to screen for criminal records; a landlord who follows the victim lock-change rules is not liable to the excluded perpetrator for loss of use of the home or of belongings; and a landlord who follows the State Bar notice rule in good faith is not liable for disposing of an attorney-tenant's client files.

In the other direction, a tenant is not liable for damage that happens accidentally despite reasonable diligence unless the lease says so. Whether a clause excusing the landlord's own negligence, or making the tenant indemnify the landlord for it, is enforceable is case law; the library offers no such clause.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: North Carolina has no unconscionability statute for residential leases. Its statutory unconscionability rules cover sales of goods, leases of goods (not of homes or other real property), consumer credit sales of goods or services, and a developer's contracts and leases in condominiums and planned communities; the one rule that reaches every contract is the jury-waiver statute, which declares a term requiring a party to waive a jury trial unconscionable as a matter of law. Whether a court will refuse to enforce an unfair residential lease term under general contract law is case law. Separately, a debt collector may not use unconscionable means to collect a consumer debt, including collecting a fee or charge it is not legally entitled to, which matters when a landlord tries to collect under a void lease term. No statute lets a court revise or end a running lease because it has become excessively burdensome. Cautious course: keep every fee, waiver and remedy term within what North Carolina statutes allow; this library offers no term that depends on a court accepting an unusually one-sided bargain.

title: Lease Terms North Carolina Voids
bodyText: North Carolina has no single list of prohibited lease terms; each rule sits in its own statute, and together they are the full set this library applies. Void or unenforceable are: (1) a term letting the landlord remove a residential tenant other than through the court eviction process, or seize the tenant's belongings; (2) any waiver of the protection against retaliatory eviction; (3) any release of the landlord's fitness and repair duties; and (4) any waiver or change of the state early-termination rights of federal military technicians (and their surviving family members) and of victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. (5) Under the fee statute, whose contrary terms are void, a late fee may be charged only when rent is five or more calendar days late, only once per late payment, only up to the cap, never by deducting it from a later rent payment so as to put that payment in default, and never for unpaid landlord-billed water or sewer; the only eviction administrative fees are the complaint-filing, court-appearance and second-trial fees, and only one of them may be charged and kept for a complaint; the only out-of-pocket expenses and litigation costs are court filing fees, service costs and capped attorneys' fees, plus all actual reasonable attorneys' fees where the landlord prevails on a tenant's appeal to district court and a court determines that the tenant knew, or should have known, the appeal was frivolous, unreasonable, without foundation, in bad faith or solely for delay; and a lease requiring renter's insurance cannot require a designated insurer or agent, and you may charge for coverage you obtain (actual cost plus an administrative fee of no more than $50 a year) only if the tenant fails to show proof within three business days of your request. (6) Unpaid landlord-billed water, sewer or electric charges cannot be the ground for ending the lease, and a payment goes first to rent unless the tenant designates otherwise; (7) the security deposit limits are mandatory; (8) a term requiring a party to waive a jury trial is unenforceable, and a term requiring a lawsuit or arbitration to be brought in another state is void; and (9) a restriction that allows residential use but bars use as a family care home is void. North Carolina has no statute banning confession-of-judgment, liability-waiver, home-warranty-deductible or repair-fee terms in leases, no general code rule voiding a term contrary to the policy of express law, and no money penalty for using a prohibited term, although collecting under a void term can create liability under the consumer-protection laws. Whether those unaddressed terms are enforceable is case law, which this library has not reviewed, and the library offers none of them.

title: No Collection Fee on Past-Due Rent
bodyText: No North Carolina statute authorizes a landlord to charge a tenant a collection fee or a collection agency's charges on past-due rent, and the fee statute's list of allowed charges covers only filing an eviction or money-owed case (court filing fees, service costs and, under a written lease, attorneys' fees capped at 15 percent, plus all actual reasonable attorneys' fees where the landlord prevails on a tenant's appeal to district court that a court finds frivolous, unreasonable, without foundation, in bad faith or solely for delay). North Carolina's collection laws point the other way: a collection agency may not collect from a consumer its own fee or any charge, fee or expense incidental to the debt unless legally entitled to it, and the consumer debt-collection law puts the same limit on other debt collectors. Whether a lease term by itself makes the landlord or an agency legally entitled to a collection fee, and whether the general statute on attorneys' fees in notes and other evidence of indebtedness reaches a lease, are case-law questions this library has not reviewed. Cautious course: the library offers no collection-fee clause; a landlord who refers a debt to an agency should expect to pay the agency's charges itself and collect from the tenant only rent, lawful late fees, actual damages and the case costs the statute allows.

title: No Fee for Serving Eviction Notices
bodyText: No North Carolina statute authorizes or expressly bars a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice or demand before an eviction, such as the 10-day demand for past-due rent or the demand for possession. The fee statute strictly limits what a landlord may charge once a case is filed: one administrative fee of the three kinds it names, plus court filing fees, the cost of serving the court papers and capped attorneys' fees under a written lease (and all actual reasonable attorneys' fees where the landlord prevails on a tenant's appeal to district court and a court determines that the tenant knew, or should have known, the appeal was frivolous, unreasonable, without foundation, in bad faith or solely for delay), with any other administrative fee or litigation cost for the complaint against public policy and any contrary lease term void; and it allows only one late fee for each late payment. Whether a separate notice fee is valid, or would be treated as a second late fee or a disguised eviction fee, is case law, and North Carolina has no codified penalty rule to settle it. Cautious course: the library offers no notice-service fee clause; serve required notices at the landlord's own cost and recover only the charges the fee statute allows.

title: Eviction Fees Beyond the Statute Are Void
bodyText:
North Carolina bans eviction penalty clauses by statute. For a complaint for summary ejectment or money owed, a lease may provide only one administrative fee of the three kinds the statute names (complaint-filing, court-appearance or second-trial), and only the out-of-pocket expenses and litigation costs the statute lists (court filing fees, the cost of serving the court papers and, under a written lease, reasonable attorneys' fees actually paid or owed up to 15 percent, plus all actual reasonable attorneys' fees on a frivolous tenant appeal the landlord wins).

It is against public policy for a landlord to put any other administrative fee, expense or litigation cost for filing such a complaint in a lease or to claim one, and any lease term contrary to the statute is void and unenforceable. An administrative fee the landlord earns may not be deducted from a later rent payment or treated as a default supporting a later eviction. The amounts and conditions are in the library's eviction-fee rows; a fixed eviction charge outside them should not appear in a North Carolina lease.

title: Liquidated Damages and Early-Termination Charges
bodyText:
North Carolina has no general statute on liquidated damages or contract penalties; the codified test (an agreed amount must be reasonable in light of the anticipated or actual harm, and an unreasonably large one is void as a penalty) applies to sales and leases of goods, not to leases of homes.

For residential leases the statutes fix the amount in two cases. A military technician who ends the lease under the military early-termination statute owes, besides prorated rent, liquidated damages only if fewer than nine months of the tenancy were completed and the landlord suffered actual damages: no more than one month's rent if fewer than six months were completed, or half a month's rent for six to nine months. A tenant who ends the lease as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking owes prorated rent but no other rent or fees due only to the early termination, and under either statute no damages or penalties are due if the termination comes 14 or more days before occupancy.

The security deposit may cover damages from the tenant not finishing the rental period (except after those terminations or a landlord-caused move-out) and the cost of re-renting, including reasonable broker fees, but never more than the landlord's actual damages.

Whether any other agreed amount, such as an early-termination fee in a fixed-term lease, is enforceable is case law; the library's early-termination clause keeps those statutory rights intact.

title: Tenant Remedies When the Landlord Breaches
bodyText: When a North Carolina landlord breaches the lease or the landlord-tenant statutes, the tenant's remedies run through the courts: any right or obligation in the landlord-tenant chapter can be enforced by a civil action, on top of other legal and equitable remedies, and under the Residential Rental Agreements Act a tenant's action includes recoupment, counterclaim, defense and setoff, so the tenant can raise the landlord's breach in the landlord's eviction case. The tenant's duty to pay rent and the landlord's fitness duty depend on each other, but the tenant may not withhold rent on their own before a court rules, and a violation of the Act is not by itself negligence. Specific remedies: a tenant removed or locked out outside the court process may recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages (not punitive, treble or emotional-distress damages), and a tenant whose belongings are seized may recover them or their value plus actual damages; a court that finds an eviction retaliatory denies it, though the landlord may still receive rent due or any other appropriate judgment; a landlord who fails to account for and refund a deposit can be sued for it, and a willful failure on the deposit, bond or notice rules forfeits the right to keep any of it and can bring attorney's fees; and a landlord who has not fixed a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm 30 days after written notice commits an infraction with a fine of up to $250. A tenant who left because the landlord broke the lockout rules or was constructively evicted by a fitness violation cannot be charged deposit deductions for not finishing the rental period. Repair-specific remedies are in the tenant repair remedies row; unfair-practice claims are covered by the consumer-protection row.

title: Tenant Remedies for Unmade Repairs
bodyText: North Carolina gives a tenant no self-help remedy for a landlord's failure to repair: there is no repair-and-deduct right, no statutory rent abatement, no rent escrow for repairs, and the tenant may not withhold rent on their own before a court decides they may. The tenant's remedy is a court action to enforce the landlord's fitness duties, in which a court can award damages and decide whether rent was owed, and the tenant can raise the same claims as a counterclaim, defense, recoupment or setoff when the landlord sues for possession or rent. The landlord's duty to repair supplied facilities and appliances starts with the tenant's written notice (none is needed in an emergency), and imminently dangerous conditions must be fixed within a reasonable time once the landlord knows of them. A landlord who has not fixed a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm 30 days after written notice from the tenant or a government agent commits an infraction (fine up to $250), and a good-faith repair request or complaint to a housing inspector is protected against retaliatory eviction. A tenant's complaint about substandard conditions is also reasonable cause for a local housing inspection.

title: Rent Paid Into Court and Tenant Counterclaims
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a tenant to pay rent into court to defend an eviction or to file a counterclaim, and a magistrate may not continue a summary ejectment case beyond five days or the next small-claims session, whichever is longer, without both parties' consent; no rent deposit is tied to a continuance. In a nonpayment case, a tenant who pays or tenders the rent due and the court costs before judgment ends the case, and if the landlord presses on after the tenant pays into court what is found due plus costs, the case is stayed and the tenant recovers the later costs.
