In small claims court a tenant may file a counterclaim within the $10,000 limit but is not required to, and a claim not raised there can still be brought in a separate suit; on appeal the district court allows counterclaims under the civil rules, which require a pleading filed there to state any counterclaim arising from the same transaction. Rent into court matters on appeal: to stop the eviction while appealing, the tenant pays the clerk the undisputed back rent the magistrate found (an indigent tenant pays only future rent) and signs an undertaking to pay the rent into court as it comes due, plus, in a nonpayment case, prorated rent if the judgment came more than five business days before the next due date; if a payment is more than five business days late the clerk issues execution on the landlord's application, and the clerk pays the landlord rent the tenant has not claimed in a pleading within five business days of a written request. The same bond stays a district court judgment during a further appeal, and a landlord may move to dismiss a tenant's appeal where the tenant raised no defense in small claims and either filed no motion, answer or counterclaim in district court or did not keep to the bond.

title: No Penalty for Void Terms; Collecting on Them Is Risky
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute that charges a landlord a money penalty or damages simply for putting a prohibited term in a lease; its contrary-term statutes make the term void and unenforceable, nothing more. Liability comes from acting on such a term: a landlord who removes a tenant outside the court process owes actual damages, a willful failure on the deposit rules forfeits the right to keep any of the deposit and can bring attorney's fees, and a landlord who keeps more of a deposit than actual damages must refund it. Collecting a fee or charge the landlord is not legally entitled to, such as one a void lease term provides for, can also violate the state's debt-collection law, which allows actual damages plus a civil penalty of $500 to $4,000 for each violation, and the Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which trebles damages; how far those laws reach a landlord collecting its own rent is case law. So leave void terms out of the lease rather than relying on them being merely unenforceable.

title: Exemption Waivers Have No Effect in a Lease
bodyText: A North Carolina lease cannot waive the tenant's exemptions from collection. State law lets a resident debtor keep certain property free from creditors' claims, including up to $35,000 of interest in property the debtor uses as a residence, $5,000 of household goods plus $1,000 for each dependent (up to $4,000 more), a $3,500 interest in one vehicle, $2,000 of tools of the trade, health aids and retirement accounts, and those exemptions can be waived only by transferring the exempt property, by a written waiver made after judgment and approved by the clerk or a district court judge, or by failing to claim them within 20 days after the court's notice of exemption rights. A waiver signed in a lease before any judgment is none of these, so it has no effect; the library offers no exemption-waiver clause. The residence exemption protects the debtor's own interest in a home, so for most tenants it adds little, but the personal-property exemptions protect a tenant's belongings and car. The debtor may instead choose the smaller constitutional exemptions, which protect a homestead owned and occupied by the debtor and personal property; either way, before an execution can issue on a judgment for rent or damages, the court must send the tenant notice of these rights unless an exception applies.

title: Domestic Violence Lock Changes
bodyText: North Carolina gives a tenant a lock-change right when a tenant or household member is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. If the perpetrator is not a tenant of the same unit, a tenant may ask orally or in writing with no documentation, and you must change the locks or give permission to change them within 48 hours; if the perpetrator is a co-tenant, the tenant must give you a copy of a court order telling the perpetrator to stay away from the unit before the locks are changed, and you have 72 hours from the request (the statute does not say how that runs when the order arrives later, so the cautious course is to act as soon as you have it). The protected tenant pays for the change and, if you miss the deadline, may change the locks without your permission; whenever the protected tenant changes the locks, the tenant must give you a key to the new locks within 48 hours. Once you have the stay-away order you need not give the excluded perpetrator keys or access unless a court order allows a return for belongings, you are not liable to the perpetrator for loss of use or property if you comply, and the perpetrator stays liable for rent and damage with the other tenants. The statute sets no damages figure and, unlike the early-termination section, has no anti-waiver sentence of its own; it is enforceable by civil action, whether a lease term waiving it is enforceable is case law, and the library offers no waiver clause. Termination rights are in edu-dv-lease-termination-nc.

title: Domestic Violence Victims: No Eviction or Refusal Based on Status
bodyText: You may not terminate a tenancy, refuse to renew, refuse to rent or otherwise retaliate based substantially on a tenant's, applicant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or on a tenant's having ended a lease under the victim early-termination right. Evidence of the abuse may include police, court or federal agency records, documentation from a domestic violence or sexual assault program, or documentation from a religious, medical or other professional. The section names no special eviction defense or damages figure; it is enforceable by civil action, and a tenant evicted within 12 months after a good-faith attempt to use these state-law rights may also raise the general retaliatory-eviction defense, which can't be waived, though you can still prevail where nonpayment or another substantial lease breach is the real reason (see edu-retaliation-nc). A district court in a domestic violence case may give one party possession of the shared residence and order the other evicted; that order is directed at the parties to the case. North Carolina has no other domestic-violence eviction defense in its statutes, and whether victim status excuses a lease breach caused by the abuser is case law.

title: Domestic Violence: Documents a Tenant Must Give
bodyText: North Carolina's three victim provisions accept different proof. To end a lease early, the tenant's written notice must come with a copy of a valid protective order under the domestic violence chapter or a civil no-contact order (other than an ex parte order), a criminal order restraining a person from contact with the protected tenant, or a valid Address Confidentiality Program card issued to the victim or a minor in the household; a domestic violence or sexual assault victim must also send a safety plan, dated during the tenancy being ended, from a qualifying domestic violence or sexual assault program that recommends relocation (the statute asks no safety plan of a stalking victim). A lock change needs no documentation when the perpetrator is not a co-tenant, and a copy of a court order telling a co-tenant perpetrator to stay away from the unit when they are; for the nondiscrimination rule, evidence may include police, court or federal agency records or program, religious, medical or other professional documentation, but no document is required. No North Carolina provision runs a deadline from the date an order was issued: the order or card must be valid when given, and the safety plan must be dated during the tenancy. For reference, domestic violence protective orders and permanent civil no-contact orders last no more than one year unless renewed, a consent protective order counts as a protective order, and an Address Confidentiality Program card stays valid while the holder is certified, four years per certification. See edu-dv-lease-termination-nc and edu-dv-lockchange-nc.

title: Domestic Violence Information: No Landlord Confidentiality Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a private landlord to keep a tenant's domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking information confidential, and no rule specific to what you do with a protective order, safety plan or Address Confidentiality Program card a tenant gives you. The Address Confidentiality Program binds the Attorney General and State and local government agencies, which must accept the program's substitute address when creating a new public record; a private landlord is not an agency, though a landlord that is itself a unit of State or local government (the definition names an authority) may be. Two of the program's rules reach any person: no one may knowingly and intentionally obtain a participant's actual address or telephone number from the Attorney General or an agency without authorization, and a person who receives it under a court order may not pass it on without the court's permission; a knowing violation is a Class 1 misdemeanor with a fine of up to $2,500. General privacy and identity-theft rules still apply to tenant records (see edu-tenant-confidential-information-nc).

title: Deposit Return After a Domestic Violence Termination
bodyText: North Carolina has no deposit-return rule special to a domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking termination; the general rule applies, so you must itemize and refund within 30 days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered to you, or give an interim accounting then and a final one within 60 days. When a protected tenant ends the lease under the victim termination right, you may not apply the deposit to damages for the unfinished rental period. If other tenants remain, the tenancy continues for them, and the statutes do not say whether the departing protected tenant's share must be accounted for when they leave or only when the continuing tenancy ends; that is case law, so the cautious course is to settle in writing with all tenants, within 30 days after the protected tenant leaves, how the deposit is held from then on. If the tenant gives you an Address Confidentiality Program substitute address, the Attorney General receives and forwards first-class mail sent there. See edu-security-deposit-rules-nc and edu-dv-lease-termination-nc.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: North Carolina has not moved or renumbered the laws its tenant protections for victims rely on. The landlord-tenant sections point to the domestic violence chapter (Chapter 50B), the civil no-contact order chapter (Chapter 50C), the Address Confidentiality Program card issued under section 15C-4, the domestic violence program standards in section 50B-9 and, for sexual assault and stalking, Chapter 14 as a whole, and each still sits at that number. Inside Chapter 14 the crimes themselves have moved: the rape and sexual-offense sections were recodified into sections 14-27.20 to 14-27.36 effective December 1, 2015, and the old stalking section 14-277.3 was repealed effective December 1, 2008 and replaced by section 14-277.3A, so a lease, addendum or notice form citing the old crime numbers is out of date even though the landlord-tenant statutes, which cite the chapter, are not. Recent acts changed protective-order procedure (since December 1, 2025 a person seeking relief for acts in North Carolina may file without living here) but not any chapter or section number your forms would cite. See edu-dv-lease-termination-nc.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText:
North Carolina's State Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to refuse reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services that may be necessary for a person with a disability to have equal use and enjoyment of a dwelling, or to refuse reasonable modifications of the premises, at that person's expense, that are necessary to their full enjoyment of it; a refusal is a violation whatever your intent.

For a rental unit you may, where it is reasonable to do so, condition permission for a modification on the renter's agreement to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted; North Carolina does not require that condition to appear in the lease and has no rule on a restoration deposit or interest-bearing account. Because the condition is lawful only where reasonable in the particular case, the library offers no standing lease clause for it; agree it in writing when the modification is requested.

You need not rent to a person whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or cause substantial physical damage to others' property, and these duties do not reach the rental of a unit in an owner-occupied building of up to four units or of rooms in an owner-occupied private house (discriminatory advertising and statements stay barred there).

A lease restriction that allows residential use but bars a family care home is void. Service animals: edu-service-animal-law-nc; the wider Act: edu-fair-housing-nc.

title: Children and Familial Status
bodyText: North Carolina's State Fair Housing Act bars refusing to rent to a household, or treating it differently in terms, conditions, facilities or services, because of familial status: children under 18 living with a parent, a legal custodian or a custodian's designee with written permission, and anyone who is pregnant or securing legal custody of a child. The rule covers an existing rental as well as a new one, but North Carolina has no separate landlord-tenant rule (such as a notice period or grace year) for a child who arrives during the tenancy, and no rule that the lease must say anything about children. A manager who is a licensed real estate broker is also bound by the Real Estate Commission's rule against discriminating on familial status. Reasonable state or local limits on the maximum number of occupants still apply, and qualifying housing for older persons is exempt from the familial-status rules (see edu-senior-housing-work-card-nc). The Act's practices do not reach a unit in an owner-occupied building of up to four units or rooms in an owner-occupied private house, except that discriminatory statements, ads and inquiries stay barred there. A city of at least 90,000 people that hosts a large recurring event may adopt its own fair housing ordinance; local ordinances were not researched for this library (see edu-local-preemption-nc and edu-fair-housing-nc).

title: Questions and Records About Protected Classes
bodyText: North Carolina's State Fair Housing Act bars using a form or application, making a record, or making an inquiry in connection with a prospective rental that indicates, directly or indirectly, an intent to limit, specify or discriminate because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability or familial status, and bars discriminatory statements, ads and signs. This inquiry ban is narrower than a flat ban: the Act reaches a question or record that indicates an intent to discriminate, and North Carolina has no separate statute listing questions a landlord may never ask. It is the one practice that still applies to the otherwise exempt rental of a unit in an owner-occupied building of up to four units or of rooms in an owner-occupied private house. North Carolina has no state rule on asking about immigration status (edu-no-immigration-inquiry-rule-nc) or source of income (edu-no-source-of-income-rule-nc); the wider Act is in edu-fair-housing-nc.

title: Faking a Service Animal
bodyText: North Carolina makes it a Class 3 misdemeanor to disguise an animal as a service animal or a service animal in training. That sentence names no place, and the rights it protects include keeping a service animal on premises a person leases or rents, so it reaches housing as well as public places. It covers service animals only: North Carolina has no misrepresentation crime for emotional support or other assistance animals and no rule on false disability documentation, and those requests are handled as reasonable accommodations under fair housing law (see edu-disability-accommodation-nc). The same section makes it a crime to deprive a person of service-animal rights or to charge a fee for a service animal (see edu-service-animal-law-nc), and it names no civil remedy for a landlord.

title: Registered Sex Offenders: No Disclosure Duty
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a landlord to tell applicants or tenants that a registered sex offender lives in or near the property: when property is offered for rent, it is not a material fact that a person convicted of a crime requiring sex offender registration occupies, occupied or lives near it. You may not knowingly make a false statement about that fact if asked. Nothing requires a registrant to tell a landlord of their status. The registry is public: name, address, photograph, offense and registration status can be looked up free online or requested from the sheriff (see edu-sex-offender-occupancy-nc for the residency limits on registrants, and edu-stigmatized-property-nc).

title: Sex Offender Residency Limits
bodyText: North Carolina puts its sex offender residency limits on the registrant, not the landlord: a registrant who did not establish the residence before August 16, 2006 commits a felony by knowingly living at a location, or in any structure any part of which is, within 1,000 feet of the property line of a public or nonpublic school or a child care center. A residence counts as established once the registrant enters into a written lease for it, for as long as they are lawfully entitled to stay, and a school or child care center opening nearby afterwards does not put them in violation; the statute creates no private cause of action against a landlord over the restriction. It is also a felony for anyone to take other people's children into care at their residence knowing that a registrant lives there, and registrants convicted of listed offenses against minors may not knowingly be on premises intended primarily for minors, such as playgrounds, or at places such as swimming pools when minors are present; whether a rental community's own playground or pool counts is case law. North Carolina has no statewide rule barring a landlord from renting to two registrants together and no landlord duty to check distances. See edu-sex-offender-disclosure-nc and edu-family-child-care-nc.

title: Senior Housing Staff: No Work-Card Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no work-card, permit or background-check requirement for staff of senior (55-and-over or 62-and-over) rental housing. The State Fair Housing Act's only staff rule for such housing is in its exemption: housing for older persons keeps its exemption from the familial-status rules even though units are occupied by employees under the minimum age, or by their family members living with them, as long as those employees perform substantial duties directly related to managing the housing. To qualify, housing must be provided under a state or federal program for the elderly, be intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, or be intended and operated for at least one person 55 or older per unit, as shown by such factors as significant facilities and services designed for older persons (or, where that is not practicable, important housing opportunities for them), at least 80 percent of units so occupied, and the publication of and adherence to policies showing that intent. See edu-children-occupancy-nc and edu-employee-screening-nc.

title: Student Housing: No Separate Rules
bodyText: North Carolina has no separate student-housing regime: its residential rental agreements act does not exclude dormitories or student housing, whoever owns them, and its only exclusions are vacation rentals and dwellings furnished free. The Tenant Security Deposit Act, however, excludes single rooms, so whether its deposit rules reach a room rented on its own (as in by-the-bed student leases) turns on whether the rental is of a single room, which this library has not resolved by case law. Since North Carolina has no rent cap or just-cause rule, there is no student-housing exemption from either. The State Fair Housing Act speaks to student housing in two places: renting single-sex dormitory property is exempt from the ban on sex discrimination only, and a religious organization, or an educational organization operated, supervised or controlled by one, may prefer members of its own religion as long as membership is not restricted by race, color, sex, national origin, disability or familial status. Neither exemption covers advertising or other housing practices beyond its own terms; local ordinances were not researched (see edu-fair-housing-nc).

title: Tenant Screening
bodyText: North Carolina regulates tenant screening lightly: you have no duty to screen applicants, occupants or guests for criminal records, a person's criminal record does not by law make future injury or damage they cause foreseeable to you, and you may still use a criminal background check as grounds to refuse to rent. A court-issued Certificate of Relief bars a negligence claim that you lacked due care in leasing to its holder if you relied on it at the time, and the holder must tell a landlord who relied on it of any later conviction, modification or revocation within 10 days; a person whose record was expunged may lawfully leave it out when answering your questions. In a drug-nuisance forfeiture case, criminal record checks and prior-residency reference checks of prospective tenants are listed as evidence of an owner's good faith. North Carolina has no rule on when criminal history may be considered, no look-back periods, no minimum-income limits and no tax-credit-property rule, and a consumer's credit freeze does not block a report used for tenant screening. Fair housing rules still apply (see edu-fair-housing-nc and edu-protected-class-inquiry-ban-nc); federal consumer-report rules are not stated in this library, and public housing authorities have their own selection rules.

title: Screening Apartment Employees
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord or property manager to run background checks on apartment employees, such as maintenance staff with keys to units. The licensing law reaches the manager instead: renting or leasing property for others for compensation requires a real estate broker license, and the Real Estate Commission may obtain a criminal record check of each license applicant. An owner that is a business entity, and its officers and W-2 employees while doing work the entity itself is exempt for, need no license (an individual owner is exempt only when personally leasing the owner's own property), nor does a salaried employee of a licensed broker whose work is limited to showing units, giving lease information, taking applications, completing preprinted form leases and accepting deposits and rent made payable to the owner or broker. If you do screen job applicants, an employer may not require them to disclose, or knowingly ask about, arrests, charges or convictions that have been expunged; other employment law was not researched for this library (see edu-tenant-screening-nc).

title: Sharing Tenant Information
bodyText: North Carolina has no landlord-tenant statute barring a landlord from sharing tenant or applicant information, and no consent rule for doing so. The Identity Theft Protection Act still binds a landlord business: you may not make a person's Social Security number available to the public, print it on mailings or require it to be sent over an unsecured internet connection, or sell or disclose it to a third party without the person's written consent when you have reason to believe the third party lacks a legitimate purpose; collecting and using it in an application, for internal verification, or to get a credit report or run a background check is allowed. No person may knowingly publish another's Social Security, driver's license, account or similar numbers to the public after that person has objected. Data security and disposal duties are in edu-tenant-records-nc, and victim address rules in edu-dv-confidentiality-nc.

title: Tenant Records and Data Security
bodyText: North Carolina gives tenants no statutory right to a rent ledger or to inspect a landlord's records, and no statute requires a ledger with a nonpayment demand (see edu-no-cash-receipt-duty-nc for receipts). A real estate broker who manages rentals for others must keep a ledger for each property or owner showing the tenant and each deposit and disbursement, may keep a separate security deposit ledger, keeps leases and receipts for three years after the funds are disbursed or the transaction ends, and must give the client (the owner) copies within 10 days of a written request. Any business holding North Carolina residents' personal information, such as names with Social Security, driver's license, bank or card numbers, must take reasonable measures against unauthorized access when disposing of it, including shredding or erasing and written disposal procedures. After a security breach, a business that owns or licenses the information must notify affected people without unreasonable delay, with the contents the statute lists, and also notify the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division, while a business that only holds someone else's data (a manager holding an owner's records, for example) must notify the owner or licensee immediately; North Carolina has no general written information security program requirement outside insurance. See edu-tenant-confidential-information-nc.

title: No Rent-Reporting Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no rent-reporting law: nothing requires a landlord to offer positive rent reporting, nothing lets or bars a lease requiring a tenant to join a rent-reporting program, and no statute requires written notice to a tenant before late rent is reported to a credit bureau. The state's credit-report statute speaks to rentals only in passing: a consumer's security freeze does not stop a credit report from being used for tenant screening (see edu-tenant-screening-nc). Federal credit-reporting rules for anyone who furnishes data are not stated in this library.

title: Family Child Care in a Rental
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to allow a tenant to run a family child care home, voiding a lease term that bars one, or setting conditions such as insurance or liability waivers; whether to allow it is a matter for the lease. A family child care home is child care for more than two but fewer than 11 children in an operator-occupied private dwelling, so a tenant operator can qualify, and child care is regulated by the State's child care licensing law. Unlike family child care, a family care home for up to six people with disabilities is a protected residential use, and a lease term barring one is void (see edu-disability-accommodation-nc). It is a felony to take other people's children into care at a residence knowing that a registered sex offender lives there (see edu-sex-offender-occupancy-nc); local zoning ordinances were not researched for this library (see edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: Firearms in Rentals
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute on firearms in private leases: nothing requires a landlord to allow firearms, bars a lease restriction, or protects a firearm stored in a vehicle in a rental property's parking area, and counties and cities may not regulate firearm possession or storage except as statutes allow.

A concealed handgun permit does not authorize carrying on private premises where the person in legal possession or control has posted a conspicuous notice prohibiting it, except for the permit holders the statute exempts from its area limits (such as prosecutors, judges, magistrates, elected clerks of court and registers of deeds, and designated Department of Public Safety and, since July 7, 2026, State Bureau of Investigation employees); who that person is for a leased unit, as against common areas you control, is case law.

Anyone who lives with a minor commits a misdemeanor by leaving a firearm that can be fired where they knew or should have known an unsupervised minor could get it, if the minor then misuses it in a way the statute lists.

Whether a lease may ban possession inside a unit is also case law, so it offers no possession ban; it offers an optional discharge and storage clause (firearms-nc). The shared parking-lot sentence other states use is not offered for North Carolina because no North Carolina statute requires it.

title: Marijuana and Hemp in Rentals
bodyText:
North Carolina has not legalized marijuana for medical or adult use: it is a Schedule VI controlled substance, and possessing it is a crime, a Class 3 misdemeanor for small amounts and more serious with quantity. No statute protects a tenant's cannabis use or limits a lease restriction, so a lease may bar marijuana smoking, growing, possession and use (the optional clause cannabis-restrictions-ak does this); the library's criminal-activity clause does not reach simple possession, so the cannabis clause is the tool for that (see criminal-activity-nc and edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-nc).

Hemp and hemp products with no more than 0.3 percent delta-9 THC are not marijuana under state law, and a caregiver may lawfully possess a qualifying hemp extract to treat intractable epilepsy; a request to allow that extract as a disability accommodation would be decided under fair housing law (see edu-disability-accommodation-nc). Knowingly keeping or maintaining a dwelling that people resort to for using controlled substances is itself a crime.

title: No Statutory Guest Rights
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute giving tenants a right to have guests or service providers visit, barring guest fees, or limiting a lease guest policy, so guest rules are a matter for the lease (see guest-policy and guest-policy-day-limit). The one statutory rule on guests runs the other way: in an expedited eviction for criminal activity, a court that finds a household member or guest engaged in criminal activity on or near the premises may issue a conditional order requiring the tenant not to invite or permit that barred person back onto any part of the premises, and breaking it ends the tenancy (see edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-nc). Fair housing rules still apply to how guest rules are written and enforced (see edu-fair-housing-nc).

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText:
North Carolina caps the security deposit by type of tenancy: no more than two weeks' rent for a week-to-week tenancy, one and one-half months' rent for a month-to-month tenancy, and two months' rent for any longer term, such as a one-year lease. The cap covers everyone in the business of renting or managing residential units on a weekly, monthly or yearly basis, except rentals of single rooms, and it has no exemption for higher-rent, furnished or luxury units and no separate allowance for furniture, alterations or added risk.

The deposit law's only express allowance outside the cap is a reasonable nonrefundable pet fee (the cap limits security deposits, not rent or other lawful fees); a refundable pet deposit is part of the security deposit and counts toward the cap.

The law does not say whether the cap is measured on the rent at signing or on a later, higher rent, so if you ask for more deposit after a rent increase, keep the total you hold within the cap figured on the rent in effect when you collect the extra amount. Prepaid last month's rent is treated as part of the deposit, as explained in the library's last-month's-rent row. Vacation rentals follow the separate vacation rental rules.

title: Prepaid Last Month's Rent
bodyText:
North Carolina's security deposit law does not define a security deposit and says nothing about prepaid last month's rent. A deposit may be kept for the tenant's possible failure to pay rent, so money you collect at signing and hold against the last month of the lease works like security. This library therefore treats a "last month's rent" collected at signing as part of the security deposit: it counts toward the deposit limit, is held in the trust account or covered by the bond, and is applied and accounted for with the deposit when the tenancy ends. The only exception is a lease that makes the payment Rent for a named calendar month (for example, Rent for June 2027), which is then simply rent paid early.

No North Carolina statute lets a tenant insist on using the deposit as the last month's rent, or forbids you from agreeing to it; if the tenant does not pay the last month, you may apply the deposit to the unpaid rent and account for it within the usual deadline. Vacation rentals follow their own rules.

title: Consequences of Breaking the Deposit Rules
bodyText: If you do not account for and refund the balance of a security deposit as North Carolina's deposit law requires, the tenant may sue you to force the accounting and recover the balance. If you willfully fail to meet the law's deposit, bond or notice requirements, you lose the right to keep any part of the deposit, even for unpaid rent or damage you could otherwise have deducted, though you can still sue the tenant for what the tenant owes. The tenant may also recover damages caused by your noncompliance, and if the tenant wins the judgment and the court finds your noncompliance willful, it may award attorney's fees as court costs. The deposit law itself sets no double or triple damages. The law does not say whether its notice requirements include the itemized move-out accounting as well as the 30-day notice of where the deposit is held, so treat a willful failure to send the itemization on time as putting the whole deposit at risk. Whether a deposit violation is also an unfair trade practice, with triple damages, is for the courts; see the library's unfair trade practices row.

title: Security Deposit When the Property Changes Hands
bodyText: When your interest in a rented unit ends, whether by sale, assignment, death, the appointment of a receiver or any other way, you or your agent must, within 30 days, do one of two things with the deposit that remains after lawful deductions: transfer it to your successor and then notify the tenant by mail of the transfer and of the new owner's name and address, or return it to the tenant. Doing either one on time relieves you of further liability for the deposit; if you do neither, you remain answerable for it. A successor who takes over the deposit must account for and refund it under the same rules, and the tenant's lawsuit remedy runs against the successor too. Vacation rentals have their own transfer rules.

title: Pet Fees and Pet Deposits
bodyText: North Carolina lets you charge a reasonable, nonrefundable fee for pets the tenant keeps on the property, in addition to the security deposit. The law sets no dollar figure; it says only that the fee must be reasonable. A refundable pet deposit is different: the deposit law does not set one apart, so it is part of the security deposit, counts toward the deposit limit, may be used only for the purposes the deposit law allows and must be held and returned with the rest of the deposit. No North Carolina statute addresses monthly pet rent. None of these charges may be made for a service animal, and assistance animals are not pets; see the library's assistance-animal rows.

title: Late Fee Limit
bodyText:
North Carolina caps late fees on residential rent. A late fee may be charged only if the lease fixes a definite time for paying rent and the parties have agreed to the fee, and only once rent is five or more calendar days late, counting from the day after it was due. For monthly rent the fee may not exceed $15 or 5% of the monthly rent, whichever is greater; for weekly rent, $4 or 5% of the weekly rent, whichever is greater.

It may be charged only once for each late payment, may not be deducted from a later payment to make that payment late, may not be charged for unpaid landlord-billed water or sewer, and, where the rent is subsidized by HUD, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, a State agency, a public housing authority or a local government, is figured on the tenant's share only. A lease term contrary to these rules is void.

The same cap applies to every residential rental agreement; North Carolina has no separate, different late-fee cap for manufactured home parks, and late fees on landlord-billed utility bills are only what the Utilities Commission allows. The library's late-fee clause and late-fee education row apply these rules.

title: Fees When Rent Is Subsidized
bodyText: If a tenant's rent is subsidized by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, a State agency, a public housing authority or a local government, any late fee or other fee North Carolina's fee statute allows (including the eviction administrative fees) must be figured on the tenant's share of the contract rent only; the subsidy is left out. So for a tenant who pays $300 of a $1,200 rent, the late-fee cap is the greater of $15 or 5% of $300, which is $15, and the court-appearance fee is 10% of $300. The statute does not say whether you may charge the tenant a late fee when only the agency's part arrives late; the cautious course is not to, since the fee is tied to the tenant's share. Federal program rules may add their own limits.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: North Carolina does not allow a landlord to lock out a residential tenant for unpaid rent, with or without notice, and has no procedure that lets a lease opt into a lockout. A residential tenant may be evicted, dispossessed or otherwise removed, actually or constructively, only through the court eviction process (summary ejectment, or the separate procedure for drug and other criminal activity). Seizing or holding a tenant's belongings for rent is also prohibited. Any lease term to the contrary is void. A tenant locked out, or whom the landlord or agent attempts to remove outside the court process, may recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages from the landlord or agent. The library's self-help eviction row covers lock changes, utility cutoffs and belongings in more detail.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: North Carolina law gives a tenant no right to pay the security deposit in installments and does not require you to offer that option; the General Statutes, the 2024-2026 session laws and the held administrative rules were searched and none addresses it. You may agree to accept the deposit in installments if you choose. Whatever schedule you agree, the total deposit stays within the deposit limit, every amount you receive is held in the trust account or covered by the bond, and the deposit may be used only for the purposes the deposit law allows. Counties and cities may not regulate the amount of rent, with limited exceptions.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule letting a lease preset cleaning, carpet or repair charges against the security deposit, and no prescribed notice for doing so. What controls is the deposit law's list of permitted uses: when the tenancy ends you may apply the deposit only to the listed items, such as unpaid rent and landlord-billed utility charges, damage to the premises, and re-renting costs, and you may never keep anything for normal wear and tear or more than your actual damages. Cleaning is not on the list on its own, and the law does not say whether a unit left dirty counts as damage to the premises; the cautious course is to take a cleaning cost from the deposit only where it remedies damage beyond normal wear and tear, and only at what it actually cost you. A flat preset charge therefore cannot be kept just because the lease names it; at most a schedule tells the tenant what typical repairs cost. This library offers no preset-charge schedule. Vacation rentals, which may state a cleaning fee in the rental agreement, follow their own rules.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute on carpet cleaning: nothing lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out on any condition, and nothing forbids a lease asking for it. The deposit law decides what you can actually recover from the deposit. You may apply the deposit only to its listed purposes, including damage to the premises, and never for normal wear and tear or more than your actual damages; a general breach of the lease is not on the list. The law does not say whether carpets left soiled count as damage to the premises, so the cautious course is to deduct carpet cleaning only where it remedies damage beyond normal wear and tear, and only the amount you actually paid, listed in your itemized deposit statement. For that reason this library does not offer the professional carpet-cleaning clause used in some other states, which charges the cost to the deposit as damages for not following the lease. Vacation rentals, which may state a cleaning fee, follow their own rules.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: North Carolina has no special procedure, election or fee for an early or expedited return of a security deposit, and none is needed: the deposit law's deadlines are outer limits. You must mail or deliver the itemized statement with the balance no later than 30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant returns possession (or, if the extent of your claim cannot be determined within 30 days, an interim accounting then and a final one within 60 days), and you may always do it sooner. You may not deduct a processing or accounting fee for doing so, because the deposit may be applied only to the listed purposes, and the only fees on that list are the ones North Carolina's fee statute permits, none of which is a deposit-processing fee.

title: No Posted Deposit Standards Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule requiring you to post or hand out the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you own many adjoining units and charge different tenants different deposits. What does apply: every deposit must stay within the deposit limit for its type of tenancy, and fair housing law bars setting deposit amounts differently because of a protected characteristic. Applying the same written criteria to every applicant is a sensible practice, not a legal requirement.

title: Nonrefundable Deposits and Fees
bodyText:
North Carolina has no notice procedure for nonrefundable deposits, because its deposit law leaves no room for one: money you hold as security may be applied only to the listed purposes and the rest must be refunded, so calling part of a deposit nonrefundable does not let you keep it. The deposit law does not define a security deposit, and this library treats any money held to secure the tenant's rent or other obligations, or against damage, as part of the security deposit whatever it is called, counted toward the deposit limit.

The only nonrefundable charge the deposit law names is a reasonable pet fee. North Carolina has no statute requiring a notice for, capping or banning other nonrefundable fees for a service, such as an application fee, with two exceptions in North Carolina's fee statute: it voids any eviction-related administrative fee it does not authorize, and where the lease requires renters insurance, it lets you charge the tenant the actual cost of coverage you obtain plus an administrative fee of no more than $50 a year only if the tenant fails to show proof of the coverage within three business days of your request.

If you charge nonrefundable fees, the library's optional clause lists each one and its purpose.

title: No Separate Notice Rule for Nonrefundable Charges
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule requiring a separate written notice, a separate signed document or particular wording before you may treat a deposit or fee as nonrefundable. That is because the deposit law does not allow a nonrefundable deposit at all: money held as security must be applied only to the listed purposes and the rest refunded. A reasonable nonrefundable pet fee and nonrefundable fees for a service may simply be stated in the lease; the library's optional nonrefundable-fees clause does that.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute on holding deposits, earnest money or other money taken from an applicant to hold a unit before the lease is signed. The deposit law speaks of security deposits from the tenant and does not say whether it reaches money taken before there is a tenancy, and no statute says whether you must return a holding deposit, may keep it if the applicant backs out, or owe more than its return if you back out. The cautious course: agree the terms in writing (the amount, how long you will hold the unit, and when the money is refunded, credited or kept), refund it if you do not offer the lease, and once the lease is signed either credit it to the first month's rent or hold it as part of the security deposit, within the deposit limit and in the trust account or under the bond. A real estate broker must place money received on a pending lease in a trust or escrow account within the deadlines in the Real Estate Commission's rules and, if the parties dispute a deposit other than a residential tenant security deposit, hold it until both release it or a court orders disbursement, or deposit it with the clerk of superior court. Rental referral agencies that charge applicants to find housing have separate rules.

title: No Fee-in-Lieu-of-Deposit Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute authorizing or regulating a fee, surety bond or insurance product that a tenant pays instead of a security deposit. The bond the deposit law mentions is different: it lets you, the landlord, buy a bond from a licensed insurer instead of keeping the tenant's deposit in a trust account, and it does not replace the deposit. Because the deposit law does not define a security deposit, money a tenant pays that you hold to secure rent or damage is treated as part of the security deposit, whatever it is called; a fee that buys a third-party product is a fee. If a lease requires the tenant to carry insurance coverage for the premises, it may not require a particular insurer or agent. The cautious course, if you offer an alternative, is to keep it optional and let the tenant pay an ordinary deposit instead. This library offers no fee-in-lieu clause for North Carolina.

title: No Fee-Disclosure or All-In Pricing Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no fee-transparency or all-in pricing law for rentals: nothing requires you to advertise or state rent as one total including mandatory fees, list fees on the lease's first page or in prescribed words, and no statute lists fees a landlord may not charge outside the late-fee, eviction-fee and deposit rules. The general unfair and deceptive trade practices law still applies to business conduct, so a fee that is hidden, misdescribed or charged without the tenant's agreement can create liability; how far that law reaches residential leasing is for the courts. Fees the fee statute does not authorize for eviction filings are void, and collecting a charge you are not legally entitled to can violate the debt-collection rules. Electric and natural gas bills you send under Utilities Commission authority must show the administrative and late fees the Commission approved. Stating every fee plainly in the lease is the safe practice.

title: No General Rule on Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute that specifically bars charging a tenant a fee for a service you do not provide. Related rules do apply. If you bill tenants for water and sewer or electricity under Utilities Commission authority, you may charge only the Commission-approved rates and fees, may not include water or electricity used in common areas or other units, and may not bill for excess water use from a plumbing malfunction the tenant did not know about or had reported to you. Eviction-related administrative fees other than those the fee statute authorizes are void. Beyond that, charging for something the tenant does not receive can be an unfair or deceptive trade practice, and collecting a charge you are not legally entitled to can violate the debt-collection rules; how far those laws reach residential leasing is for the courts. Make sure every fee in your lease pays for something you actually provide.

title: North Carolina Dollar and Percentage Limits
bodyText: North Carolina sets no limit on the amount of rent, and counties and cities may not regulate it, but state law caps these charges. Security deposit: two weeks' rent (week to week), one and one-half months' rent (month to month) or two months' rent (longer terms); a nonrefundable pet fee must be reasonable. Late fee: the greater of $15 or 5% of monthly rent, or of $4 or 5% of weekly rent, once per late payment and only after five calendar days. Eviction administrative fees, under a written lease and only one per case: a complaint-filing fee of the greater of $15 or 5% of monthly rent, a court-appearance fee of 10% of monthly rent, or a second-trial fee of up to 12%. Attorneys' fees under a written lease: up to 15% of the amount owed (15% of monthly rent for a non-rent eviction), or all actual reasonable fees if the tenant's appeal is found frivolous and you win. Renter's insurance you buy for a tenant who fails to show proof within three business days of your request: actual cost plus an administrative fee of up to $50 a year. Returned check: up to $35. Landlord-billed water and sewer: no more than the supplier's unit rate plus a Commission-approved administrative fee (generally up to $3.75); electricity: actual cost plus the administrative and late fees the Commission allows. A military technician's early termination: liquidated damages, only if you suffered actual damages from the loss of the tenancy, of at most one month's rent (under six months of tenancy) or half a month's (six to nine months), and none if the termination comes 14 or more days before occupancy. If rent is subsidized by HUD, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, a State agency, a public housing authority or a local government, fees are figured on the tenant's share only.

title: Which Fees Must Be in the Lease
bodyText: North Carolina has no general rule that every fee, fine or charge must be listed in the lease, no notice period for adding a fee later, no single "total monthly payment" figure and no ban on common-area maintenance fees. Several fees, though, exist only if the lease provides for them. A late fee must be agreed by the parties in a lease that fixes a definite time for paying rent. The eviction complaint-filing, court-appearance and second-trial administrative fees, and attorneys' fees of up to 15% for an eviction or money-owed case, may be charged only under a written lease; the separate award of all actual reasonable attorneys' fees when you prevail on a tenant's appeal to district court and a court determines that the tenant knew, or should have known, the appeal was frivolous, unreasonable, without foundation, in bad faith or solely for delay does not depend on the lease. You may bill tenants for water and sewer, electricity or natural gas only under a written rental agreement and with Utilities Commission authority: water and sewer charges may not exceed the supplier's unit rate, the administrative fee is capped by the Commission, electricity is billed at actual cost, and you must give each tenant at lease signing a copy of your rates and the Commission's rules (and, for electricity, tell tenants at the start and each year how bills are allocated and what fees apply). A reasonable nonrefundable pet fee needs no particular wording. List every fee you intend to charge in the lease; a fee the tenant never agreed to is hard to collect.

title: Collecting Rent Carries the Fitness Duty
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute saying in so many words that a lease, assignment, deed, deed of trust or other security instrument cannot let someone collect the rent free of the duty to keep the unit fit and habitable. The Residential Rental Agreements Act reaches the same people another way. It defines the landlord as any owner and any rental management company, rental agency or other person with actual or apparent authority as an agent to perform the landlord's duties, makes the tenant's duty to pay rent under the rental agreement or an assignment and the landlord's fitness duties depend on each other, and says no acceptance by the tenant of a defective unit releases the landlord, unless a government body blocks repairs for a set period of no more than six months (a later written contract, supported by adequate consideration other than the rental itself, in which the tenant agrees to do specified work is also allowed if it is not made with the purpose or effect of evading the landlord's duties). Whether a term in a lease, deed or mortgage could shift the fitness duties away from whoever collects the rent is case law, and the library offers no such term.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages
bodyText: North Carolina has no landlord-tenant statute on interest on unpaid rent, fees or damages, either requiring a lease term for it or setting a rate for leases. General law fills the gap: when you win a lawsuit for breach of the lease, the amount awarded bears interest from the date of the breach, and North Carolina's legal rate of interest is 8% a year. After judgment the interest is at the legal rate unless the lease says a contract rate applies after judgment, and where credit was extended for personal or household purposes it is the lower of the two. Whether a lease may add its own interest charge on overdue rent is not settled by statute: the usury law's contract rates cover loans and forbearances, and an interest charge on late rent could be treated as an extra late fee beyond the late-fee cap, which would be void. The cautious course, which this library follows, is no contractual interest clause; claim interest at the legal rate in any court action instead. Collecting interest you are not legally entitled to can also violate the debt-collection rules.

title: Utility Deposits
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule for a separate utility deposit held by a landlord, and the library offers none. The security deposit itself may be used for unpaid rent and for unpaid water, sewer and electric charges you bill under Utilities Commission authority, so money you collect to secure those charges is part of the security deposit: it counts toward the deposit limit, is held in the trust account or under the bond, and is accounted for and refunded with the deposit within 30 days after the tenancy ends and possession is returned. If you bill tenants for electricity or natural gas, you may not pass on to them a deposit you paid the utility. A landlord billing for water, sewer or electricity is treated as a public utility for those charges, and the Commission's rules do not say whether its customer-deposit rules then apply to you, which is another reason not to take a separate utility deposit. When the tenant has an account directly with a utility whose deposits the Commission's rules govern, the deposit is limited, earns interest once held more than 90 days, and must be refunded with accrued interest when service is discontinued, and an unclaimed utility deposit is presumed abandoned one year after it becomes payable.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: An unclaimed deposit refund never becomes yours. If you do not know the tenant's address, North Carolina's deposit law requires you, after 30 days, to apply the deposit to the permitted charges and to hold the balance for the tenant to collect for at least six months. After that the balance is unclaimed property under the North Carolina Unclaimed Property Act, which names security deposits expressly and covers property held in the course of a holder's business: it is presumed abandoned five years after the tenant's right to demand it arose, unless the tenant shows interest in it first. You then become a holder with duties to the State Treasurer: mail the tenant a written notice 60 to 120 days before you report (for property of $50 or more, falling to $25 or more on December 1, 2026), file the report before November 1 covering the 12 months before July 1, and pay the money over with it; a holder whose reportable property totals $250 or less in a year reports it in a later year once the total is higher. Late reporting carries interest, and willful failure carries a civil penalty of $1,000 a day, up to $25,000, plus 25% of the property's value. You may deduct a charge for the tenant's failure to claim only under a valid written contract and only if you regularly impose it. A lease term forfeiting an unclaimed or undeliverable refund to you is not something the deposit law allows, and this library offers none.

title: Deposit Refund Cannot Depend on Move-Out Notice
bodyText: North Carolina's deposit law does not let you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out or a forwarding address. Your deadline runs from the end of the tenancy and the tenant's return of possession: within 30 days you must mail or deliver the itemized statement with the balance, or an interim accounting if your claim cannot yet be figured, with a final accounting within 60 days. If you do not know the tenant's address, you must, after 30 days, apply the deposit to the permitted charges and hold any balance for the tenant to collect for at least six months. A lease may still ask the tenant to give notice and a forwarding address, and a tenant's failure to give the notice a periodic tenancy requires can leave rent owing that the deposit may cover, but you may not keep the deposit just because the notice or address was not given.

title: Rental Registration and Permits
bodyText: No North Carolina statute requires landlords to register or license rentals with the State or with a county (such as through the county assessor), no rule that an out-of-state owner hire an in-state broker or agent, and no state business licence for renting homes. State law also limits what cities and counties may do: a local government may not require you to get a permit or permission under its building or housing code powers to lease residential property, or to register rental property, except for an individual property with more than four verified violations in a rolling 12 months or two or more in a rolling 30 days, or one identified in the top 10% of properties for crime or disorder under a local ordinance. All violations found in a unit during a 72-hour period count together, and a violation counts as verified only if it is not corrected within 21 days of written notice (the same violation a third time in 12 months cannot be corrected away, and for a violation caused by the tenant's behavior, filing an eviction within 30 days of the notice counts as a correction). Even for those properties a local government may not make a registration violation a crime, may not charge rental property a special fee or tax that other property does not pay beyond $500 per 12-month period with verified violations (unless general law allows it), and you may appeal action against your unit to the local appeals board. Any local registration or permit ordinance within those limits remains local and was not researched for this library; see edu-local-preemption-nc.

title: Code Inspections of Rental Property
bodyText:
North Carolina has no state rental inspection program, and state law limits local ones. A city or county inspection department may make periodic inspections of a residential building only with reasonable cause: the owner has more than two verified violations in 12 months, someone has complained or asked for an inspection, the department knows of an unsafe condition, or violations are visible from outside; it may also check other units of a multifamily building for the same hazard after finding an immediate threat in one, and may run periodic inspections in designated blighted areas (no more than 1 square mile or 5% of its jurisdiction, whichever is greater) that meet the statutory blight definitions and fit the local government's neighborhood revitalization strategy, after notice to owners and residents, a legislative hearing and a plan to help low-income owners comply, but it may not treat owner-occupied and rented homes, or single-family and multifamily buildings, differently.

Fire-code inspections and other inspections state law requires are not limited by these rules, and a local government may not make you submit to an inspection before it provides utility service.

Inspectors may enter at reasonable hours on showing credentials, and where a warrant is constitutionally required an official can get an administrative inspection warrant valid for 24 hours; a health director refused consent must get one unless there is an imminent hazard.

No North Carolina statute lets the lease itself authorize an inspector to enter so that the tenant must allow entry without separate consent, and the library does not offer a clause that tries to.

See edu-local-preemption-nc and edu-landlord-registration-nc.

title: No State Tenant-Rights Statement
bodyText: North Carolina has no state-agency statement of tenant rights that you must give tenants or attach to a lease, no rule that each tenant sign an acknowledgment of one or initial its pages, and no rule barring an eviction or other suit until one is provided (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Two statutes come close. A vacation rental agreement must carry, clearly and conspicuously on its face, a prescribed notice that it is governed by the Vacation Rental Act and that the parties' rights and obligations are defined by law (see edu-vacation-rental-scope-nc). And converting a rental building to condominiums requires a notice to each residential tenant, at least 90 days before the tenant must vacate, that sets out generally the tenants' rights under the conversion statute; failure to give it is a defense to an action for possession (see edu-condo-conversion-notice-nc). Whether any city or county requires a local tenant-rights notice was not researched for this library; state limits on local rental rules are in edu-local-preemption-nc.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: North Carolina has no state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities that you must give a tenant before signing or at renewal, and no signed acknowledgment of one is required (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). No state agency is directed to publish such a guide for residential tenancies. Your disclosure duties come from specific statutes instead, such as the vacation rental notice and the lead-paint rules (see edu-vacation-rental-scope-nc and edu-lead-hazards-nc); for the separate question of a state statement of tenant rights, see edu-tenant-rights-statement-nc. Whether any city or county hands out or requires a local guide was not researched for this library; state limits on local rental rules are in edu-local-preemption-nc.

title: Changing Terms of a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute on changing the terms of a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy: no set advance notice to modify a term, no longer notice for raising a fee the lease already provides, and no rule that a change in a term must be made by a full termination notice offering a new tenancy (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The only statutory periods are the notices that end a periodic tenancy: seven days for month-to-month, two days for week-to-week, one month before the end of the year for year-to-year, and at least 60 days for a manufactured-home space (see edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-nc); during a fixed term, terms change only as the lease allows. One statute freezes terms: once a condominium conversion notice is given, the terms of the tenancy may not be altered during the 90-day period before the tenant must leave (see edu-condo-conversion-notice-nc). Whether a mid-tenancy change binds a periodic tenant without agreement, or only after the tenancy is ended with proper notice and new terms are offered, is case law; the cautious course is written notice of the change at least as long as the notice that would end the tenancy, given before the rental period in which it starts. Local governments may not regulate the amount of rent, and no local notice rule was researched for this library (see edu-no-rent-increase-notice-nc and edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: Local Health Rules
bodyText: North Carolina does not require you to give a tenant a copy of local health rules on request, and no statute tells you to refer tenants to the health department (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Local boards of health (county, district or public health authority boards) may adopt rules to protect public health, including rules stricter than the state's in areas the state regulates where the board finds a stricter rule is required to protect public health (but not, for example, rules on grading, operating and permitting food and lodging facilities), and the local health director enforces them. A health director who finds a public health nuisance may order the owner, lessee or other person in control of the property to abate it, and for an imminent hazard may order abatement or, after notice or a reasonable attempt at notice, enter and abate it, with a lien on the property for the cost, which an owner or other person in control can defeat by showing no imminent hazard existed or that they were not culpable in creating it. Whether your local board of health has rules that reach rental housing remains local and was not researched for this library; housing-code enforcement runs through city and county minimum housing codes (see edu-rental-inspection-nc and edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: Rent After Condemnation
bodyText: No North Carolina statute bars you from collecting rent after a dwelling is condemned, placarded or ordered vacated (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Other rules still bite: once a local officer closes an unfit dwelling and posts the placard, occupying it is a crime, and the local government's summary court action to remove a tenant of the owner may be brought only after the tenant has had 30 days' notice that the governing board has ordered the officer to act; under the Residential Rental Agreements Act the tenant's duty to pay rent and your duty to provide fit premises depend on each other, although the tenant may not withhold rent on their own before a court decides. If the home is destroyed, or damaged so it cannot be made fit except at a cost above one year's rent, without the tenant's fault, and the home was the main reason for the rental, the tenant may surrender in writing within 10 days, paying any rent in arrears and the prorated rent then due, and owe no later rent, unless the lease addresses repairs or the case or otherwise provides (the library's casualty clause is casualty-termination-nc). Whether rent is owed for a period when a condemned unit cannot lawfully be occupied is case law; the cautious course is not to charge rent for any period the unit is under an order to vacate or posted as unfit.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code Orders
bodyText: North Carolina does not require you to tell a tenant or applicant about an outstanding inspection report, repair order or condemnation order on the property (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Tenants learn of these in other ways: under a local minimum housing code the officer's complaint and hearing notice go to the owner and to every party in interest, which includes anyone in possession of the dwelling; a closed unfit dwelling is placarded at its main entrance, and the governing board's ordinances ordering closing or demolition are recorded with the register of deeds; and a building condemned as unsafe gets a posted notice that it is a crime to remove. The only statute found that makes a private party disclose a pending public-agency order is for contracts for deed (a sale on installments), not leases. Renting a unit you know is posted as unfit puts your tenant in breach of a criminal ban on occupying it and conflicts with your fitness duties (see edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-nc).

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty
bodyText: North Carolina has no inspection-notice penalty because it has no inspection-notice duty: no statute requires a move-in or move-out inspection, a condition checklist, a notice telling the tenant of a right to an inspection, or a set notice before you enter, so none sets a forfeiture, multiple of rent or fine for skipping one (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The penalties that do exist attach to the deposit rules themselves: a landlord's willful failure to comply with the deposit, bond or notice requirements of the Tenant Security Deposit Act voids the right to keep any part of the deposit (see edu-security-deposit-rules-nc). Entry and inspection notice is set by the lease (see landlords-access and edu-no-entry-notice-statute-nc), and a signed move-in and move-out condition report remains the best evidence for deductions (see edu-no-move-in-inspection-rule-nc).

title: Code Repair Orders and Receivership
bodyText: Repair orders in North Carolina come from city and county minimum housing codes: after a complaint and a hearing, the local public officer may order you to repair an unfit dwelling within a set time if repair costs are reasonable in relation to its value (requiring it vacated during repairs only if continued occupancy is a significant threat of bodily harm), or to remove or demolish it if they are not. If you do not comply, the governing board may by ordinance direct the officer to repair, close or demolish the dwelling, and the cost becomes a lien on the property (inside a city, also on your other property in the city or within one mile, except your primary residence). Separately, a building inspector may condemn an unsafe building and, after a hearing, order it repaired, closed, vacated or demolished within at least 60 days (sooner for imminent danger); failing to comply is a misdemeanor. Receivership exists only for vacant property: a city may petition the superior court for a receiver to rehabilitate, demolish or sell a vacant building or dwelling after the owner fails to comply with such an order (or when an owner asks), and once appointed and recorded the receiver alone may collect rents, may manage the property with a landlord's powers for up to two years after rehabilitation, and holds a lien ahead of everything except taxes and other government assessments. No North Carolina statute provides receivership for occupied substandard rentals, of two or more units or otherwise (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Each local government's housing code, standards and procedures remain local and were not researched for this library (see edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: No Code-Variance Notice Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule that a housing or health code variance, exception or waiver for a rental must be given to tenants or attached to the rental agreement (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched, including the words exception, exemption and waiver). The nearest power is local: on an appeal from the housing officer, a housing appeals board may, where the strict letter of the minimum housing ordinance would cause unnecessary hardship, adapt its application to the case, but the statute requires no notice to tenants of that decision. State variances from food and lodging sanitation rules reach lodging establishments such as hotels, not ordinary residential rentals. Whether a local housing code or board of health requires notice of a variance remains local and was not researched for this library (see edu-health-district-rental-rules-nc and edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: Fire Code Standard
bodyText: North Carolina's fire code is the North Carolina Fire Code, one volume of the North Carolina State Building Code, which the Building Code Council (commercial and multifamily) and the Residential Code Council (residential) adopt as state rules; they may use national model codes as guidance but are not required to adopt them, and the statutes name no model-code edition. The Code applies throughout the state; a city or county may adopt its own fire prevention code only with the responsible Council's approval, and may not add fire-code provisions for dwellings under the North Carolina Residential Code that the Residential Code does not prescriptively require. The 2024 edition of the State Building Code was to take effect July 1, 2025, but a 2025 law delays it until 12 months after the first day of the month following the State Fire Marshal's certification that the Councils have published and distributed it and the Residential Code Council is fully constituted; the State Fire Marshal's office said in March 2025 that the 2018 State Building Code remains in force until then and in March 2026 that this was still current, so the 2024 edition cannot become mandatory before 12 months after a certification not yet announced. Confirm with your local building or fire official which edition is enforced. Local governments may enforce the fire code with civil penalties, and fire-code periodic inspections fall outside the limits on rental inspections (see edu-rental-inspection-nc). From January 1, 2027 the two Councils are administered through a new Building Codes and Interpretations Bureau in the Department of Labor; the Code in effect on that date is not changed by the move.

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: A lease cannot freeze North Carolina's building and housing standards at the edition in force when it was signed: the Residential Rental Agreements Act requires you to comply with the current applicable building and housing codes, whether enacted before or after October 1, 1977, but only to the extent those codes themselves apply, and it imposes no new requirement on a structure that a current building code exempts. The statutes rarely name a model-code edition: the State Building Code is adopted as state rules by the two Code Councils, which may use national model codes as guidance, and any state agency rule that incorporates an outside code or standard by reference must say whether later amendments and editions are included (state rules for public pools, for example, incorporate the 2018 North Carolina Plumbing Code including later amendments and editions). Local boards of health may also adopt outside codes and standards by reference in their rules. One frozen text sits in the statute itself: the 1976 safety rules for existing high-rise buildings, which apply on a building official's written order (see edu-fire-sprinkler-duty-nc). Smoke alarms must carry a UL or equivalent national testing laboratory listing, carbon monoxide alarms must be listed to the named ANSI/UL standards, and both must be installed to NFPA standards or the manufacturer's instructions; the statute ties none of these to a dated edition (see smoke-co-alarms-nc); which edition of the State Building Code is now in force is covered in edu-fire-code-standard-nc.

title: No Sprinkler Retrofit Duty
bodyText: No North Carolina statute requires you to install or retrofit fire sprinklers in an existing rental house or apartment building (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched); whether new construction or an alteration needs sprinklers is set by the State Building Code volumes, which were not read for this library. Three- and four-family dwellings (one building of no more than two stories above grade on its own lot) built under the North Carolina Residential Code may not be required to have automatic sprinklers, and need 2-hour fire-rated separations instead. Existing high-rise buildings, including residential ones of at least 60 feet or 6 stories, must add listed life-safety features (alarms, corridor smoke detectors, exits, emergency power and more) within a reasonable time fixed by the building official's written order; only the tallest class (250 feet or 25 stories and up) must add sprinklers, and then only in mercantile, hazardous, commercial kitchen, hazardous-storage and school lab areas. A city or county fire prevention code needs state Council approval and may not add provisions for Residential Code dwellings that the Residential Code does not prescriptively require, and a city may not require sprinklers in a Residential Code building as a condition of a no-impact home-based business.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: North Carolina does not require you to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, when it was last inspected or maintained, or that it has none (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched; every unit using the word sprinkler was screened). The only state sprinkler funding program found is a revolving loan fund run by the North Carolina Housing Finance Agency for adult care homes, group homes for developmentally disabled adults and nursing homes; it does not reach ordinary rental housing, and no session law offers private landlords sprinkler retrofit grants or loans. Whether a building needs sprinklers at all is covered in edu-fire-sprinkler-duty-nc.

title: Certificates of Occupancy
bodyText: North Carolina does not require you to give a tenant a copy of a certificate of occupancy, state in the lease that one exists, or post one, and no statute makes a lease void or rent uncollectible because a unit lacks one (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Certificates still matter before you rent: no new building, addition, or existing building that has been altered or moved under a building permit may be occupied until the inspection department issues a certificate of compliance (or a temporary certificate of occupancy for a stated period), and anyone who owns, leases or controls the building and occupies it or allows it to be occupied before then commits a Class 1 misdemeanor. A local government may not require you to enroll or participate in any governmental program as a condition of getting a certificate of occupancy for residential rental property.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Until January 15, 2027 North Carolina has no statewide accessory dwelling unit rule; whether you may build and rent one is up to local zoning.
