A 2026 law then requires each covered city to allow at least one accessory dwelling unit, built to the North Carolina Residential Code, for each single-family detached house in areas zoned for residential use that allow single-family houses; it applies to permit applications filed on or after January 15, 2027, only in cities of 50,000 or more people outside the coastal-area counties. Such a city may not prohibit the house and the accessory unit from being used for long-term rentals by separate households, require conditional zoning, set parking requirements, bar connection to the house's utilities where capacity allows, charge more than the fee for a similar single-family permit, or set a maximum unit size below 800 or above 1,000 square feet; it may require a setback of up to 10 feet (or the zone's general minimum if less), placement to the side or rear, and a unit smaller than the house, and the lot may not later be split so the unit sits on a different parcel. The law does not override private covenants or HOA restrictions on dwelling types, and does not apply in historic preservation districts, to National Historic Landmarks, or to a unit not connected to water (or well) and septic or sewer. It sets no minimum rental term, and it does not say whether a city may bar short-term rental of an accessory unit or require the owner to live on the lot, since only long-term rentals by separate households are protected; the cautious course is to treat short-term use and owner-occupancy rules as local, and check covenants before renting. Covered cities must adopt implementing regulations by July 1, 2027, or accessory units are allowed there without limitations; everywhere else, local zoning still governs and was not researched for this library (see edu-single-family-zone-lease-limit-nc and edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: No North Carolina statute limits renting a home in a single-family zone to owners who live on the lot, and there is no state lot-split or two-unit program with an owner-occupancy affidavit, a short-term rental bar or a tenant-displacement exclusion (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Zoning of residential areas is otherwise local, but state law limits it in two ways that matter to landlords: a city or county generally may not require a permit or registration to rent a home (see edu-landlord-registration-nc), and from January 15, 2027 a city of 50,000 or more outside the coastal-area counties must allow an accessory dwelling unit with each single-family detached house and may not prohibit the house and the unit from being rented long-term to separate households (see edu-accessory-dwelling-unit-nc). The accessory dwelling unit law does not affect private covenants or other agreements among owners restricting dwelling types (see hoa-compliance).

title: Size Thresholds for Landlord Duties
bodyText: North Carolina has no general small-landlord exemption and no duty tiered by how many units you own in total: the Residential Rental Agreements Act applies to every rental agreement for a dwelling unit, and the Tenant Security Deposit Act applies to everyone engaged in the business of renting or managing residential units (except single rooms) on a weekly, monthly or annual basis (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The size tests that do exist count the building, not your portfolio: the state fair housing act's main rental exemption needs both a building with housing for no more than four families and the owner or a family member living in one of them (both conditions, not either), and a room in a private house where the owner or family lives is also exempt, though discriminatory advertising is still barred in both cases. Foreclosure rules turn on 15 rental units: tenants in property with fewer than 15 get a notice-of-sale statement and an early-termination right, and occupants of property with 15 or more get 30 days' notice before an order for possession instead of 10. Accessibility design rules reach buildings of four or more units, and some rules count local population instead, such as the minimum-heat ordinance duty for local governments of 200,000 or more and the accessory dwelling unit rule for cities of 50,000 or more (see edu-accessory-dwelling-unit-nc).

title: No State Approval for Tribal or Communal Land Leases
bodyText: No North Carolina statute makes a residential lease wait for a government officer's approval because the land is communal, tribal or native-owned, and state law has no communal or family land tenure (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). If you own the land and rent a home on it, the lease needs no state approval. State law does recognize the trust lands of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians and the Catawba Indian Nation (for tribal police jurisdiction, and the Eastern Band counts as a local government for building inspections on land held in trust for it), but whether a lease of tribal trust land needs federal or tribal approval is a matter of federal and tribal law; the cautious course is to get that approval question answered before leasing such land.

title: No Special-District Statement
bodyText: North Carolina does not require you to tell a residential tenant, in the lease or otherwise, that the property lies in a municipal or county service district, sanitary district or other special district, or what that district taxes or assesses, and it gives residential tenants no vote or seat in such a district because of their tenancy (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The only tenant role found is in county research and production service districts, which must have an association of owners and tenants that includes at least 75% of the owners of nonresidential property there; it recommends on the district's affairs and votes on removing territory from it. Any district tax or assessment you pass through to a tenant is a matter for the lease and the fee rules (see edu-fees-as-rent-nc).

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: North Carolina has no rent-timing, late-fee or eviction protection for federal or state workers who go unpaid during a government shutdown (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The ordinary rules apply: rent is due as the lease says, late fees are limited as in late-fee-limit-nc, and eviction follows the summary ejectment process (see edu-eviction-process-nc). Servicemembers have separate protections (see edu-servicemember-rights-nc). Any payment plan for an affected tenant is a matter of agreement; local ordinances were not researched for this library (see edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: North Carolina has no truth-in-renting law: there is no state-published statement of landlord and tenant rights you must give tenants (see edu-tenant-rights-statement-nc), and no general rule that penalizes you for offering a lease with a term that violates a tenant's clearly established legal rights (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Instead, particular statutes strike particular terms. For example, a tenant's waiver of the retaliatory-eviction protections is void, a contract term waiving a jury trial is unenforceable, and the state early-termination rights of federal military technicians and of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking victims cannot be waived; any residential rental agreement provision contrary to the statutory rules on late fees, eviction fees and litigation costs is against public policy and unenforceable (see edu-late-and-eviction-fees-nc), and any lease provision contrary to the ban on self-help eviction is void as against public policy (see edu-self-help-eviction-nc). Unfair or deceptive practices in leasing may also be reached by the Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act, as far as the courts allow (see edu-consumer-protection-act-nc).

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule that the terms offered to a month-to-month tenant may not be more burdensome than those offered on a fixed-term lease (or the reverse), and no cap on how much more rent you may charge for one kind of tenancy than another (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The statutes treat tenancy types differently in two places: the security deposit may not exceed two weeks' rent for a week-to-week tenancy, one and one-half months' rent for month-to-month, and two months' rent for longer terms (see edu-security-deposit-rules-nc); and the notice to end a periodic tenancy is two days for week-to-week, seven days for month-to-month and one month for year-to-year (see edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-nc). Cities and counties may not regulate the amount of rent except for their own, subsidized or grant-assisted properties and owners that take local funding or incentives, so a local rent-parity rule could reach only those; other local rules were not researched for this library (see edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: Notice Before an Eviction for Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
North Carolina's statutes and the state rules searched for this library prescribe no form, wording or delivery method for a notice about unpaid rent, and none requires a state form to go with it (court rules, AOC forms and local ordinances were not read for this library).

If the lease fixes a definite time for paying rent and does not itself say that unpaid rent ends the tenancy, the law ends the term if the rent stays unpaid 10 days after you or your agent demand all past-due rent; if the lease does say so, no statutory waiting period applies, but in every case you must demand that the tenant give up possession before you file, and you may then remove the tenant only through the court (summary ejectment, see edu-eviction-process-nc).

Give both demands in writing on paper, because North Carolina's electronic-transactions law does not reach eviction or default notices under a lease of a primary residence (edu-electronic-notices-nc).

If the tenant pays or tenders the rent due and the court costs before judgment, the case stops, and North Carolina sets no limit on how often a tenant may do this. Unpaid water, sewer or electric charges you bill the tenant under the Utilities Commission's procedures for landlord utility billing can't be the basis for ending the lease. This library's default clause gives the tenant 10 days after a written demand in every case (default-by-tenant-nc); no statute lets a lease waive the demand for possession (edu-notice-to-quit-waiver-nc).

title: No Bar on Demanding Rent for a Unit With Violations
bodyText: No North Carolina statute bars you from demanding or collecting rent, or from serving a demand for past-due rent, while a unit has code violations or is unfit to live in (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Conditions still matter: under the Residential Rental Agreements Act the tenant's duty to pay rent and your duty to keep the unit fit depend on each other, so a tenant can raise unfit conditions against your claim for rent, although the tenant may not withhold rent on their own before a court decides. Once a local officer orders a dwelling vacated and closed and posts it as unfit, the rules in edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-nc apply, including the cautious course of not charging rent while that order stands. Local housing codes may say more and were not researched for this library (edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: Eviction Grounds and Cure Periods
bodyText:
North Carolina has one statutory notice-and-cure track and three grounds for summary ejectment. The grounds are: the tenant stays after the term has ended; the tenant has done or failed to do something that, under the terms of the lease, ends the tenancy; or a tenant behind on rent deserts the premises and leaves them unoccupied; and every case needs a demand that the tenant give up possession first.

Apart from lease-option contracts (below), the only cure period the statutes set is for unpaid rent where the lease fixes a definite time for paying rent and does not itself make nonpayment end the tenancy: the term is forfeited if the rent stays unpaid 10 days after you demand all past-due rent, and a tenant who pays or tenders the rent and court costs before judgment stops the case (see edu-nonpayment-notice-nc).

For any other breach North Carolina sets no cure period or notice form (though you must notify the tenant in writing of a breach of the statutory upkeep duties, such as keeping the unit clean and safe and not damaging it, except in emergencies), so whether a breach ends the tenancy depends on what the lease says; the statute does not say the breached term must be material, and whether a court will refuse to enforce a forfeiture for a trivial breach is case law.

Cautious course: say in the lease which breaches end the tenancy and give written notice and a chance to cure before filing, as this library's default clause does (default-by-tenant-nc); drug and other criminal activity can instead go through the expedited procedure with no cure (edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-nc).

Unpaid water, sewer or electric charges you bill under the Utilities Commission's procedures for landlord utility billing are never a ground, and where a lease is combined with an option to buy a one-to-four-family home the tenant will live in as a principal dwelling, the tenant's option rights can't be forfeited without a statutory notice and chance to cure, which this library does not cover.

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction
bodyText:
North Carolina gives a tenant facing eviction for unpaid rent one statutory chance to keep the tenancy: if the tenant pays or tenders the rent due and the court costs at any time before judgment, the case stops (and if you press on and the tenant pays the amount found due and the costs into court, you pay the later costs).

There is no right to redeem after judgment, before the writ is carried out, and no rule that paying a money judgment bars the eviction; but you may choose to stop it, by signing a statement for the sheriff that the tenant has paid all court costs and satisfied what is owed, and the writ then goes back unexecuted.

If you take rent after judgment, be careful: to enforce a judgment for possession more than 30 days old you must swear that you have neither made a new lease with the tenant nor accepted rent for any period after the judgment.

No statute prescribes wording for accepting a partial payment; instead, for an eviction based on a breach for which the lease reserves the right to re-enter, the lease itself may say that accepting partial rent or a partial housing subsidy payment does not waive the breach (partial-payment-nonwaiver-nc). No statute makes you accept payment from a charity, government program or other third party, or limits the payment methods you may require for it. See edu-nonpayment-notice-nc for the 10-day demand and edu-forfeiture-redemption-nc.

title: Saving a Tenancy Forfeited for Rent
bodyText: In North Carolina a tenancy forfeited for unpaid rent can be saved in two statutory ways, both before judgment. Where the lease fixes a definite time for paying rent and does not itself make nonpayment end the tenancy, the term is forfeited if the rent stays unpaid 10 days after you demand all past-due rent, so paying within those 10 days avoids the forfeiture; and in any eviction for unpaid rent, a tenant who pays or tenders the rent due and the court costs before judgment stops the case. No statute lets a tenant undo the forfeiture after judgment, makes you accept late rent after the 10 days have run, or lets a court relieve a tenant from forfeiture on equitable grounds; whether a court may still do so is case law. Forfeiture for a breach other than rent depends on the lease (edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-nc). Details, including what to do if you accept rent after judgment: edu-redemption-nc.

title: Landlord's Remedies When a Tenancy Ends
bodyText: When a tenancy ends for default, a North Carolina landlord can seek possession and money together or separately. Possession goes through summary ejectment, usually before a magistrate in small claims court, and in the same complaint you may claim back rent and damages for the tenant's occupation after the tenancy ended, up to the small-claims limit of $10,000; if you leave the money claim out, you can still sue for it later. If the tenant was served only by mail and posting, you may ask the magistrate to split off the money claim and decide possession alone. Money alone can be sued for in an ordinary civil action: small claims for up to $10,000 if you ask for assignment to a magistrate, district court up to $25,000, and superior court above that. The security deposit may be applied to unpaid rent, damage, losses from the tenant not completing the rental period (except after an early termination under North Carolina's statutes for military technicians or for victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or a move-out caused by an unlawful removal or by unfit premises), re-renting costs, post-eviction removal and storage, court costs and the fees the fee statute allows (edu-security-deposit-rules-nc), and eviction fees and attorneys' fees are limited to what that statute allows (eviction-fees-nc). No North Carolina statute addresses accelerating the rest of the term's rent on default; whether a lease acceleration term is enforceable is case law, so the library offers none (see edu-abandonment-and-mitigation-nc).

title: Tenant Moves Out Early: Rent and Re-Renting
bodyText:
No North Carolina statute says what happens to the rest of the term when a tenant moves out early: none ends the lease on abandonment, keeps the tenant liable for the remaining rent, or requires you to mitigate by re-renting. Those questions are case law.

The statutes touch the subject in three places: a tenant who is behind on rent and deserts the premises, leaving them unoccupied, can be removed by summary ejectment; personal property counts as abandoned if you find evidence that clearly shows the tenant voluntarily left after the paid rental period ended and you have no notice of a disability that caused the vacancy (with a presumption 10 or more days after you post a notice of suspected abandonment inside and outside without response), but only for the rule letting you give belongings worth $750 or less to a charity (edu-abandoned-property-nc); and the security deposit may cover losses from the tenant not completing the rental period and the cost of re-renting, including a broker's reasonable fee.

Cautious course: assume a court may expect you to try to re-rent, make and document reasonable efforts to do so, credit rent from a new tenant against what the old tenant owes, and recover only your actual loss; this library's default clause promises reasonable mitigation efforts to the extent the law requires (default-by-tenant-nc). A tenant ending the lease under a statutory early-termination right owes only what that statute allows (edu-statutory-early-termination-nc).

title: Statutory Rights to End a Lease Early
bodyText:
North Carolina gives tenants these statutory rights to end a lease early; the military, servicemember and domestic-violence rights can't be waived.

Military: a military technician may end the lease by written notice with orders or a commanding officer's verification, effective at least 30 days after you receive it, after permanent change-of-station orders to move 50 miles or more or an early discharge; on deployment with a military unit for 90 days or more, by the same kind of notice, effective 30 days after the next rent due date or 45 days after you receive the notice, whichever is shorter; and immediate family or the estate may end it if the technician dies on active duty; the technician owes prorated rent plus limited liquidated damages, and other servicemembers rely on the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which North Carolina's own Servicemembers Civil Relief Act applies, to the extent military service materially affects the servicemember's ability to meet the lease's obligations, and extends (edu-servicemember-rights-nc).

Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may end it on 30 days' written notice with the required documents, owing only prorated rent (edu-dv-lease-termination-nc).

In a property with fewer than 15 rental units being sold in a power-of-sale foreclosure, a tenant who receives the notice of sale may end it by written notice effective 10 to 90 days after the sale date, unless the owner has cured the default by the time the tenant gives notice, owing only prorated rent (edu-foreclosure-tenant-rights-nc).

A tenant may also surrender when the home is destroyed or so damaged it can't be made reasonably fit for less than a year's rent without the tenant's fault, if the home was the main reason for the rental and the lease neither addresses repairs nor provides for the case, by a writing delivered within 10 days of the damage and by paying the rent in arrears and the prorated rent then due (casualty-termination-nc), and may end the lease if you remove or try to remove the tenant outside the court process.

You may not apply the deposit to early-termination losses after a termination under the military-technician or domestic-violence statutes above, or after a move-out caused by an unlawful removal or unfit premises; North Carolina has no statutory termination for a landlord's fraudulent misrepresentation and no rule forfeiting accrued rent for leaving a prescribed statement out of the lease, and a tenant's ordinary early-termination option is a lease term (early-termination-ks).

title: Belongings and Re-Entry After an Eviction
bodyText: After a North Carolina eviction judgment, the sheriff must carry out the writ within five days of receiving it, after notice to the tenant of the approximate time; except where the lease is of a space for a manufactured home, the notice must warn that property not claimed within seven days may be thrown away, disposed of or sold, and is given in person or at the home at least two days ahead or by first-class mail at least five days ahead. If the tenant doesn't take the belongings, the sheriff may store them in a storage warehouse in the county (or in an adjoining county if the county has none) and may make you advance the moving cost and one month's storage, and if you refuse the sheriff returns the writ unexecuted; alternatively you may tell the sheriff in writing that the belongings can stay and have the unit simply locked. For seven days after you are put in possession you may move the belongings for storage but may not throw away or sell them, and must release them on the tenant's request; after that you may dispose of or sell them under the notice and surplus rules in edu-abandoned-property-nc, and if everything left is worth less than $500 it is abandoned after five days. The sheriff is liable only for willful or wanton negligence in storing property; no statute gives a landlord its own immunity for the eviction, and no North Carolina statute sets a separate post-eviction rule for animals left behind, though anyone who has charge or custody of an animal and willfully and without justifiable excuse abandons it commits a misdemeanor (local animal-control ordinances were not researched for this library). A person who, after being removed under a writ, goes back without authorization into the building, or onto premises enclosed or secured to keep out intruders, commits first-degree trespass as a Class I felony with a fine of at least $1,000.

title: Trespass Notices to Non-Tenants
bodyText:
North Carolina's trespass law lets you, as owner or person in charge of the property, tell someone who is not your tenant not to enter or stay; a person who then enters or remains without authorization commits second-degree trespass (a Class 3 misdemeanor), as does a person who enters premises posted against entry in a way likely to be noticed, and entering or staying without authorization in a building of another, or on premises enclosed or secured to keep intruders out, is first-degree trespass (a Class 2 misdemeanor).

The statute requires no written form and lists no defenses, but it lets a lawful occupant give or refuse permission too, and it doesn't say whether a tenant can authorize a guest you have barred to visit the tenant's unit or use the common areas; that is case law.

Cautious course: give the barred person a written no-trespass notice that names the property and the areas covered, call the police for refusals in areas you control, and rely on the lease covenant barred-person-covenant-ne (the tenant agrees not to admit a person you have barred in writing for dangerous or damaging conduct) rather than trying to bar guests from the tenant's own unit. Apply any ban list consistently, since fair housing rules apply (edu-fair-housing-nc).

Going back onto the property after removal under a writ for possession is a felony (edu-post-eviction-property-nc), and people who never rented or paid rent can be removed under the 2025 procedure in edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-nc.

title: Ending a Lease for Owner Move-In
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute that gives a landlord a right to end a lease early so that the owner or a relative can move in, and none that sets a notice period, minimum ownership or occupancy period, or relocation payment for doing so. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy ends on the ordinary notice anyway (edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-nc), but a fixed-term lease that is silent binds you to the full term; the right exists only if the lease reserves it, as the library's optional owner-occupancy-termination-ar clause does (you name who will move in and choose a notice of at least 30 days ending on the last day of a monthly rental period).

One statute bears on it: a tenant who has made a repair request, code complaint or other protected move in the 12 months before you file may defend the eviction as retaliatory, and you still win if you seek in good faith to recover possession at the end of the tenant's term to live there yourself; that protection names the landlord's own home, not a relative's, and speaks of the end of the term, so whether it covers an early termination for a family member is case law (edu-retaliation-nc).

If the tenant doesn't leave by the termination date, you may remove the tenant only through summary ejectment.

title: Who Can Appear in Court for an Entity Landlord
bodyText: In a North Carolina summary ejectment or past-due rent case, the complaint may be signed by an agent for the landlord, such as a property manager, who has actual knowledge of the facts it alleges, and no party in small claims court, or in the district court appeal for a new trial, is required to have a lawyer. What the statutes don't say is whether a corporation or LLC landlord may present its case at the hearing through a non-lawyer officer, member, employee or manager: the law bars anyone but a licensed lawyer from appearing for another person in court, and bars a corporation from appearing as an attorney for anyone, and how those rules apply to an entity's own employee is case law and court-rule territory this library has not reviewed. Cautious course: have an agent with personal knowledge sign the complaint and attend as a witness, and use a licensed North Carolina attorney to present the case for an entity, at least on any appeal. An out-of-state corporation or LLC that transacts business in North Carolina without a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State can't maintain a lawsuit here until it gets one before trial, and owes back fees and a civil penalty of up to $1,000 a year; merely owning real property isn't transacting business, but whether renting homes is depends on the facts, so obtain the certificate before you file. If you rent under an assumed business name, file the assumed business name certificate with the register of deeds first; failing to file doesn't bar a suit, but you are liable to anyone harmed for the reasonable cost, including attorneys' fees, of finding out who you are.

title: Serving Eviction Papers
bodyText: In a North Carolina summary ejectment, the court papers are usually served by the sheriff's officer under the eviction service statute: the officer mails a copy to the tenant's last known address in a stamped envelope you provide, may phone the tenant to arrange service, and otherwise visits the home at least once (at least two days before the hearing) to hand the papers to the tenant or leave them with a resident of suitable age, posting them on the premises if that fails. Small claims law also allows service by registered or certified mail, signature confirmation or a designated delivery service, or by the tenant's written acceptance of service or voluntary appearance. The small-claims and eviction service statutes say nothing about an agent the tenant appoints in the lease to accept court papers, so the library offers no such clause; the lease's notice address (notices) is simply where you send notices and the most useful last known address to give the officer. A tenant enrolled in North Carolina's Address Confidentiality Program has the Attorney General as agent for service of process at a substitute address, and if a paper is served by mail through the program, five days are added to any response period of 10 days or less. If the tenant was served only by mail and posting, you may still get possession but may have to sever the money claim (edu-landlord-remedies-termination-nc).

title: No Hardship Delay of an Eviction
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule letting a court postpone an eviction because of the tenant's hardship, such as illness, age, children, weather or inability to find other housing (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). What does affect timing: the magistrate decides a motion to continue the hearing under the general civil rule, which allows a continuance only for good cause shown (whether a tenant's illness or other hardship is good cause is for the magistrate, and this library has not reviewed the case law), and may not continue a summary ejectment hearing for more than five days, or to the next small-claims session if later, without both sides' consent; the tenant has 10 days to appeal; the eviction is stayed during an appeal only if the tenant pays the undisputed back rent to the clerk (an indigent tenant need not) and keeps paying rent into court as it comes due, and missing a payment by five business days ends the stay; and the sheriff must carry out the writ within five days of receiving it. A servicemember whose ability to take part in the case is materially affected by military service is entitled to a stay on request, during service and for 60 days after (edu-servicemember-rights-nc). Courts' general powers and local practice were not researched for this library; see edu-eviction-process-nc.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacancy Notice Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in cold weather, and no freezing-pipes or heating-season rule for tenants (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The general tenant duties still apply: the tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises and is responsible for damage inside the unit under the tenant's exclusive control, except ordinary wear and tear, your own acts, defective products or repairs you authorized, acts of non-invitees, or natural forces (edu-tenant-caused-damage-nc). The tenant must also comply with any obligations the applicable building and housing codes place on tenants; local housing codes may include cold-weather or heating duties and were not researched for this library (edu-local-preemption-nc). If you want notice before a long absence, see the library's extended-absence guidance (edu-extended-absence-notice-nc).

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Notice
bodyText: North Carolina has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law for private rentals, so there is no notice telling tenants whether such a law covers them, and nothing to put in the lease about it (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). A fixed term ends on its last day and a periodic tenancy ends on the statutory notice, with no reason required, subject to the retaliation, domestic-violence and condominium-conversion limits described in edu-no-for-cause-eviction-nc. North Carolina's housing-authority statute lets a public housing authority end or refuse to renew a rental agreement for a serious or repeated violation of a material term, such as nonpayment, breach of federal tenant obligations or other good cause, and public housing and other federally assisted tenancies carry federal rules this library does not state here.

title: During a Notice to Vacate
bodyText: North Carolina has no general rule limiting what you may do to the unit or the tenancy while a notice to vacate is running, such as a ban on alterations that make the unit unlivable (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The tenancy and the lease stay in force until the notice period ends, so your duties continue: you must keep the unit fit and may not cut off utilities, lock the tenant out or otherwise force the tenant out before then (edu-landlord-repair-duties-nc, edu-self-help-eviction-nc), and a notice to quit given after a tenant's repair request or complaint can be challenged as retaliatory (edu-retaliation-nc). One specific rule applies in a condominium conversion: tenants must get at least 90 days' notice, may not be required to leave sooner except for nonpayment, waste, disturbing other tenants or another breach allowing repossession, and the terms of the tenancy may not be changed during that period (edu-condo-conversion-notice-nc).

title: No Possession Bond
bodyText: North Carolina has no end-of-term possession bond, no bond with a confessed judgment for possession, and no other bond a tenant must post to keep or give up a home, apart from court-procedure bonds (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The bonds that exist are these: a tenant who appeals an eviction stays it by paying the undisputed back rent to the clerk (unless indigent) and signing an undertaking to pay rent into court as it comes due, with no other appeal security required; the statutory form for that undertaking is in the eviction statute; and a person removed under the 2025 unauthorized-occupant procedure must post a bond of at least $10,000 to appeal (edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-nc). A confession of judgment needs a separate signed and sworn statement filed with the clerk and covers money, not possession, so don't put a confession of judgment or warrant of attorney in a residential lease (edu-confession-of-judgment-nc).

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule giving a tenant a defense, continuance or reinstatement in an eviction because a Social Security check, other government benefit or a housing voucher payment arrived late (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). The ordinary rules apply: the 10-day demand where the lease fixes a definite time for paying rent and has no forfeiture term, and the tenant's right to stop a nonpayment case by paying the rent and costs before judgment (edu-nonpayment-notice-nc). Subsidies do change three things: where the rent is subsidized by HUD, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, a State agency, a public housing authority or a local government, late fees and other fee-statute charges are figured on the tenant's share of the rent only; to stay an eviction on appeal the tenant pays the tenant's share of the contract rent into court; and the lease may say that accepting a partial subsidy payment does not waive the breach (partial-payment-nonwaiver-nc). Federal program rules for voucher and other assisted tenancies, including whether you may evict for the agency's unpaid share, are not stated here.

title: Tenant's Bankruptcy
bodyText: Bankruptcy is federal law, and North Carolina law adds nothing specific: no North Carolina statute addresses a residential tenant's bankruptcy, a lease clause making bankruptcy a default, collecting rent from a bankrupt tenant, or whether a writ of possession may be carried out after you learn of a bankruptcy filing (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). Federal bankruptcy law controls what you may do once a tenant files, and no library row covering North Carolina states it yet. Cautious course: once you learn a tenant has filed, stop eviction and collection steps and get advice on federal bankruptcy law before filing, continuing a case or asking the sheriff to carry out a writ.

title: Tenancy at Will
bodyText: North Carolina's statutes don't use the term tenancy at will or say how one is created or ended, and set no notice period for it (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). What they do say: when someone occupies your land with your permission but without an express agreement on rent, or under an oral lease that is void, you may recover reasonable compensation for the occupation, and any rent the oral lease named is evidence of its value; periodic tenancies end on statutory notice (seven days before the end of a month-to-month period, two days for week to week, one month before the end of the year for year to year; edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-nc); and a tenant who stays after the tenancy ends can be removed only by summary ejectment after a demand for possession. Whether an informal arrangement is a tenancy at will, a periodic tenancy measured by the rent period, or something else, and what notice ends it, is case law. Cautious course: put the arrangement in a written lease that states the term or the rent period, and before filing give at least the notice the statute sets for the matching periodic tenancy. A person who has paid you rent is not an unauthorized occupant under the 2025 squatter procedure (edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-nc).

title: No Early Termination for Illness or Care Needs
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule letting a residential tenant end a lease early because of age, illness, disability or incapacity, or because the tenant must move to a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility, and no rule that a tenancy ends when a party becomes unable to contract (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules searched). So unless the lease gives that right, such a tenant is treated like any other tenant leaving a fixed term early (edu-abandonment-and-mitigation-nc), and a month-to-month tenant can end the tenancy on the ordinary notice (edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-nc). A request from a tenant with a disability to be released early or on shorter notice may be a request for a reasonable accommodation under fair housing law; consider it on its facts (edu-disability-accommodation-nc). If a lease whose rent falls due at the end of each rent period ends because of a death partway through a period, you may recover the rent apportioned to the date of death, subject to just allowances (edu-tenant-death-nc). A prior occupant's serious illness or death in the unit is not a material fact you must disclose, though you may not knowingly misstate it (edu-stigmatized-property-nc).

title: Minors as Tenants and Eviction Defendants
bodyText: In North Carolina a person becomes an adult at 18, so anyone 18 or older can sign a lease in his or her own name; there is no higher age of majority and no special rule for 18-to-20-year-olds. No statute addresses leasing to someone under 18, and the statutes assume a minor's contract can be disaffirmed on reaching 18; a minor emancipated by court decree can contract and sue and be sued as an adult. Cautious course: don't make an unemancipated minor a tenant on the lease; have a parent or other adult sign as tenant (or guarantor) and list the minor as an occupant. No statute bars naming a minor in an eviction, and the expedited criminal-activity procedure expressly lets you sue an adult or minor member of the tenant's household (edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-nc); but a minor defendant must defend through a guardian or a court-appointed guardian ad litem, and in small claims a minor can be served only in person, with separate service on a parent, guardian or other person having care of the child.

title: Deadlines for Suing Over Rent and Damage
bodyText: In North Carolina a suit on a contract, including a landlord's claim for unpaid rent or for damage the lease makes the tenant liable for, must generally be brought within three years after it accrues, as must a claim on a liability created by statute unless the statute sets another period, a claim for taking or injuring personal property, and a claim for trespass to real property. A sealed instrument, or an instrument conveying an interest in real property, gets ten years against the principal; whether a residential lease counts as one is case law, so the cautious course is to sue within three years. An acknowledgment or new promise restarts the period only if it is in a writing signed by the person to be charged, though the statute leaves the effect of a payment to the general law; and when there is more than one tenant or a guarantor, an act or acknowledgment by one that restarts the period does so only against that one, not against others who did not authorize or ratify it. Actions for a statutory penalty or forfeiture given to the aggrieved party have one year, unless the statute imposing it sets a different period. No statute addresses a residential lease that shortens or lengthens these periods (the goods-sale and goods-lease rules that allow shortening don't reach leases of homes); whether such a lease term is enforceable is case law, so the library offers no such clause.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: North Carolina's general automatic-renewal statute applies to any person in commerce who sells or leases products or services to a consumer under a contract that renews automatically unless the consumer cancels; whether a residential lease of a home is a lease of products or services is case law, so treat an automatic-renewal clause in a lease as covered. If it is covered, you must disclose the renewal clause clearly and conspicuously in the lease, disclose clearly and conspicuously how to cancel, and, for a renewal period longer than 60 days, send written notice by personal delivery, email or first-class mail at least 15 but no more than 45 days before the renewal date, stating that date and that the lease will renew unless the tenant cancels before it; any terms that will change on renewal must appear on that notice in at least 12-point bold type. A clause that doesn't comply is void and unenforceable, unless the failure was an error despite written compliance procedures and you refund or credit what was billed after the renewal. Without a renewal clause a fixed-term lease simply ends; no statute renews it or turns a holdover into a new term, and no statute limits how early you may ask a tenant to commit to a renewal (see holdover-ca and holdover-rate-nc). The library offers no automatic-renewal clause.

title: Heat
bodyText: A North Carolina landlord must keep the heating facilities it supplies, or is required to supply, in good and safe working order and repair them promptly after the tenant's written repair request (no written request is needed in an emergency). From November 1 through March 31, lacking working heat able to warm the living areas to 65 degrees when it is 20 degrees outside is an imminently dangerous condition, which you must fix within a reasonable time based on its severity once you know of it or are told. Cities and counties of 200,000 or more people must also require by ordinance that every rental unit can heat at least one habitable room other than the kitchen to 68 degrees, with the owner keeping that heat source in good and safe working order; portable kerosene heaters do not count as the permanent source, and those local governments may set stricter rules. The statute has no exception letting the lease move the heat duty to the tenant, even for equipment the tenant controls or pays to run; a lease may make the tenant pay the gas or electric bill, but your repair and fitness duties stay with you.

title: Shifting Repair Duties to the Tenant
bodyText:
A North Carolina lease cannot move any of the landlord's fitness duties to the tenant: code compliance, fitness and habitability, safe common areas, repair of supplied facilities and appliances, alarms and imminently dangerous conditions stay with you whatever the lease says (the one lease-variable detail is that a written agreement may change who puts new batteries in battery-operated smoke and carbon monoxide alarms at the start of the tenancy and who replaces them during it; edu-habitability-modifiable-nc), and a tenant's acceptance of your failure to meet them does not release you.

The one route is a subsequent written contract (the statute does not say subsequent to what; the cautious course this library takes is a contract made after the lease is signed) in which the tenant agrees to do specified work for adequate consideration other than the right to rent the home, and which is not made to get around your duties; a conspicuous lease term or a rent concession written into the lease is not that route.

This rule covers every dwelling unit under the Residential Rental Agreements Act, not only single-family homes, and it has no special list of conditions (such as common-area garbage) that may be shifted.

Separately, the lease may restate the tenant's own statutory duties, such as keeping the part of the premises the tenant uses clean and safe, and may spell out routine care of the areas the tenant alone uses as part of those duties; repairs needed to keep the premises fit stay with you. Use the library's separate tenant-work agreement for anything more.

title: Repair Requests and Notice
bodyText: North Carolina ties different repair duties to different kinds of notice. Your duty to repair supplied electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances runs from the tenant's written repair request, except in an emergency; smoke and carbon monoxide alarms must be repaired or replaced within 15 days of the tenant's written notice, and failing to act within 30 days of written notice from the tenant or a government agent is an infraction. Imminently dangerous conditions (such as unsafe wiring, no water, no heat in winter or broken exterior locks) must be fixed within a reasonable time once you actually know of them or receive notice of any kind, and your general duty to keep the home fit, safe and up to code has no notice condition in the statute at all. A lease may ask tenants to put repair requests in writing, but it cannot make written notice a condition of those other duties, and a tenant's good-faith complaint or repair request, written or not, is protected against retaliatory eviction (a waiver of that protection is void). Whether a lease that invites phone or verbal requests gives up the written-notice condition is case law; the cautious course is to treat every request you actually receive as notice.

title: Casualty and Re-Renting Rules a Lease May Change
bodyText:
North Carolina's casualty statutes are default rules that the lease may replace. Without a lease term on the subject, a tenant may give up the lease if the building is destroyed, or damaged so badly that making it reasonably fit would cost more than a year's rent, without the tenant's negligence, where use of that building was the main reason for renting; the tenant must deliver a written surrender within 10 days and pay rent owed to the date of the damage, and then owes no later rent.

That rule does not apply if the lease shows a contrary intention or deals with repairs or such a case, a lease promise to repair does not bind a party to rebuild or repair after an accidental fire, not caused by that party's lack of ordinary diligence, destroys or damages more than half the building's value, and a tenant is not liable for accidental damage despite reasonable care unless the lease says so.

What a casualty clause cannot do is release you from your fitness and repair duties, which no lease term or tenant acceptance waives; how a court squares those duties with a destroyed building is case law.

No North Carolina statute requires you to re-rent after a tenant leaves early or says whether a lease may waive that common-law question; the deposit may cover reasonable re-renting costs after the tenant's breach, and the library offers no clause waiving re-renting efforts.

title: No Landlord Exit When Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No North Carolina statute lets you end a tenancy, or skip a repair, because the repair would cost too much; your fitness and repair duties apply whatever the cost, and a tenant's acceptance of defects does not release you unless a government body blocks the repair for a set period of no more than six months (a later written contract, supported by consideration other than the rental itself, for the tenant to do specified work is allowed if not made to evade your duties). The landlord-tenant statutes have two cost thresholds. Where the lease does not deal with repairs or the case, a tenant whose building is destroyed or damaged so that making it reasonably fit would cost more than one year's rent, without the tenant's negligence, and whose use of that building was the main reason for renting, may surrender the lease in writing within 10 days, paying the rent then owed, and owe no later rent. And a lease promise to repair does not bind the promising party to rebuild or repair after an accidental fire, not caused by that party's lack of ordinary diligence, destroys or damages more than half the building's value; that rule construes a lease promise and does not end the tenancy or your statutory duties (edu-casualty-and-mitigation-waivable-nc). Cost also matters where a city or county has adopted a minimum housing ordinance under the state enabling law: after a hearing finding a dwelling unfit, its public officer orders it repaired if that can be done at a reasonable cost in relation to its value and otherwise order it removed or demolished (or, for a dwelling of particular significance in a historic district, vacated and closed), and an eviction is not treated as retaliatory where code compliance requires demolition or major work that cannot be done without displacing the household. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy can still be ended by the usual notice.

title: No Statutory Exit for Environmental Events
bodyText: No North Carolina statute gives you or a tenant a right to end a residential lease because of an environmental event such as contamination, a chemical spill or mold, and none sets up an opt-in termination right a lease can choose. The general rules apply instead: excessive standing water, sewage or flooding from plumbing leaks or poor drainage that contributes to mosquitoes or mold is an imminently dangerous condition you must fix within a reasonable time, based on its severity, after you learn of it or are notified, your fitness and code duties cannot be waived, and a tenant whose building is destroyed or made unfit beyond a year's rent to repair, without the tenant's negligence, may surrender the lease if use of the building was the main reason for renting and the lease neither addresses repairs nor provides for the case, by a writing delivered within 10 days of the damage and by paying the rent then owed. The library's fire and other casualty clause is the lease term for damage that makes the home unfit; the library offers no separate clause letting you end the lease for an environmental event, because ending a tenancy in place of a repair you owe may be treated as evading the fitness duties, which is case law. A periodic tenancy can still be ended by the usual notice, and removing a tenant still requires the court eviction process.

title: Tenancies After a Declared Disaster
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute that ends a tenancy, suspends rent or sets special landlord duties when a declared disaster makes a rental unusable or unreachable. The ordinary rules govern: your fitness and repair duties continue, the tenant may, on the casualty statute's conditions (no fault of the tenant, repair costing more than a year's rent, the building the main reason for renting, written surrender within 10 days with the rent then owed), surrender a destroyed or badly damaged building unless the lease addresses repairs or the case or otherwise provides (the library's fire and casualty clause does), and removing a tenant still takes the court eviction process. During a declared state of emergency the Governor, with the Council of State's agreement, may order evacuations, control the occupancy of premises and set economic controls covering shelter and rents, and breaking such an order is a misdemeanor. The emergency price-gouging statute bars anyone, in the declared area during the emergency period, from renting goods or services used as a direct result of the emergency or to preserve life, health, safety or economic well-being, with the knowledge and intent to charge a price that is unreasonably excessive under the circumstances; it does not say whether a lease of a home is a rental of goods or services, so the cautious course is not to raise rents sharply in a declared area during that period.

title: No Disaster-Guest Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute letting a tenant house people displaced by a fire, storm, flood or declared disaster in spite of the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none written for what you may charge or require while such guests stay, though during a declared emergency the price-gouging statute may reach an unreasonably excessive charge (whether it reaches a residential lease is case law; edu-disaster-duties-nc). The lease's guest and occupancy terms therefore govern, subject to any local occupancy or housing code and to any executive order issued during a declared state of emergency, which can control the occupancy of premises in the emergency area.

title: No Duty to Rehouse Tenants
bodyText: North Carolina's landlord-tenant statutes do not make you house a tenant elsewhere, or pay moving or hotel costs, while repairs are made or after a fire or other casualty, whether or not the tenant asks. Where a local housing official finds a dwelling unfit, the order may require it to be vacated only if staying during the repair period would present a significant threat of bodily harm, and the local government must give a tenant at least 30 days' notice before using the summary court action to remove them after the governing board orders the dwelling closed or demolished. Relocation payments for people displaced by a government acquisition or project are owed by the government agency, not by the landlord. One housing regime does carry a rehousing duty: under the Migrant Housing Act, where the Department of Labor finds housing provided to migrants uninhabitable, the migrants must be allowed to stay for a reasonable period of up to 14 days while the operator either repairs the housing or locates alternative housing, but the operator must provide alternative housing at once if the housing could reasonably be expected to cause death or serious physical harm, and any alternative housing must be at the same or a lower rate.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: North Carolina's statutes create no presumption in habitability disputes: none presumes that you breached your fitness duties because the unit violates a code or lacks a facility, that you took too long to repair, that you had notice of a defect, or what a defective unit was worth. A tenant who claims a breach, by suing or as a defense or counterclaim in your eviction case, proves it in the ordinary way, and the tenant may not withhold rent before a court rules. Two statutory rules still frame the proof: your duty to fix an imminently dangerous condition runs from your actual knowledge or any notice, and a violation of the fitness statute is not negligence per se. The only presumption in the eviction-related statutes concerns abandoned property, not habitability. Court decisions were not searched, so do not assume a court will never shift the burden on particular facts.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in the Lease
bodyText: North Carolina does not require your lease to say that the unit is or will be fit to live in, and prescribes no habitability wording. The duty exists without it: by statute you must comply with building and housing codes, make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas safe, keep supplied facilities and appliances in repair, provide alarms and fix imminently dangerous conditions, and the lease cannot take those duties away. The library's maintenance clause states your repair commitment in general terms, and the move-in condition acknowledgment is evidence of condition only; neither is a substitute for meeting the statute.

title: No Form Rule for Promises to Repair
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be given before the lease is signed. Your statutory fitness and repair duties apply whether or not you promise anything, and no promise or tenant acceptance reduces them. Whether a particular promise outside the lease binds you, or is displaced by the lease's entire-agreement clause, is ordinary contract law this library has not reviewed.

title: Who Makes Repairs
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute that lets, or forbids, a lease naming who must make repairs or requiring tenants to use your repairer, and none gives tenants a right to make repairs themselves and deduct the cost from rent, so there is no statutory self-repair remedy for a lease to channel. Repairs are your duty, and a tenant takes on repair work only through a subsequent written contract for specified work, supported by adequate consideration other than the tenancy itself and not made with the purpose or effect of evading your duties (tenant-repair-agreement-nc). You may recover from the tenant the actual and reasonable cost of repairing an imminently dangerous condition the tenant caused. You or your employee may do lock work on your own rental property without a locksmith license, as long as you do not hold yourselves out as locksmiths, and a domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking victim may change the locks without your permission if you do not act in time.

title: No Rent Escrow, So No Exemption Notice
bodyText: North Carolina has no rent-escrow remedy for repairs, so it has no small-landlord or owner-occupant exemption from one and no exemption notice to give; do not put one in the lease. A tenant may not withhold rent on their own before a court decides they may, and the tenant's repair remedies run through a court action, counterclaim or defense. The only rent a tenant pays to the clerk of court is rent paid to stay an eviction judgment on appeal or tendered in the eviction case, which has nothing to do with repairs. The Residential Rental Agreements Act applies to every residential rental agreement for a dwelling unit except vacation rentals and free housing, with no exemption based on how many units you own.

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText: North Carolina sets the temperature at the source, not at each tenancy: the thermostat of any new residential water heater offered for sale or lease for a single-family or multifamily dwelling must be preset by the manufacturer or installer no higher than about 120 degrees Fahrenheit (higher only where it supplies space heaters that need it), and every residential water heater must carry a tag or sticker at the thermostat warning that higher settings may cause severe burns. No statute requires you to reset a water heater before each new tenant moves in. An occupant with an individual water heater may reset the thermostat, and if that happens in a rented unit, the owner, like the manufacturer and installer, is relieved of liability for damages attributed to the resetting. Tank water heaters of 120 gallons or less must have an approved pressure-temperature relief valve, and local ordinances may add other safety-feature rules.

title: No Radiator-Cover Rule
bodyText: No North Carolina statute, and none of the state agency rules held for this library, requires radiator covers or guards, on request or otherwise, or a lease rider about them; the word radiator appears nowhere in the statutes, session laws, constitution or agency rules held for this library. Your general duties still apply: keep supplied heating facilities in good and safe working order, keep the premises fit and habitable, and comply with the building and housing codes, which may say more about heating equipment. Steam boilers in apartment houses of six or more families are also subject to the State's boiler safety law, while boilers in private residences and smaller apartment houses are exempt from it.

title: No Window-Guard Rule
bodyText: No North Carolina statute, and none of the state agency rules held for this library, requires window guards, window stops or other fall-prevention devices in rentals where children live, no duty to offer them on request, and no window-guard lease notice; it also has no statute on burglar or security bars, their release mechanisms or a disclosure about them. What the fitness statute does cover is windows as security: broken windows, and the lack of operable locks on all ground-level windows, are imminently dangerous conditions you must fix within a reasonable time, based on their severity, once you know of them or receive notice.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: No North Carolina statute, and none of the state agency rules held for this library, requires periodic engineering inspections of balconies, decks, porches, railings or other exterior elevated elements at rental properties, and no report or repair deadline tied to such an inspection. Your general duties cover them: keep common areas safe, keep the premises fit and habitable, comply with the building and housing codes, and fix unsafe flooring or steps within a reasonable time, based on their severity, once you know of them or receive notice, since those are imminently dangerous conditions. Local inspectors may inspect rental buildings only when there is reasonable cause, such as a complaint or a visible violation, or in a designated blighted area, though periodic inspections under the State fire prevention code, or otherwise required by State law, are not limited that way.

title: Locks and Security Devices
bodyText: North Carolina's security-device duty sits in the fitness statute: the lack of operable locks on all doors leading to the outside, broken windows, and the lack of operable locks on all ground-level windows are imminently dangerous conditions, which you must repair within a reasonable time based on the severity once you know of them or are told. No statute requires a particular type of lock such as a keyed deadbolt, a door viewer or peephole, or rekeying between tenancies, and none sets a tenant duty to report a broken lock beyond the general written repair request your lease may ask for; your fitness duty includes complying with the applicable building and housing codes, and local housing codes, which may require particular locks, were not researched for this library (edu-local-preemption-nc). A violation of the fitness statute is not negligence per se, so a lock failure is not automatically negligence, though ordinary negligence claims are not displaced. When a tenant gives you notice that a tenant or household member is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking and asks for the locks to be changed, you must change them or allow the tenant to do so within 48 hours, or within 72 hours where the perpetrator lives in the unit and the tenant has given you a court order to stay away, under the separate lock-change rules (edu-dv-lockchange-nc). You or your employee may rekey or repair locks on your own rental property without a locksmith license, as long as you do not present yourselves as locksmiths.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: North Carolina does not require apartment owners, at any size, to adopt a key-control policy, keep a master-key log, limit who holds passkeys, or run background checks on employees who can enter units. Related rules: a tenant's criminal record does not by itself make a later injury foreseeable to you, and you have no duty to screen for criminal records, though you may use a background check to refuse to rent; you or your employee may do lock work on your own rental property without a locksmith license if you do not present yourselves as locksmiths; and once you have a court order requiring a co-tenant perpetrator of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking to stay away, you have no duty to give that person keys or access unless a court order allows a return for belongings. Older high-rise buildings may have fire-safety master-key requirements under the building code statute, which this library has not applied to rentals.

title: Common-Area Lighting and Electricity
bodyText: North Carolina sets no lighting level for hallways, stairways, entries or other common areas; your duty is the general one to keep all common areas safe and to comply with the building and housing codes, which may set lighting rules. If you bill tenants for electricity under the Utilities Commission's procedure for units metered in your name, you may not include electricity used in any other unit or in a common area in a tenant's bill. In buildings of two or more units permitted since September 1, 1977, each unit must generally have its own electric service and meter in the tenant's name, unless the lease includes electricity in the rent with service in your name or the Commission has approved another arrangement. No statute addresses common-area lights wired to a tenant's own meter, and the library offers no clause making a tenant pay for them, because that arrangement is not covered by the billing procedure and sits uneasily with the bar on billing tenants for common-area electricity.

title: Elevators, Pools, Boilers and Other Facilities
bodyText: Beyond keeping the unit fit, North Carolina law reaches several building facilities. Elevators: you must comply with the elevator safety requirements for private residences, cottages and similar accommodations subject to the State accommodation sales tax (a unit rented to the same person for 90 or more continuous days is exempt from that tax), which limit door gaps and require you to stop a noncompliant elevator until a guard, baffle or compliant door is installed and reported to the State Fire Marshal; separately, an elevator anywhere but a single-family residence needs a Department of Labor certificate of operation. Pools: a pool at an apartment complex is a public swimming pool and may not open without a state operation permit; only a private pool serving a single-family dwelling, used by its residents and guests, is excluded. Boilers and pressure vessels fall under the State boiler safety law unless they are in a private residence or an apartment house of fewer than six families. If you charge tenants for water or sewer and know the water exceeds a maximum contaminant level, you must notify them, and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are covered by the library's alarm clause. No statute puts a duty on landlords for garage door openers, mailboxes, laundry rooms or similar amenities beyond the general duty to keep supplied facilities in repair and common areas safe.

title: Stoves and Refrigerators
bodyText: No North Carolina statute requires you to supply a stove or a refrigerator. If you do supply one, or a building or housing code requires you to, it is among the facilities and appliances you must maintain in good and safe working order and promptly repair once the tenant asks in writing (no written request is needed in an emergency). Local minimum housing codes may require cooking facilities and were not researched for this library, and the State Building Code was not read. The library's appliances clause lists the appliances that come with the unit.

title: Excluding Appliances from the Lease
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule presuming that an appliance left in a unit is yours unless the lease excludes it. Your repair duty reaches the facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply, so the lease may say which appliances come with the unit, but it cannot exclude anything a building or housing code requires, and it cannot excuse the facilities the fitness statute treats as essential, such as heat able to reach 65 degrees in winter, potable water, an operable toilet and a bathtub or shower, or working wiring. Whether an item you leave in the unit but declare "not supplied" escapes the repair duty is not settled by the statute, and a tenant's acceptance never releases your fitness duties; the cautious course is to remove an appliance you will not maintain, and the library offers no exclusion clause for North Carolina.

title: What North Carolina Habitability Law Does Not Have
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no North Carolina counterpart. In the law searched for this library, North Carolina has: (1) no repair-and-deduct right, no statutory rent abatement and no rent escrow (so no exemption notice); (2) no presumption of breach, delay or notice from a code violation; (3) no required habitability statement in the lease; (4) no materiality threshold dividing defects; (5) no procedure for accepting listed defects in return for lower rent; (6) no repair deadline other than 15 days for alarms after the tenant's written notice, prompt repair of supplied facilities and appliances after a written request (except in emergencies), and a reasonable time for imminently dangerous conditions; (7) no landlord exit because repairs cost too much, and no lease exit for environmental events or declared disasters beyond the tenant's general right, on its conditions, to surrender a destroyed or badly damaged building; (8) no duty to rehouse a tenant during repairs; (9) no duty to supply a stove or refrigerator and no presumption about appliances left in a unit; (10) no rules on window guards, radiator covers, balcony inspections, deadbolts, door viewers, rekeying, key control or common-area lighting levels; and (11) no duty to reset a water heater at each new tenancy, though new heaters must be preset at the factory or on installation. Each point is worked out in its own row, and local housing codes and the State Building Code may add requirements.

title: State Lead Notices: Event-Based, Not at Signing
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead disclosure for housing built before 1978, North Carolina requires no state lead notice, pamphlet, form or information packet that must be given with a lease or at signing or renewal. Its lead notices are tied to later events instead. If the state health department finds lead poisoning hazards where a child under six or a pregnant woman with confirmed lead poisoning (a blood lead level of 10 micrograms per deciliter or more) lives or regularly visits and orders remediation, you must tell the department and the occupants the dates of the work at least three days before it starts. If you follow the state lead maintenance standard for a pre-1978 unit (for example to qualify for an annual certificate of compliance), you must give occupants the EPA pamphlets Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home and Renovate Right, summaries of any state lead hazard reports on the property and copies of earlier certificates; the certificate application needs the occupants' signed acknowledgment, and while a certificate is in force you must give occupants three days' notice before maintenance, renovation or remodeling work. A certified renovation firm doing paid work in pre-1978 housing must hand out the EPA-approved renovation pamphlet.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Leases
bodyText: North Carolina has no lead-safe certificate that a rental must have or that must be attached to a lease as an exhibit. What it has is a voluntary annual certificate of compliance: an owner of a pre-1978 unit who follows the state lead maintenance standard may apply to the state health department each year, with a $10 fee, and the certificate expires one year after it issues. The application must include a sworn statement from the owner, the occupants' signed acknowledgment that they received the required lead information, a visual inspection summary by a certified lead inspector or risk assessor, and lead dust test results. Keeping up the maintenance standard and the certificate yearly, or showing the unit was lead-safe housing, shields an owner from liability to occupants for lead injuries in the ways the statute describes; see the library's North Carolina lead hazards row. For housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure at leasing still applies.

title: Asbestos: Permits for Removal, No Tenant Notice
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute or rule requiring a landlord to tell tenants about asbestos in a rental, before signing or during the tenancy. Its asbestos law regulates the work, not the lease: no one may remove more than 35 cubic feet, 160 square feet or 260 linear feet of regulated asbestos-containing material per job without a state removal permit, the work must be done by accredited people (a building owner and its permanent employees doing small-scale, short-duration work are exempt from accreditation), and a building owner of a renovation or demolition must follow the federal asbestos air-emission rules the state has adopted. North Carolina's asbestos statute treats a single-family home or a building of fewer than 10 units as a residence, and the state airborne asbestos limit and air monitoring for permitted removals apply only to public areas, meaning areas of buildings other than residences that are not covered by workplace safety law; so the areas of an apartment building of 10 or more units, its units as well as its common areas, can fall under them. A seller of a one-to-four unit home uses the state's sale disclosure statement, which lists asbestos but lets the owner either disclose what the owner actually knows or make no representations; it reaches a lease only when the lease carries an option to buy and the tenant does not occupy or intend to occupy the home (see the library's North Carolina required disclosures row). Asbestos that makes the unit unfit is part of your general repair and fitness duty.

title: Contaminated Property: Statement in the Lease
bodyText:
North Carolina has no general rule requiring a landlord to tell a tenant that the property is or was contaminated. But when property carrying certain recorded environmental notices is sold, leased, conveyed or transferred, the deed or other instrument of transfer must state the property's status in its description section, in type no smaller than the body, usually with the book and page of the recorded notice: contaminated sites and oil or hazardous substance discharge sites with land-use restrictions, inactive hazardous waste disposal sites, brownfields properties, dry-cleaning solvent sites, landfills and hazardous waste disposal sites, demolition debris disposal sites, property with more than 1,000 cubic yards of coal ash fill, and radioactive waste disposal sites.

Whether a residential lease counts as an instrument of transfer has not been settled in the law this library reviewed, so the library's cautious course is to put the statement in the lease, using the North Carolina environmental notice clause. Anyone who owns or leases property subject to a recorded land-use restriction must abide by it, so your tenants are bound too.

A seller's disclosure statement covering hazardous materials and environmental contamination applies to sales and to leases with an option to buy where the tenant does not live in the home (see the library's North Carolina required disclosures row).

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure Rule
bodyText: North Carolina's statutes and the state rules searched for this library do not require a landlord to disclose defective, corrosive or imported drywall to a tenant, and the sale disclosure statute names no drywall item either (the State Building Code and local ordinances were not read for this library). If drywall makes the unit unfit or damages wiring or other facilities you supply, your general duty to keep the premises fit applies, and so does your duty to keep those facilities in good and safe working order once the tenant notifies you in writing of needed repairs (no written notice is needed in an emergency). A seller's disclosure statement covers structural components and building systems generally; it reaches a lease only when the lease carries an option to buy and the tenant does not occupy or intend to occupy the home (see the library's North Carolina required disclosures row).

title: No Military Zone Disclosure for Leases
bodyText: North Carolina requires no lease disclosure that a rental is in a military air installation's noise or accident zone, near a military installation, or in any military impact area, and gives tenants no termination right on that ground. The state's sale disclosure form asks the owner about noise, odor, smoke or other nuisance from military sources, but that form reaches a lease only when the lease carries an option to buy and the tenant does not occupy or intend to occupy the home (see the library's North Carolina required disclosures row). Starting April 1, 2027, a separate law bars prohibited foreign parties (certain foreign governments and entities they control, not individual renters) from leasing land within 50 miles of a listed military installation for a term of a year or longer; it adds no disclosure to an ordinary residential lease.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure Rule
bodyText: North Carolina's statutes and the state rules searched for this library require no lease disclosure about shoreline or beach access, public trust rights, oceanfront erosion or coastal hazard areas, whether for a year-round rental or a vacation rental. Coastal development permits and rules for areas of environmental concern govern what may be built, not what a landlord must tell a tenant. Flood information is covered separately (see the library's North Carolina flood disclosure row).

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Meter Disclosure
