bodyText: North Carolina requires no lease disclosure of former military ordnance sites nearby, of a pending or planned demolition of the building, or of a utility meter that also serves areas outside the tenant's unit. Demolition comes up elsewhere: a landlord may defend a retaliation claim by showing that the housing code requires demolition or major work that cannot be done without displacing the tenant's household, or that the landlord in good faith seeks possession at the end of the tenant's term to demolish or remodel in a way that requires displacing the household; and local housing code officers may order an unfit dwelling repaired, closed or demolished (before the local government brings its summary court action to remove a tenant of the owner, the tenant must have been served at least 30 days earlier with notice that the governing board has ordered the officer to proceed). Billing tenants for utilities, including metering rules, is covered in the library's North Carolina utility billing rows; in multi-unit buildings permitted since September 1, 1977, state law requires a separate electric (and gas) meter for each unit normally rented for a month or longer (hotels, rooming houses, dormitories and some other uses are excluded, and the Utilities Commission may approve a central meter for an energy-saving central heating, cooling or hot-water system), in the tenant's name unless the lease includes the service in the rent in your name or the Utilities Commission has approved another arrangement.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65: no North Carolina statute, and none of the state rules searched for this library, requires a landlord to post or give tenants a warning about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. The chemical warnings found are aimed at other settings, such as the alcohol-and-pregnancy warning sign displayed in ABC stores. Federal and state rules on specific hazards still apply, such as the federal lead disclosure and the state lead and asbestos rules described in the library's North Carolina rows.

title: No Pre-Signing Foreclosure Disclosure
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a landlord whose property is in foreclosure to tell a prospective or new tenant before signing a lease, and has no lease form or notice for it. The tenant hears of a power-of-sale foreclosure from the trustee instead: for residential property with fewer than 15 rental units, the notice of sale must be mailed to each occupant under a rental agreement (by name, or to "occupant"), and must tell tenants that they may end the lease by written notice effective 10 to 90 days after the sale date, owing only prorated rent, unless the default is cured first. Because that right and the later possession rules apply no matter when the lease was signed, see the library's North Carolina foreclosure row for what happens to your tenants.

title: No Association Disclosure Required in Leases
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a lease of a condominium unit or a home in a planned community (homeowners' association) to disclose the association's obligations, budget or governing documents, and does not require a copy of the lease or any statement to go to the association. The association's power to fine runs against owners for violations of the declaration, bylaws and rules, and a tenant votes only if the declaration gives lessees the vote on stated matters. Because your tenant's conduct can lead to fines against you, the library offers an optional clause recording that you gave the tenant the association documents, alongside the shared association compliance clause; the association's own declaration may also set leasing rules. Condominium conversions have their own tenant notice rules, covered elsewhere in the library.

title: No Property Tax Share of Rent Statement
bodyText: North Carolina has no renter's property tax credit and no rule requiring a landlord to tell tenants what share of the rent goes to property taxes, whether yearly, on a rent change or on request. The state's property tax relief for elderly or disabled residents (a homestead exclusion and a homestead circuit breaker deferral) runs to owners who occupy the home, not renters.

title: Required Disclosures: What North Carolina Requires
bodyText: North Carolina has no single list of lease disclosures, no state form that must be the first page of a lease, and no notice telling tenants whether a rent or eviction law covers the unit (it has no rent control or just-cause law). What it does require, when the facts apply: within 30 days after the lease term begins, the name and address of the bank or institution holding the security deposit (or the bond insurer); if you charge tenants for water or sewer and know the water exceeds a maximum contaminant level set under the state drinking water law, notice of that; any charge for water, sewer, electricity or natural gas only under a written rental agreement and the utility billing rules; a statement in the lease if the property carries one of the recorded environmental notices described in the library's contamination rows; and, for housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure. An option to buy changes the picture: for residential property of one to four dwelling units, the state's seller disclosure law covers a lease with option to purchase, and even where the tenant lives in the home the owner must give the mineral and oil and gas rights disclosure statement; if the tenant does not occupy or intend to occupy it, the residential property and owners' association disclosure statements are due too. Those statements must be delivered no later than when the tenant exercises the option, and a buyer who does not get them in time may cancel within a short window. Separately, an option to buy a home the tenant will live in as a principal dwelling, signed with or combined with the lease, must be (the chapter's option contract definition says single-family property while its property definition says one to four families; the law this library reviewed does not settle which governs, so the cautious course follows these rules for any one-to-four family home) a signed and acknowledged written contract with the listed terms (price, option fee, forfeiture triggers, exercise period, a once-a-year right to cure) and a statement in at least 14-point boldface type immediately above the tenant's signature of the right to cancel until midnight of the third business day; you must hand the tenant an exact copy at signing and record the contract or a memorandum within five business days, and the landlord-tenant law still governs the lease except where the option chapter provides otherwise. Vacation rentals have their own required notice on the face of the agreement (see the library's vacation rental row).

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice or Lease Font Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule that a single-family home lease carry an occupancy notice at the top of the first page or in oversized type, and no presumption that an occupant is unlawful unless the lease is notarized or signed by a licensed manager. Its squatter-removal law instead lets an owner seek expedited removal of a person who has no rental agreement and has never paid rent, and does not reach tenants or holdover tenants. No general font-size or first-page rule applies to residential leases; the type rules that do exist are specific: an option to buy combined with a lease must show the tenant's three-business-day cancellation right in at least 14-point boldface immediately above the tenant's signature, a vacation rental agreement must carry the statutory notice clearly and conspicuously on its face, and a recorded environmental notice statement must appear in type no smaller than the body of the instrument. See the library's North Carolina rows on required disclosures, unauthorized occupants and recorded environmental notices.

title: Pest Control: No Statutory Tenant Notice
bodyText: North Carolina's statutes do not require a landlord to notify tenants before pest control or pesticide treatment, to post a pesticide notice, or to give tenants a pest control disclosure; the statutory pesticide notices found are for other settings (school pesticide-use schedules, and notice to registered beekeepers before aerial spraying of a pesticide labeled toxic to bees). Anyone who applies a pesticide, including a landlord, must use it consistently with its labeling, so any occupant precautions on the label must be followed. The rules of the Structural Pest Control Committee and the Pesticide Board, which could set notice or safety duties for applicators, were not read for this library. Pests do matter under the repair duty: a rat infestation caused by structural defects that leave the premises open to rodents is an imminently dangerous condition you must remedy within a reasonable period of time based on the severity of the condition after you learn of it or receive notice of it (you may recover the actual and reasonable cost of repairs that are the tenant's fault). Anyone doing structural pest control for others must be licensed, and only a certified applicator (or someone under one's direct supervision) may use restricted-use pesticides, even on the owner's own property; the license exemption for work on one's own property comes with a bar on charging any fee for it, and whether a landlord's rented units count as the landlord's own property for that exemption is unsettled in the law this library reviewed, so the cautious course is to use a licensed operator in tenants' units.

title: Pools at Rental Properties
bodyText: A pool at an apartment complex or other multi-unit rental is a public swimming pool under North Carolina health law, whether or not you charge for it: it needs a yearly operation permit from the health department before it opens, and must meet the state rules on fencing (at least 48 inches high with self-closing, self-latching pedestrian gates), lifesaving equipment, an emergency telephone, water quality, a trained person responsible for operation, and reporting a death, serious injury or illness complaint to the local health department within two working days; an apartment or condominium pool limited to residents and guests needs no dressing rooms, but needs a toilet and lavatory if the farthest unit is more than 300 feet away. If no lifeguard is on duty, which the rules allow, you must post a permanent sign reading WARNING-NO LIFEGUARD ON DUTY in letters at least four inches high, plus signs that children should not use the pool without adult supervision and adults should not swim alone, and a sign barring pets and glass. A private pool serving a single-family home and used only by its residents and their guests (and, since August 11, 2026, a swim instructor) is outside these rules, though one used for a fee must be kept in good and safe working order; the exemption is for a single-family dwelling, so a pool shared by two or more rental units is not covered by it. No North Carolina law requires a pool safety notice or pool rules in the lease, and the state rules do not generally require lifeguards (one exception: if in-pool exercise equipment such as an underwater treadmill stays in the pool when not in use, the pool must be limited to adults or have a lifeguard on duty whenever children are allowed in it).

title: Private Wells: Testing and Results
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a landlord to test a private well or to give tenants well test results before or during a tenancy. Testing happens when a well is new: within 30 days after the local health department issues a certificate of completion for a newly built private drinking water well, the department tests the water (or makes sure a certified laboratory does) for a set list of metals, nitrates and nitrites, other chemicals and bacteria, and gives the results to the well owner and, where practicable, to any tenant of a dwelling served by the well when the water is sampled; if contaminants exceed public drinking water limits, the department tells the owner or the tenant about the need to limit exposure, treat the water or resample. As the well owner you must give access and power for the sampling, and you may not put a new or repaired well into service without a certificate of completion. The registry of well permits and test results kept by the local health department is searchable by address.

title: No Recycling Notice Rule (Local Ordinances Govern)
bodyText: No North Carolina statute, and none of the state rules searched for this library, requires a landlord to tell tenants where or how to recycle, or to provide recycling at a rental property. Recycling is local: a county may by ordinance require participation in a recycling program by having the owner or occupant of property separate designated materials before disposal, and a city may require an owner of improved property to put solid waste in specified receptacles, separate materials, or join a recycling program in the same way. Where a local ordinance requires a type of waste to be recycled or bars its disposal, local-government collectors and disposal facilities may not knowingly take that waste for disposal.

title: Disabled Alarms: Actual Cost, Not a Flat Fee
bodyText: North Carolina sets the charge for a disabled or damaged smoke or carbon monoxide alarm itself, and it is not a flat fee: if an alarm is disabled or damaged other than by you, your agents or an act of God, the tenant must reimburse your reasonable and actual cost of repairing or replacing it within 30 days after your written notice (or a state or local government agent's), and a tenant who does not pay in that time commits an infraction with a fine of up to $100. The security deposit may also be applied to damage to or destruction of smoke or carbon monoxide alarms. No statute authorizes a set lease fee for removing or tampering with an alarm; whether a fixed charge would be enforced or struck as a penalty is case law, so the library offers no flat fee and its North Carolina alarm clause uses the statutory actual-cost reimbursement. A tenant may temporarily disconnect an alarm to replace batteries or when it has been set off by accident.

title: No Smart Lock or App-Entry Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute regulating smart locks, keypads, key fobs or app-based entry in rentals, and no law letting a domestic-violence survivor ask whoever manages a connected device's accounts to cut off another person's access. The general rules still apply to any lock system you use: lack of operable locks on all doors leading outside is an imminently dangerous condition you must remedy within a reasonable period of time based on its severity after you learn of it or receive notice of it, and when a tenant reports that a protected tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking you must change the locks, or let the tenant change them, within 48 hours (72 hours, and only with a stay-away order, if the perpetrator lives in the same unit), and the statute does not say whether reprogramming an electronic lock counts as changing the locks, so the cautious course for an electronic lock is to change its codes and credentials (and any physical keys or cylinders) within the same deadline. Installing or servicing mechanical or electronic locks and access control devices for pay is licensed locksmith work, but you or your employees may do it on your own rental property so long as you do not hold yourselves out as locksmiths. See the library's North Carolina rows on security devices and domestic-violence lock changes.

title: No Cable or Internet Access Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute giving tenants a right to cable, satellite or internet access in a rental, requiring a landlord to let providers wire a building, or barring a rent difference for tenants who subscribe. The one related state rule concerns telephone service: if a property owner gives one provider exclusive access to serve a subdivision or other area, the local telephone company may be relieved of its duty to serve there, and the owner must tell purchasers of property in that area about the agreement (the statute names purchasers, not tenants). For vacation rentals, a landlord may deduct unpaid long distance and cable television charges the tenant owed under the rental agreement from the deposit. Federal rules on tenants' satellite dishes and antennas are not stated in this library row.

title: EV Chargers: No Tenant Right; Electricity Resale Limits
bodyText: North Carolina gives tenants no right to install an electric vehicle charger and puts no limit on a landlord's refusal, cost-sharing terms or installation standards; the lease decides (see also the library's North Carolina row on EV charging rights). The legal constraint is on selling the electricity: someone who resells electricity through an immobile charging station only for charging plug-in vehicles, using power bought from the authorized supplier, is not treated as a public utility, but otherwise a landlord may bill tenants for electricity only under a written rental agreement and the Utilities Commission's procedures. North Carolina has no weights-and-measures registration, accuracy or price-posting rule for chargers in the statutes and rules read for this library. The library's optional North Carolina charger clause therefore has the tenant connect the charger to electric service in the tenant's own name, or includes the electricity in the rent.

title: No Shared-Area EV Charging Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule on electric vehicle charging in shared parking areas: nothing requires you to allow a charger in a common lot, to reserve a space for it, or limits a reserved-space fee, and nothing makes later tenants of that space responsible for the charger. If you allow a charger in a shared lot, the lease decides the location, any parking fee and who pays for damage, and the library's optional North Carolina charger clause covers a designated space. The library does not offer the shared-area clause used in some other states for North Carolina, because its sentence making a later tenant of the space responsible depends on a statute North Carolina does not have; whether a later tenant could be bound any other way is case law, so the cautious course is to put any duties for the charger in each tenant's own lease. In a condominium or planned community, the association's rules on common elements also apply.

title: No Portable Cooling Device Rule
bodyText: North Carolina gives tenants no right to install a portable or window cooling unit, and no rule that a lease restricting window units must say so; whether one is allowed is up to the lease. North Carolina's statutes and the state rules searched for this library set no minimum cooling standard for rentals (the State Building Code, which the landlord must follow under the fitness statute, was not read for this library). If you supply air conditioning, though, you must keep it in good and safe working order and repair it promptly after the tenant's written request (no written request is needed in an emergency). A tenant-owned unit that damages the premises falls under the tenant's general duty not to damage the property.

title: No Tenant Solar Device Right
bodyText: North Carolina gives tenants no right to install a plug-in, balcony or portable solar device, so the lease may allow, condition or forbid one. The state's solar protection runs to owners, not tenants: a deed restriction, covenant or similar agreement running with the land may not prohibit, or have the effect of prohibiting, a solar collector for a residential property (it may regulate location and screening so long as it does not prevent reasonable use of a solar collector, and may bar collectors visible from the ground on a facade facing areas open to common or public access, on a roof surface sloping toward those areas, or in the area between that facade and those areas), and the protection does not apply to condominiums in multi-story buildings with stacked units; local development regulations are limited in the same way, without the condominium exclusion. Whether that rule could ever reach a restriction in a residential lease has not been settled in the law this library reviewed; the library treats an ordinary lease term as outside it. If you own the property in an owners' association, the association's covenant cannot bar your own solar collector except as just described.

title: Splitting Utility Bills Among Tenants
bodyText: North Carolina has no law making a lease term unenforceable just because it charges a tenant for a utility that is not separately metered, but you may charge tenants for water and sewer, electricity, natural gas or a central heating or cooling system only under a written rental agreement, with authority from the Utilities Commission, and by one of the methods the law allows. For water and sewer, charges must generally rest on each tenant's own metered use at no more than the supplier's unit rate; the only other methods are a hot-water allocation for contiguous units built before 1989 (and, since August 11, 2026, a mobile home in a mobile home park sited before 1989) where you determine that measuring each tenant's total water use is impractical or not economical, passing through a Commission-approved flat rate, or dividing one unit's bill equally among the tenants of that unit. For electricity and gas, you may only divide the bill for a unit's own meter in your name equally among that unit's tenants, or bill each tenant's measured share of an approved central system; no tenant's bill may include common areas or other units, and no procedure lets you split a building's master-metered electric bill among units. A 2026 law took the statute's express ban on ratio billing (dividing a bill by a formula such as floor area or headcount) out of the hot-water method, but the statute still calls for metered or hot-water-based charges and the Commission's rules still forbid ratio billing, so do not use it unless the Commission authorizes it. The billing clause and the rest of the rules are in utility-billing-nc and edu-utility-billing-nc.

title: Utility Charges Capped at Actual Cost
bodyText: North Carolina caps what you may charge a tenant for a utility you buy and bill under Utilities Commission authority. Electricity and natural gas may be billed only at the actual amount of the unit's own utility bill, divided equally among that unit's tenants, and water and sewer at no more than the supplier's unit rate (or a Commission-approved flat rate); on top of that you may add only the administrative fee, and any late fee, the Commission allows (for water, generally no more than $3.75 a month). You may not collect more than the rates the Commission approved (for water and sewer, not less either; for electricity and natural gas you may choose to pay part of a tenant's bill). The Commission's rules treat a landlord billing these utilities as a public utility, and a public utility that willfully overcharges and does not refund within 30 days after the customer's written demand owes double the overcharge plus $10 for each further day; whether that remedy reaches a landlord who bills utilities is case law, so the cautious course is to assume it does. Because charging a tenant for the cost of a utility needs Commission authority, the library offers no utility allowance clause that has the tenant repay usage above a set amount; to fix your cost, either include the utility in the rent with the account in your name or have the tenant hold the account. Electricity on a master meter cannot be divided among units at all except for an approved central system.

title: Utility Billing Documents at Signing
bodyText:
If you bill tenants for water and sewer, electricity or natural gas under Utilities Commission authority, the Commission's rules require you to give each tenant, when the lease is signed, a copy of your approved rates, rules and regulations for that service, a copy of the Commission's billing rules for it, and a written statement telling tenants to contact your office first with billing questions or service complaints and how to reach the Commission's Public Staff in a dispute. You must also keep those same documents in public view in your business office near where payments are received.

For electricity and natural gas you must also tell tenants, at the start and every year, how you divide bills among tenants and what administrative fee, returned check charge and late fee you charge, with a copy of the supplier's current schedule of charges, and your application for billing authority must include the lease forms you use. The clause utility-disclosure-attachment-nc delivers the signing documents with the lease; the billing clause itself is utility-billing-nc.

title: Copies of Tenant Shutoff Notices
bodyText:
The Utilities Commission requires every electric and natural gas utility it regulates to offer each residential customer the chance to name a third party to receive a copy of any notice that service is to be cut off; the option is open to every residential customer, not only elderly or disabled ones, so a tenant who holds the account can name you. The utility must tell customers about the option when service starts and at least once a year, must try to reach the named third party as well as the customer at least 24 hours before cutting service, and the designation does not make the third party responsible for the bill.

Only the customer can make the designation: no North Carolina statute or Commission rule lets an owner sign up on its own to be told when a tenant's service is about to be cut off, and the Commission's water and sewer rules have no designation option at all. City and county utilities and electric membership corporations are not covered by these Commission rules, and their own policies were not reviewed for this library. The optional clause utility-disconnection-notice-authorization-nc has the tenant name you on electric and gas accounts.

title: Keeping Landlord-Billed Utilities On
bodyText: If you bill tenants for electricity or natural gas under the Utilities Commission's procedure, the account stays in your name: you are the utility's customer and solely responsible for paying its bills promptly. If you expect not to pay the supplier's bill on time, or you receive the supplier's notice of pending disconnection, whichever comes first, you must within 24 hours give written notice to the Commission and to every affected tenant, and you may not abandon or stop providing the service to your tenants without the Commission's permission in advance. You may not disconnect a tenant's service, or ask the supplier to disconnect it, because the tenant has not paid your bill, and you may not end the lease for that reason. For water and sewer you bill under Commission authority, the same bar on disconnecting for nonpayment applies, but the Commission's water and sewer billing rules contain no 24-hour notice rule.

title: Utilities in the Landlord's Name
bodyText: When a utility account for a rental is in your name, the bill is yours. A city, county or natural gas district's water, sewer, gas or other enterprise charges are the legal obligation of the person who contracted for them, but they are the owner's obligation wherever more than one tenant is served through the same meter and, for a city or county, wherever sewer charges are billed separately from water charges, and the provider may cut off service once an account is more than 10 days (a gas district, 30 days) past due. A city, county or gas district may not make a new tenant pay a former tenant's past-due bill before starting service, except (for a city or gas district) where several tenants share one meter. If you bill tenants for electricity or gas under the Utilities Commission's procedure and expect to miss the supplier's bill or receive a disconnection notice, you must notify the Commission and every affected tenant within 24 hours (see edu-utility-interruption-submeter-nc). North Carolina law gives tenants no right to pay your unpaid utility bill and deduct it from rent, and no receiver remedy for unpaid utilities; a tenant may not withhold rent without a court ruling, but losing water or heat can breach your duty to keep the unit fit, and cutting utilities to force a tenant out is unlawful self-help.

title: Utility Shutoff Rules for Tenant Accounts
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute limiting when an electric or natural gas company regulated by the Utilities Commission may cut off a residential customer for nonpayment (the statutes for city, county and other public systems set only delinquency periods, below) and no statutory winter, heat or storm moratorium; the limits are in the Utilities Commission's rules, which bind the electric and natural gas companies it regulates. Those companies must give at least 10 days' written notice before cutting off a residential customer, must try to reach the customer (and any third party the customer named) at least 24 hours before, may not cut off service on a Friday, a weekend, a holiday or the day before a holiday, and must hold off while the customer's informal appeal to the Commission's Public Staff is pending. For bills issued from November 1 through March 31, the notice must say service will not be cut off without the Commission's approval if a household member is elderly (65 or older) or handicapped, the customer cannot pay, and the household is certified eligible for energy crisis assistance; this is a postponement for that household, not a moratorium. Any regulated utility must give at least five days' written notice before discontinuing service for nonpayment, and city and county systems may cut off accounts more than 10 days past due (natural gas districts and water and sewer authorities after 30 days) under their own procedures, which were not reviewed for this library. If you bill tenants for utilities yourself, you may not cut off their service for nonpayment at all (see edu-utility-interruption-submeter-nc).

title: Moving Utilities into the Tenant's Name
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute requiring a tenant to move utility accounts into the tenant's own name by a deadline, and none letting you cut off service still in your name if the tenant does not. Cutting off utilities to make a tenant leave is unlawful self-help, and a lease term allowing it is void; whether cutting off a landlord-name account for some other reason is lawful is a question for the courts, so the library offers no cutoff clause.

It also offers no clause making the tenant repay you for service used while an account is in your name, because charging tenants for the cost of water, sewer, electricity or natural gas needs Utilities Commission authority. Use utilities-responsibility to make the tenant arrange and pay utilities directly and utility-service-continuity to bar the tenant from letting service lapse.

In buildings of two or more units permitted since September 1, 1977, for units normally rented for a month or longer (hotels, rooming houses, dormitories and some other uses are excluded), electric and gas service must be in the tenant's name unless the lease includes it in the rent with the account in your name or the Commission has approved your billing, and a city, county or gas district may not make a new tenant pay a former tenant's unpaid bill before starting service (except, for a city or gas district, where tenants share a meter).

title: Reselling Electricity to Tenants
bodyText: A North Carolina landlord that resells electricity to tenants is regulated as a utility. Anyone who provides utility service to tenants through individual meters with a separate metered charge is a public utility for rates and service, and a landlord billing electricity under the Utilities Commission's procedure is a public utility that must have the Commission's certificate of authority before charging anything; supplying electricity to tenants without reselling it, such as by including it in the rent, does not make you a utility. The procedure reaches only units individually metered in your name or an approved central system, and each bill must show the supplier's bill for the unit and the tenant's share, the supplier's name, the usage dates, a past-due date at least 25 days after the bill is sent, your contact details, any approved fees, and the tenant's right to raise questions with you and complain to the Commission. You must also give tenants your rates and rules, the Commission's rules and a dispute statement when the lease is signed (see utility-disclosure-attachment-nc), tell them at the start and every year how you divide bills and what fees you charge, and keep the records of each tenant's charges for 36 months for tenants to inspect. Natural gas resale follows the same rules.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge; Water Billing Limits
bodyText: North Carolina has no meter conservation charge: no law attaches a charge for energy-efficiency improvements to a property's utility meter or bill so that it carries over to later tenants, so there is no notice to new tenants and no rent deduction to give. If you bill tenants for water and sewer under Utilities Commission authority, the rules on that charge are strict: no more than the supplier's unit rate for metered use, plus only the Commission-approved administrative fee (generally no more than $3.75 a month), and no charge for connection, disconnection, late payment or anything similar on top of the rate (a returned check charge is allowed). Bills must go out at least monthly, show the meter readings at the start and end of the period, the dates they were taken and the amount of water supplied, and give a past-due date at least 25 days after the billing date. Charging only the supplier's rate does not take you outside the Commission's rules, which require its certificate before billing; whether a landlord serving fewer than 15 residential customers falls outside that requirement is not settled by the texts this library reviewed, so the cautious course is to obtain the certificate.

title: Tenant Utility Bills and Liens on the Property
bodyText: In North Carolina, a city's or county's charges for water, sewer and other public enterprise services are the legal obligation of the person who contracted for them and, except for the solid waste, stormwater and sanitary district rules below, are not a lien on the property served, so a tenant's unpaid account in the tenant's own name does not become a lien on your property. The owner is liable instead in two cases: where the property is rented to more than one tenant whose services are measured by the same meter, and where sewer charges are billed separately from water charges; natural gas districts follow the same rule for shared meters. A city or county may, by ordinance, bill solid waste collection and disposal fees with property taxes, and then delinquent fees are a lien on the property on the bill; a few named cities may do the same for stormwater fees, and in a sanitary district that runs a sewer system but no water system, sewer charges are a lien on the property served. Because there is no general utility lien, North Carolina has no affidavit or lease-filing procedure for an owner to shield the property. If a tenant's unpaid bill does become a lien on the property because of the tenant's occupancy, you may use the security deposit to pay it.

title: Passing Local Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute on passing a local government fee to a tenant: none allows it and none forbids it, so it is a matter for the lease, and the optional clause government-fee-reimbursement-ky is available.

State law keeps such fees narrow. A city or county generally may not require a permit or permission under its building code enforcement or minimum housing code powers to rent residential property, or require rental registration, and may not levy a special fee or tax on residential rental property that other properties do not pay unless general law expressly authorizes it, except a fee on an individual property with repeated verified code violations or in the worst 10% for crime or disorder, capped at $500 in any 12-month period in which violations are found. If you bill tenants for water or sewer under Utilities Commission authority, the supplier's base charge you pass through may not include stormwater fees, trash collection or property taxes. See edu-local-preemption-nc for the wider limits on local rental rules.

title: Government Fines Caused by Tenants
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute that bars, or allows, passing a government fine or nuisance-abatement cost to the tenant who caused it, and none makes a tenant liable to you for such fines by default; it is a matter for the lease, and the optional clause tenant-caused-fines-as covers fines and abatement costs caused by the tenant, the tenant's household or guests, but never those for conditions you must handle yourself.

A few statutes touch the subject. If a tenant disables or damages a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, the tenant must repay your reasonable repair or replacement cost within 30 days after written notice, and a tenant who does not commits an infraction with a fine of up to $100; you face a fine of up to $250 if you fail to provide or repair an alarm within 30 days after written notice. Where a local housing code makes a tenant's prohibited behavior the owner's violation, the violation counts as corrected if you bring an eviction action within 30 days after written notice of it.

In a public-morals nuisance action (for example drug sales or prostitution), the costs of abatement are a lien on the property used, and if the court finds after an adversary hearing that a tenant used the place for those purposes, the lease is void at your option.

title: Sales and Occupancy Tax on Short Rentals
bodyText:
North Carolina does not tax ordinary residential rent: the State sales tax reaches the rental of an accommodation, which includes a residence, but an accommodation supplied to the same person for 90 or more continuous days is exempt, so a lease of 90 days or longer carries no State tax. A rental of a dwelling for fewer than 90 continuous days is taxed at the general sales tax rate, and where a county or city levies a room occupancy tax, that tax applies to the same receipts; a private residence rented for fewer than 15 days in a calendar year is exempt unless the rental is made through an accommodation facilitator, which includes a real estate broker.

The landlord (or the facilitator that collects the rent) must collect the tax, which is meant to be borne by the tenant and is a debt the tenant owes, and must state it separately on the lease or other documents unless it shows that the price includes tax; a local occupancy tax must always be stated separately. Use rent-tax-nc for a term shorter than 90 days.

Whether a month-to-month tenancy that ends up lasting 90 days is exempt from its start is not settled by the statute, and local occupancy tax acts were not reviewed for this library.

title: Passing Tax and Insurance Increases to Tenants
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute on passing property tax or insurance increases through to a residential tenant: none authorizes it, prescribes how the tenant's share must be stated, or requires a refund when taxes are abated. It is a matter for the lease, so a charge for a tax or insurance increase during the term is collectible only if the lease provides for it, and the optional clause tax-insurance-escalation-la sets the share, the notice and the refund of any reduction.

The security deposit may be used only for the purposes the deposit statute lists, such as unpaid rent, damage and certain utility charges, and a tax or insurance share is not among them; whether a lease that labels the share rent brings it within the deposit's rent purpose is not settled by the statute, and the library's clause does not call it rent, so collect it directly.

Counties and cities may not regulate rent amounts, except for their own property, rent agreements for subsidized properties, properties assisted with Community Development Block Grant funds, and owners that receive local funding or financial incentives (see edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: Rent Changes During the Lease
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute on rent escalation: none sets notice for a rent increase, limits its size, or makes a lawful increase depend on a lease clause, and the retaliation law protects tenants only as a defense to an eviction, not against a rent increase as such, so there is no escalation-clause safe harbor to earn.

During a fixed term, rent changes only as the lease provides; the optional clause rent-escalation-la sets scheduled amounts or an index formula, and tax-insurance-escalation-la passes on tax and insurance increases. The library offers no clause letting you raise rent during the term at your discretion, because whether such a one-sided term binds the tenant is a question for the courts.

In a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy you may end the tenancy on the statutory notice and offer a new rent (see edu-periodic-tenancy-notice-nc), and counties and cities may not regulate rent amounts, except for their own property, rent agreements for subsidized properties, properties assisted with Community Development Block Grant funds, and owners that receive local funding or financial incentives.

title: No State Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: North Carolina has no tax credit, grant, rent subsidy or other state incentive for landlords who rent to veterans or give veterans a rent concession. Servicemembers have their own lease-termination rights (see edu-servicemember-rights-nc). Any discount you choose to give veterans is a private concession; state it in the lease (rent-concession-wi) and apply it consistently, since fair housing law was not reviewed here for veteran or military status (see edu-fair-housing-nc).

title: No Rule on Refused Subsidy Inspections
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute on what happens when a subsidy program's inspection is refused, whether by a tenant in a voucher or other subsidized unit or by you: none makes a tenant's refusal a ground for ending the lease, gives a program inspector a right of entry, or bars you from declining a subsidized tenancy because of the program inspection. Counties and cities may not require you to accept tenants who pay with federal housing assistance, except for property belonging to the county or city and owners who receive funding or financial incentives from it. Your own access to the unit, including to let a program inspector in, depends on the lease (see landlords-access and edu-no-entry-notice-statute-nc), and a tenant's breach of an access term ends the tenancy only if the lease says that breach ends it. The program's federal rules and your contract with the housing agency govern its inspections once you take part; no library row states those federal rules yet. Local housing code inspections are separate and limited by state law (see edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: No Rule on Subsidy Abatement for Failed Units
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule on prorating or abating rent, or a subsidy's share of it, when a subsidized unit fails a housing-quality inspection or is partly unfit, and none says whether you may collect from the tenant a subsidy payment the housing agency withholds. Federal program rules and your contract with the housing agency decide whether the agency's payment stops and whether the tenant can be charged for it; no library row states those rules yet. State law does treat the tenant's share separately in three places: any fee the fee statute allows must be calculated on the tenant's share of the contract rent only, a tenant appealing an eviction stays it by paying the undisputed rent in arrears (an indigent appellant need not) and undertaking to pay into court the tenant's share of the rent as it comes due, and a lease may provide that accepting a partial housing subsidy payment does not waive a breach. Your duty to keep the unit fit applies whatever the subsidy does, and a tenant may not withhold rent without a court ruling.

title: When a Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In North Carolina a lease of land lasting more than three years from the day it is made is void unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against or by someone that party lawfully authorized (the statute does not say the authority itself must be in writing). A residential lease of three years or less may be oral, and nothing in the statute of frauds requires a shorter lease to be written. The writing rule is a validity rule, not only a recording rule: a separate statute makes a lease of more than three years good against the landlord's later buyers and lien creditors only from the time it is registered with the register of deeds (see edu-lease-registration-nc). An electronic lease and electronic signatures can satisfy a writing and signature requirement under the electronic transactions law (see electronic-signatures). The statute does not say in terms whether an assignment or a surrender of a long lease must be written; that is case law, so put every assignment, surrender or extension of a lease in a signed writing.

title: Recording a Long Lease
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a residential lease to be recorded, but a lease of land for more than three years protects the tenant against the landlord's later buyers for value and lien creditors only from the time it is registered with the register of deeds in the county where the land lies; until then it passes no property interest against them, and the statute makes no exception for a tenant already in possession or for a buyer who knew of the lease. Instead of recording the whole lease, the parties may record a memorandum naming the parties, describing the property, stating the term including extensions, renewals and any option to purchase, and identifying the full agreement; to serve as notice it must be signed by each record owner and each other party and acknowledged before a notary, and the register of deeds will not accept an instrument needing acknowledgment without it. A lease of three years or less is outside the recording statute, and on land registered under the Torrens system a lease of three years or less under which the land is actually occupied binds the registered owner even though it is not noted on the certificate. If the lease carries an option to purchase, Chapter 47G may require the option contract or a memorandum of it to be recorded within five business days (see edu-required-disclosures-nc).

title: Lease Length and Who Must Sign
bodyText: North Carolina sets no maximum term for a residential lease and requires no seal or notarized signature for a lease to be valid; to register a lease, the lessor must acknowledge it or have the signature proven on oath by a witness, and an option to purchase combined with a residential lease must itself be signed and acknowledged by all parties (see edu-required-disclosures-nc). A lease longer than three years must be in writing and signed (see edu-statute-of-frauds-lease-term-nc), and it protects the tenant against later buyers and lien creditors only once recorded (see edu-lease-registration-nc). A lease that is to begin at a future date or event becomes invalid if the term does not actually begin in possession within 30 years after it is signed. If the property is owned by spouses as tenants by the entirety, neither spouse may lease it without the other spouse's written joinder, except where another statute named in the joinder section provides otherwise. If a married owner leases separate property, the law requires the other spouse to sign any instrument affecting the owner's title, with the signing proved or acknowledged, in order to waive that spouse's elective life estate, so have both spouses sign and acknowledge the lease. The Constitution makes a deed of a married owner's homestead invalid without the spouse's signature and acknowledgment; whether that reaches a lease is case law, so if you rent out part of a home you own and live in with a spouse, have the spouse sign and acknowledge the lease. North Carolina has no community-property rule for leases.

title: No Type-Size Rule for Leases
bodyText: North Carolina sets no minimum type size for a residential lease as a whole, and no rule keeps a small-print lease out of evidence or makes it unenforceable. Two type rules can reach a lease's paperwork: an option to buy a one-to-four family home that is combined with or signed with the lease must carry the tenant's three-day cancellation statement in at least 14-point boldface type immediately above the tenant's signature (see edu-required-disclosures-nc), and if the general automatic-renewal statute reaches a lease, any terms that change on renewal must appear on the renewal notice in at least 12-point bold type (see edu-automatic-renewal-nc). A memorandum of lease offered for recording must meet the register of deeds' format rules or pay a nonstandard-document fee, which the register may waive where the only defect is print smaller than 9 points and the instrument is legible. Use a readable type size throughout.

title: No Consumer-Restrictions Statement
bodyText: North Carolina has no plain-language statute for residential leases: no readability test, no required statement of consumer restrictions listing the rights a tenant waives, no Attorney General preapproval of lease forms, and no dollar threshold excluding larger leases from such a rule (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). The state's readability tests apply to insurance policies, not leases. Instead, particular statutes void particular lease terms (see edu-prohibited-lease-terms-nc), and the general rule is in edu-no-plain-language-law-nc.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule requiring a landlord to translate a lease or give a tenant a copy in the language used to negotiate it, no type-size floor tied to a translation duty, and no language rule for leases signed in a foreclosure rent-back; the foreclosure-rescue statute governs those transfers and their written contract but sets no language or translation rule (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). The state's same-language rule for door-to-door sales of consumer goods and services expressly excludes the sale or rental of real property, and the consumer-credit home-solicitation rule covers credit sales, not leases. If you negotiate in another language, giving the tenant a translation is good practice; say in the lease which version controls.

title: No Required Lease Contents or First-Page Dates
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute listing what a residential lease must contain and no rule that the start and end dates of the lease appear on its first page (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). The few items the law requires in writing when the facts apply, such as where the security deposit is held, written authority for utility charges, contamination statements and option-to-purchase terms, are collected in edu-required-disclosures-nc; a memorandum of lease offered for recording must state the term (see edu-lease-registration-nc). State the term's start and end dates clearly near the beginning of the lease anyway, since the deposit cap, the periodic-tenancy notice and the recording rule all turn on the kind and length of the tenancy.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText:
No North Carolina statute requires a landlord who signs its own lease to give the tenant a copy, and a missing copy is not a statutory defense to enforcing the lease or to an eviction.

One exception: if the lease comes with an option for the tenant to buy a one-to-four family home the tenant will live in, the seller must give the tenant an exact copy of the option contract, with its required disclosures, when the tenant signs it (see edu-required-disclosures-nc).

A licensed real estate broker is different: under the Real Estate Commission's rules a broker must deliver a copy of any lease or rental agreement to the broker's customer or client within three days after receiving the executed document, and again within three days after a request; the rules do not define customer, so a broker handling a lease should give the tenant a copy within three days. A broker managing for an owner may, with the owner's prior written authority, using a pre-printed lease form whose material terms the broker may not change without the owner's approval, keep the owner's copies and give the owner an accounting of each lease (property, each tenant's name, phone and home address, rents) within 45 days instead, but must still deliver a copy within five days of the owner's request.

Give every tenant a fully signed copy anyway; the optional acknowledgment in lease-copy-receipt-hi records that you did.

title: No Rule Requiring Tenant Initials
bodyText: North Carolina has no rule that a tenant must initial a lease term, such as a notice period longer than the statutory one, for it to be enforceable, and no rule that a tenant initial each page (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). The only initialing rule found for occupancy is the innkeeper's: a hotel or similar lodging's written statement of the guest's stay, signed or initialed by the guest, is a valid contract, which does not reach ordinary residential tenancies; from July 1, 2026 (S.L. 2026-41, s. 5A.17, not yet in the compiled section) the innkeeper section also covers an apartment's rental, after a declared emergency or disaster, to a disaster-recovery grant recipient while the occupant's home is repaired or rebuilt (see edu-vacation-rental-scope-nc). Having tenants initial an unusual term, such as a longer notice to end a month-to-month tenancy than the statute's seven days (see periodic-tenancy-notice-nc), is still good evidence that they saw it.

title: Which Notices Must Be in Writing
bodyText: North Carolina requires writing for particular notices, not for all of them. You must notify the tenant in writing of a breach of the tenant's statutory maintenance duties (keeping the unit clean and safe, disposing of trash, not damaging the premises or disabling alarms) except in an emergency; itemize deposit deductions in writing and mail or deliver them within 30 days after the tenancy ends and possession is returned (or, if the claim cannot be determined by then, an interim accounting within 30 days and a final one within 60 days); and, before selling property left after an eviction, mail written notice of the sale at least seven days ahead. The tenant must request non-emergency repairs of supplied facilities and appliances in writing, must report a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm needing repair in writing, and must give written notice to end the lease early as a servicemember, a protected victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or a tenant of a property in foreclosure; a tenant surrendering after a casualty does so by a writing. The statutes on the notice to end a periodic tenancy and the demand for past-due rent do not say the notice must be written, but give both on paper so you can prove them, and remember that default, cure and eviction notices for a primary residence fall outside the electronic transactions law (see edu-electronic-notices-nc). The lease may require writing for other notices (see notices).

title: No Agreed Actual-Notice Method Rule
bodyText: North Carolina's landlord-tenant statutes do not define actual notice or list ways of giving it, and no statute lets or forbids the parties to agree on an added method such as a text message (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). Most statutory notices name no delivery method, so the lease's notice clause governs ordinary notices (see notices). Where a statute names a method, follow it: the deposit itemization must be mailed or delivered and the notice of sale of property left after an eviction must go by first-class mail (see edu-written-notice-required-nc). The electronic transactions law, which is what lets an electronic record satisfy a writing rule, does not apply to a notice of default, cure or eviction under a lease of the tenant's primary residence, so give those notices on paper even if the tenant has agreed to text or e-mail (see edu-electronic-notices-nc).

title: House Rules Under North Carolina Law
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute on a private landlord's house rules: none sets conditions for a rule to be enforceable, limits rule changes during a tenancy, binds a tenant only to rules in force at signing, or lets a written notice alone make a new rule part of a month-to-month lease.

With no statute, whether a rule binds the tenant, and whether a lease may let the landlord change rules during the term, is contract case law; so treat rules as lease terms: attach them or state them in the lease and make later changes during the term only with the tenant's written agreement or at a renewal (see rules-wi).

Breaking a rule supports an eviction only if the lease says that a breach ends the tenancy, and the retaliatory-eviction defense does not stop an eviction for breach of a substantial lease covenant that is the real reason for it (see edu-retaliation-nc).

A public housing authority may adopt rules on guests and visitors after consulting its tenants, and an association's rules reach a tenant through the owner's lease (see hoa-compliance), except that in a condominium under the older Unit Ownership Act a unit owner's tenants are bound by statute to the declaration and bylaws (see edu-hoa-nc).

title: Illegal Use Can Void the Lease
bodyText: Under North Carolina's public nuisance law, if a court finds after an adversary hearing in a nuisance abatement action that a tenant uses the premises for lewdness, assignation, prostitution, gambling, illegal sale or possession of alcohol or controlled substances, or repeated breaches of the peace, that use makes the lease void at the owner's option and possession reverts to the owner without any act by the owner. Where repeated drug activity leads to forfeiture of the property itself, a tenant found to have taken part in the nuisance loses the lease, and the court weighs an owner's good faith, including lease terms barring illegal drugs, eviction of tenants who break them, criminal record checks and prior-residency reference checks. An order of abatement may also close the place against further nuisance use. Outside a nuisance case, use the lease's own limits (residential-use-only, criminal-activity-nc) and the expedited eviction for criminal activity (see edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-nc); North Carolina has no statute that voids a lease merely because the premises are used for a prohibited purpose without a court finding.

title: No Double-Letting Rule
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute on renting the same room or unit to two tenants for the same period: no ban, no rent-abatement remedy and no rule written for competing tenants (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). For a lease of more than three years the recording statute decides priority against later purchasers for value by registration (see edu-lease-registration-nc); whether a later tenant counts as such a purchaser, and which tenant prevails under shorter leases, is case law. The nearest rule is the crime of renting or leasing residential property to someone while knowing you have no ownership or leasehold interest in it, a felony that is also an unfair trade practice. A second lease of space already let to someone else exposes you to the first tenant's claims under the lease and general contract law, which this library has not reviewed, so never let space already under lease.

title: Leasing by a Life Tenant
bodyText: North Carolina law has no usufruct and no statute on leases granted by a usufructuary, and no statute says whether a lease granted by someone holding only a life estate survives that person's death (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). If a lease ends because of a death during a rent period, the lessor or the lessor's personal representative may recover rent for the part of the period before the death, and any security for the rent is apportioned the same way. Where the property is subject to a contingent remainder, a lease binding everyone can be authorized by a special proceeding before the clerk of superior court. Whether a life tenant's lease binds the remaindermen otherwise is case law, so if you hold only a life estate, tell the tenant, have the remaindermen join the lease or obtain court authority, and keep the term within what you can deliver.

title: Seasonal Rentals
bodyText: North Carolina has no seasonal-tenancy statute: no seasonal lease form, no rule ending a seasonal lease without notice, and no seasonal exception to the landlord-tenant rules (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). What matters is whether the stay is a vacation rental: renting residential property for vacation, leisure or recreation for fewer than 90 days to someone who has a permanent home to return to is governed by the Vacation Rental Act, not by the residential rental agreements law, and a rental to someone with no other primary residence is not a vacation rental (see edu-vacation-rental-scope-nc). A seasonal rental that is not a vacation rental is an ordinary residential tenancy, so a fixed seasonal term ends on its last day; the repair and eviction rules apply in full, and the deposit rules apply if you are in the business of renting or managing dwelling units on a weekly, monthly or annual basis. One code point: for local minimum housing codes, a manufactured home, mobile home or recreational vehicle used solely for a seasonal vacation purpose is not a dwelling. Housing used as living quarters for migrant farmworkers employed seasonally is separately regulated by the Migrant Housing Act (preoccupancy inspection and certification, safety and heating standards), unless you regularly rent housing to the general public on the same terms (see edu-tenant-employee-housing-nc).

title: Lease Guaranties and Renewals
bodyText:
A promise to answer for a tenant's debt or default is enforceable in North Carolina only if the guaranty, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor or someone the guarantor authorized. No statute says whether a lease guaranty covers renewals, extensions or a month-to-month holdover, requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or end date, makes a guaranty revocable as to future rent, or limits what you may collect from a guarantor up front other than through the general security-deposit cap, which limits security deposits for a dwelling unit without saying who pays them, so count any money a guarantor gives as security toward that cap (see edu-security-deposit-cap-nc); those questions are for the guaranty's own words and case law, so state in the guaranty whether it covers renewals and holdover.

Under the general surety statute, which does not say in terms whether a lease is an obligation it covers (case law, so assume it does), once a rent payment or other obligation is due a guarantor may serve you written notice, by sheriff or registered mail with return receipt, requiring you to use all reasonable diligence to recover from the tenant and to realize on any security you hold; the guarantor must also notify any co-guarantors, and if you do not take appropriate action within 30 days, the guarantor is discharged to the extent prejudiced, and a waiver of defenses for extensions of time does not prevent that. The optional guaranty clause is guaranty-as.

title: Notice of Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: No North Carolina statute requires a residential tenant to tell the landlord about a lawsuit, foreclosure, tax proceeding or other claim against the property, so that duty exists only if the lease creates it (the library-wide clause tenant-forward-proceedings-ca, tagged for North Carolina, does). The law runs the other way in foreclosure: when residential property with fewer than 15 rental units is sold under a power of sale, the notice of sale must also be mailed to each person occupying it under a residential rental agreement, by name if known or to "occupant" (the same subdivision has the other notices mailed first-class at least 20 days before the sale), and the tenant may then end the lease early (see edu-foreclosure-tenant-rights-nc).

title: Optional Terms North Carolina Law Lets a Lease Add
bodyText: Several North Carolina rights exist for a landlord only if the lease provides for them, and the library offers a clause for each: a late fee within the statutory cap (late-fee-limit-nc); the complaint-filing, court-appearance and second-trial fees and capped attorneys' fees, which require a written lease (eviction-fees-nc); a provision that, in an eviction based on a forfeiture clause, accepting partial rent or a partial subsidy payment does not waive a breach for which the lease reserved the right of reentry (partial-payment-nonwaiver-nc); a forfeiture clause making a breach end the tenancy, which is what lets a non-rent breach support eviction under the summary ejectment statute (the expedited eviction for criminal activity does not depend on it; see edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-nc) (default-by-tenant-nc); and charges for water, sewer, electricity or gas, allowed only under a written rental agreement and the utility billing rules (utility-billing-nc). By contract the lease may also make the tenant liable for accidental damage the tenant would otherwise not owe (tenant-caused-damage-nc), displace the statutory casualty surrender rule (casualty-termination-nc), shift smoke and carbon monoxide alarm batteries by written agreement (smoke-co-alarms-nc), require renters insurance on the statutory conditions (renters-insurance-nc), charge a reasonable nonrefundable pet fee (pet-policy-nc), and name an emergency contact for a tenant's death (emergency-contact-nc). A lease combined with an option to purchase brings in the option-contract and seller-disclosure rules in edu-required-disclosures-nc, which are not repeated here. Each clause is optional; none is required.

title: Out-of-State Owners and Entity Landlords
bodyText: North Carolina does not require an individual owner who lives out of state to name an in-state agent in the lease or anywhere else, and it has no income-tax withholding on rent paid to nonresident owners (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). Entity landlords have registration rules instead. An out-of-state corporation or LLC may not transact business in North Carolina until it obtains a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State, and once authorized it must keep a registered office and a registered agent in the state, whose job is to forward any notice, process or demand served on it. Merely owning real property is not transacting business, but renting homes appears on the safe list only for property acquired in foreclosure while it is being liquidated, so obtain the certificate before you rent; an entity transacting business here without a certificate cannot maintain a lawsuit, including an eviction, unless it obtains the certificate before trial (the issue is raised by motion and decided before trial), and owes back fees and taxes with interest plus a civil penalty of $10 a day up to $1,000 a year, though its acts, including its leases, stay valid and it may still defend a suit. Anyone, individual or entity, who rents under a name other than its own real or registered name must first file an assumed business name certificate with the register of deeds (see edu-entity-landlord-court-representation-nc for court appearance).

title: Working With Law Enforcement
bodyText: North Carolina has no general duty for a landlord to cooperate with police, report tenants' crimes or hand over tenant records on request, and no crime-free lease program in state law (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). Cooperation runs mostly toward the landlord: in an expedited eviction for criminal activity a police agency may give you police and lab reports and make officers available to testify, people who in good faith start, join or give information for such an action are immune from civil liability, and if a local program lists your property among the top ten percent for crime or disorder, the local government must tell you what is being counted and it and the sheriff or police must help you address the criminal activity, including testifying in an eviction. Cooperating with law enforcement is also a sign of good faith a court weighs before ordering a drug-nuisance property forfeited. Two duties do bind you: if a court order directs it, you must give officers the information and help needed to install a pen register or trap-and-trace device, for which you are paid your reasonable expenses; and like anyone else you must report suspected abuse, neglect or dependency of a child, or a child's death from maltreatment, to the county department of social services, report to law enforcement within a reasonable time a child under 16 you reasonably suspect has disappeared and may be in danger, if you are 18 or older immediately report to local law enforcement a juvenile you know or should reasonably know has been the victim of a violent offense, sexual offense or misdemeanor child abuse (even where a tenant committed it), report a disabled adult you reasonably believe needs protective services, notify the medical examiner of a sudden, violent or suspicious death you suspect, and not disturb the body until the medical examiner authorizes it (unless, with the medical examiner unavailable, law enforcement decides the body cannot safely stay at the scene).

title: Beyond the Landlord-Tenant Chapter
bodyText: This library searched all of North Carolina's General Statutes, the Constitution, the 2024-2026 session laws and the held state administrative rules, not only the landlord-tenant chapter, for rules landlords ask about. (1) Squatters: North Carolina does have a squatter-specific procedure, in force since December 1, 2025, for removing a person who never had a right to occupy and never paid rent (see edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-nc). (2) Cash rent receipts: no statute requires a landlord to give a receipt for rent, cash or otherwise, and no general law gives a payer a right to demand one; a licensed broker's trust-account records must include receipts for cash payments in leasing transactions (see edu-no-cash-receipt-duty-nc). (3) Registration before an eviction: no state law makes landlord registration or a rental license a condition of filing for or winning possession, and local registration is limited by state law (see edu-landlord-registration-nc); the only registration rules found that would bar a landlord's lawsuit are for out-of-state business entities (other suit bars, such as those for unlicensed security-system and installment-paper businesses, do not reach renting), such as a corporation, LLC or limited partnership that transacts business here without a certificate of authority or registration (see edu-nonresident-owner-agent-nc). (4) Rules outside the chapter that do bind every landlord, such as assumed business name filing and the duties to report suspected child or disabled-adult abuse and suspicious deaths, are in edu-nonresident-owner-agent-nc and edu-law-enforcement-cooperation-nc.

title: No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Notice
bodyText: North Carolina has no tenant protection act of the California kind: no statewide cap on rent increases, no just-cause eviction rule for private rentals and no general right for a tenant to buy or get first offer on a rental you sell, so there is no statutory notice about any of them to put in a lease (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). Cities and counties may not regulate the amount of rent on private property, except their own, subsidized or grant-assisted property and owners who take local funding or incentives (see edu-local-preemption-nc). The state housing-authorities law lets a public housing authority end or refuse to renew a lease for a serious or repeated violation of a material term or other good cause; it does not itself say these are the only grounds, and the federal public housing rules are stated elsewhere (see edu-good-cause-notice-nc). The only tenant purchase right is in condominium conversions, where the converter must offer each residential tenant the unit for 30 days after the conversion notice (see edu-condo-conversion-notice-nc); converting a manufactured home community requires 180 days' notice to home owners but gives no purchase right.

title: No Rent-Cap Exemption Notice
bodyText: Because North Carolina has no statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction law for private rentals, there is nothing to be exempt from and no exemption notice to put in a lease, whether for a single-family home, a newer building or any other property (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules searched). Do not copy another state's exemption statement into a North Carolina lease; the rules that do apply are in edu-tpa-notice-nc.

title: No Sunset on Core Tenant Laws
bodyText: North Carolina has no tenant protection act on a repeal clock, and none of its core landlord-tenant statutes (the residential rental agreements law, the security deposit act, the eviction, retaliation and expedited criminal-eviction articles, or the Vacation Rental Act) carries an expiration or automatic repeal date in the General Statutes as compiled through Session Law 2026-30 or in the 2024-2026 session laws held for this library. Changes come instead from ordinary amendments, which the library tracks row by row.

title: Emergency Contacts
bodyText:
North Carolina does not require a landlord to give tenants an emergency telephone number, a management website or a social-services hotline notice, and does not require a tenant to name an emergency contact.

Naming one still matters: if a tenant who is the sole occupant dies leaving belongings in the unit, the landlord's affidavit to take possession of them must name the person identified in the rental application, lease or other landlord document as the authorized person to contact in the event of the tenant's death or emergency and describe the landlord's good-faith attempt to reach that person, and the landlord must mail that person a copy of the affidavit; with no contact named, the landlord must post notice of the filing instead. Use the optional clause emergency-contact-nc to collect the contact (see edu-tenant-death-nc), and give tenants a number for urgent repairs as good practice.

title: Other Rules North Carolina Does Not Have
bodyText: Several lease-formation and notice rules found in other states have no North Carolina counterpart in the law searched for this library (General Statutes, 2024-2026 session laws, the Constitution and the held state administrative rules). North Carolina has: (1) no ban on or remedy for renting the same unit to two tenants (edu-double-letting-nc); (2) no duty to translate a lease (edu-translation-duty-nc); (3) no type-size rule for the lease as a whole (edu-lease-type-size-nc); (4) no rule requiring tenant initials on any term (edu-lease-notice-initial-requirement-nc); (5) no list of required lease contents and no first-page date rule (edu-lease-content-requirements-nc); (6) no plain-language or consumer-restrictions statement (edu-plain-language-consumer-statement-nc); (7) no statute on private house rules or changing them (edu-rules-regulations-nc); (8) no seasonal-tenancy rule apart from the vacation rental line and the Migrant Housing Act for seasonal farmworker housing (edu-seasonal-tenancy-nc); (9) no usufruct (edu-usufructuary-lessor-nc); (10) no agreed actual-notice method rule (edu-actual-notice-method-nc); (11) no tenant duty to report proceedings against the property (edu-adverse-proceeding-notice-nc); and (12) no rule on whether a guaranty covers renewals (edu-guarantor-renewal-nc). General contract law, which this library has not reviewed, governs each of these, so the lease should address any that matter to you.

title: Associations and Rented Homes
bodyText:
North Carolina's condominium and planned community laws do not let an association collect rent from your tenant when you fall behind on assessments, do not cap or regulate an association's lease-approval or tenant-application fee or deposit, and do not say whether a declaration's leasing restriction binds only owners who bought after it or agreed to it; any leasing limits or approval requirement come from the association's own declaration and rules.

The association acts against you as owner: unless the declaration sets its own procedure, it may fine an owner only after notice and a hearing, the fine is an assessment secured by a lien on your unit or lot, and a common expense caused by an occupant's misconduct (or, in a planned community, negligence) may be assessed against your unit or lot alone.

In an older condominium still under the Unit Ownership Act, tenants are expressly subject to that Act and to the declaration and bylaws.

The shared association compliance clause has your tenant follow association rules and pay fines the tenant causes, the deposit statute lets a security deposit cover unpaid bills that become a lien on the property because of the tenant's occupancy, and whether an association fine is such a bill is not settled by the statute (case law), so say in the lease that association fines the tenant causes are the tenant's responsibility and deduct one only after it has become a lien, and the library also offers an optional clause recording that you gave the tenant the association documents and an optional approval condition for associations whose documents require approval of a lease. No North Carolina statute protects a tenant's home child care against an association.

title: Tenant Duties Set by Statute
Nuisance Abatement and Rental Property
bodyText: Under North Carolina's nuisance abatement law, using, owning or leasing a building or place for prostitution, gambling, illegal possession or sale of alcohol or controlled substances, or obscene matter, or one where repeated breaches of the peace (such as assaults, threats or firing guns) are carried on or permitted, is a nuisance, and the building, its contents and the ground itself can be enjoined and abated.
