The State, a district attorney, a county or city, or any private citizen of the county (except for a nuisance involving the illegal possession or sale of obscene or lewd matter; a private citizen must post a bond of at least $1,000 before getting a restraining order or temporary injunction) may sue in superior court; for drug, alcohol, gambling, prostitution and breach-of-peace nuisances an owner is treated as knowing if the owner knew or by due diligence should have known, the court may close the property before trial and in its final order, the costs of abatement (including attorney fees) are a lien on the property, and a later owner who neglects to abate after notice of an injunction is liable too. Where the nuisance includes at least two prior occurrences within five years of drug manufacture, sale or possession with intent to sell, or two prior Schedule I or II possession occurrences, the property itself can be forfeited to the county school board, but only if every owner is a defendant, the plaintiff is not a private citizen, and the court finds by clear and convincing evidence that every owner took part in the nuisance or had prior written notice of it and made no good-faith efforts to stop it (otherwise, only if it continues or recurs within five years of the abatement order without good-faith efforts to abate it), and good-faith factors the court may weigh include lease terms banning illegal drugs with eviction of violators and criminal record and reference checks of applicants. If a court finds after a hearing that a tenant used the place for these purposes, the lease becomes void at your option and possession reverts to you, and an owner who pays the costs and posts a bond for the property's full value, conditioned on abating the nuisance and keeping it away for a year, may ask the court to return a closed property, which it may do if satisfied of the owner's good faith; the release does not clear any judgment or lien on the property. This law sets up no nuisance receivership or rent escrow and requires no summary of it in the lease; to remove a tenant or household member involved in drug or other criminal activity, the faster route is the expedited eviction action (see edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-nc and the lease clause criminal-activity-nc).

title: Contractor Liens for Tenant Work
bodyText:
In North Carolina a contractor, worker, designer or supplier who improves real property under a contract with the owner can claim a lien on it, and the statute defines the owner as a person who has an interest in the property, for whom the improvement is made and who ordered it, including the owner's agents acting within their authority; real property includes leaseholds, and the lien reaches the property only to the extent of that owner's interest. Work your tenant orders can therefore be liened against the tenant's leasehold, but the statute does not say when it also reaches your own interest: whether you become an owner of the work by consenting to, requiring or paying for it, or because the tenant acted as your agent, is case law.

North Carolina has no notice-of-nonresponsibility procedure and no statute letting a lease keep the landlord's interest free of liens; a claim of lien must be filed with the clerk of superior court within 120 days after the claimant last furnished labor or materials at the site, and a contractor's agreement to waive its lien rights in exchange for getting the contract is unenforceable.

The cautious course is the optional no-liens clause, which keeps tenant-ordered work the tenant's responsibility, says the tenant is not your agent and has the tenant tell each contractor that you are not paying (no-liens-ar); avoid paying for or directing a tenant's work unless you mean to answer for it.

title: No Landlord Lien on a Residential Tenant's Belongings
bodyText: North Carolina prohibits distress and distraint: a residential landlord has no lien on, and no right to seize or hold, a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent, and has rights in a residential tenant's personal property only under the statutes on abandoned property of small value, disposal of property left after a writ of possession is executed, sheriff's storage after an eviction, and a deceased tenant's property. Because those rules sit in the residential ejectment law, a lease term contrary to them (such as a contractual landlord's lien or a security interest in household goods enforced by seizure) is void as against public policy. The one residential exception is a manufactured home lot: a lessor of a space for a manufactured home has a statutory lien on the tenant's manufactured home, furniture and other belongings if the home is still on the space 21 days after the lessor is put in possession by a writ and the lessor has a lawful damages claim, for rent due when the tenant left plus up to 60 days, damage beyond normal wear and tear and sale costs, enforced by public sale; there is no lien if the lessor and tenant agree there will be none, and it does not outrank an already perfected security interest. The landlord's crop lien and crop-insurance lien apply only to land rented for agricultural purposes, and the statutory lien on furniture and fixtures left behind applies only to nonresidential premises. Recover unpaid residential rent through a court judgment and lawful deductions from the security deposit (see edu-self-help-eviction-nc and edu-post-eviction-property-nc).

title: When Rented Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText:
North Carolina's general eminent domain chapter treats a lease as property and anyone holding an interest in the land, including a tenant, as an owner, so a tenant's leasehold can be part of a condemnation and share in the compensation, which is generally the fair market value of what is taken (or, for a partial taking, the loss in value of the whole tract if greater); where owners and tenants make conflicting claims to the award, the clerk or judge may have the money paid into court and decide who gets it.

No North Carolina statute says whether a lease ends, or whether rent stops or is reduced, when all or part of the rented property is taken, and none lets a court cancel a lease because of a taking; that is left to the lease and to case law, so use the optional condemnation clause to settle termination, rent and the award between you and the tenant (see eminent-domain-vi).

Separately, a public agency whose project displaces a residential tenant may owe the tenant moving expenses and, if the tenant lawfully occupied the dwelling for at least 90 days before negotiations to acquire it began, a rental replacement payment of up to $5,250 under the state relocation assistance law, where the agency has made that law apply to the project (a short-term tenant who moved in after the agency acquired the property is generally not a displaced person); those payments belong to the tenant.

title: Foreign Adversary Land Limits and Leases
bodyText: North Carolina generally lets aliens buy, inherit, hold and convey land just as citizens can, and nothing requires a lease to an alien to say so or to give the alien's name and address. Starting April 1, 2027, the North Carolina Farmland and Military Protection Act bars a prohibited foreign party from buying, acquiring, leasing or holding any direct interest in agricultural land (which excludes land leased for agricultural research and development or for producing farm inputs, up to 250 acres in the aggregate per lessee) or in property within 50 miles of a listed military installation (such as Fort Bragg, Camp Lejeune, Cherry Point or Seymour Johnson), and the interests it covers include a lease of one year or longer, or one renewable by option to a total of one year. A prohibited foreign party is a government on a federal arms-export list of adversary countries or a state-controlled enterprise of one, an entity or trust organized under such a government's laws or in which such governments or entities hold a significant interest or control (generally a third or more), and an agent, trustee or other fiduciary for one; the definition does not reach a person because of his or her citizenship, and it excludes an entity cleared by, or holding a national security agreement with, the federal Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), and a U.S. subsidiary of such an entity. A prohibited foreign party that already held a covered interest before April 1, 2027, or before its country was added to the federal list, may keep it but must register with the Secretary of State and may not acquire more; the Act's separate bar on acquiring any interest, and its one-year divestiture rule for land acquired by devise, descent or debt enforcement, each exclude a de minimis direct interest, which the Act defines as small or passive holdings in an entity that owns the land, not a lease; the first bar, on any direct interest, carries no such exception, and the text does not say how the two fit (case law not reviewed for this library). You face no civil or criminal liability for failing to find out whether a tenant is a prohibited foreign party, but knowingly selling a covered interest in violation of the Act, or aiding such a sale with actual knowledge, is a misdemeanor; the Act does not say whether granting a lease counts as selling, so do not knowingly lease covered land for a year or more to an entity you know is a prohibited foreign party. Separate rules already bar an adversarial foreign government from holding any interest in land with commercially valuable high-purity quartz, and the Act gives no private right to sue.

title: Home Businesses in Rentals
bodyText: Since July 7, 2026, a North Carolina city may not ban a no-impact home-based business or require a permit, license, registration or other approval to run one, though it may adopt narrowly tailored rules for health and safety, to keep the business secondary to and compatible with residential use, and to bar uses such as selling illegal drugs or liquor or adult businesses. A no-impact home-based business is one owned and operated by the owner or occupant of the home that sells only lawful goods or services, keeps on-site employees and clients within the city's occupancy limit, creates no on-street parking or substantial added traffic, operates inside the home or in its yard, is not visible from the street and stores nothing outside, so a tenant can qualify. The rule limits city ordinances only: it does not apply where a deed, covenant or other agreement restricting use of the land, or association documents, prohibit the business, it does not cover county ordinances, and no North Carolina statute makes a home business a right against the landlord. A lease may therefore limit or bar business use (see residential-use-only); county zoning rules and other local ordinances remain local and were not researched for this library (see edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: Hunting, Fishing and Trapping on Rented Land
bodyText:
No North Carolina statute decides whether you or your tenant holds the right to hunt, fish or trap on rented land, or requires a written grant before a tenant of farmland may hunt; that is left to the lease.

The trespass law treats the lessee much like the owner: either may post the land with signs or purple paint marks, and on posted land a person who hunts, fishes or traps without written permission of the landowner, lessee or agent, carried and dated within the last 12 months, commits a misdemeanor. Trapping on another's land, posted or not, requires written permission from the owner or the owner's agent dated within the past year, and the wildlife law's definition of owner leaves out lessees (unless the lease is in substance a disguised sale, such as a security device for the tenant's purchase), so an ordinary tenant cannot authorize trapping on its own.

A tenant who is principally engaged in cultivating land leased for agricultural purposes counts as a landholder and, with a spouse and dependents under 18 living there, may take wildlife on that land without the general hunting, fishing and trapping licenses (special licenses such as those for alligator, elk, bear and falconry still apply). If you want to keep the hunting, fishing and trapping rights, or control who the tenant lets in, say so in the lease (see farmland-sporting-rights-co).

title: Flags and Signs at Rentals
bodyText: No North Carolina statute gives a tenant a right, as against the landlord, to display a flag, political sign or other sign at a rental home, so a lease may set reasonable display rules (see edu-rules-regulations-nc). The statutory display protections run elsewhere: in condominiums and planned communities, since August 11, 2026 no covenant restriction may be read to regulate or prohibit an owner's display of a United States or North Carolina flag up to 4 by 6 feet shown under the federal flag customs on property the owner owns exclusively, whatever the restriction says, and a restriction may regulate an association member's political signs on the member's own property only if it uses the statute's required wording, with associations still able to limit timing (from 45 days before to 7 days after an election) and size and number; those protections name owners and members, not tenants. Counties and cities may not prohibit an official governmental flag (such as the United States, North Carolina or another recognized nation's flag) flown under the federal customs with the consent of the owner or of a person in lawful control of the property, though they may set reasonable health and safety limits on size, number, location and pole height.

title: No Religious Display Rule for Rentals
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute giving a tenant a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah on the door frame or a holiday decoration, or limiting a lease rule on them. A neutral display rule that applies the same way to every tenant is a lease matter (see edu-rules-regulations-nc), but the State Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to discriminate because of religion or national origin in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental (subject to its exemptions, such as a building of up to four units where you or a family member lives, or a room in your own home; see edu-fair-housing-nc), so do not apply a display rule more strictly to one faith or culture, and do not refuse or end a tenancy because of a religious item.

title: No Canvassing Access Rule for Rentals
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to let candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or other canvassers into an apartment building, a gated community or a manufactured home park, and none barring a landlord from limiting that access; who may enter common areas is governed by the lease and the landlord's own rules (see common-area-use and edu-trespass-notice-nc). Whether a tenant may invite a canvasser into the tenant's own home is likewise a matter for the lease's guest rules (see edu-guest-rights-nc). The only related statute is a criminal ban on targeted picketing directed at a particular single-family or multifamily residence or its occupants, from the sidewalk or street in front of or beside it, in a manner the picketer knows or should know would make a reasonable person fear for safety or suffer substantial emotional distress; general picketing that moves through a neighborhood is not barred.

title: Tenant Organizing Is Protected from Retaliation
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute giving tenants an affirmative right to organize on the property, to meet in a community room or common area, or to distribute literature, and none requiring a landlord to recognize or bargain with a tenants' organization. It does protect organizing against retaliation: a good-faith attempt to organize, join or otherwise be involved with any organization promoting or enforcing tenants' rights is a protected act, and a tenant facing an eviction filed within 12 months after it may defend on the ground that the eviction is substantially in response to it; if the court agrees it must deny the eviction, though the landlord can still recover rent due. The landlord may still prevail where the eviction rests on unpaid rent or another substantial lease breach, a holdover after a fixed term with no renewal option, a good-faith notice to quit given before the protected act, or the other grounds the statute lists. Any waiver of these protections by a tenant or household member is void, so a lease must not bar tenant organizing or penalize it (see edu-retaliation-nc).

title: Trying to Settle Disputes Before Court
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute requiring, regulating or limiting a lease term that has the landlord and tenant try to resolve a dispute informally before going to court. A residential tenant may be removed only through the court eviction process (summary ejectment or the expedited criminal-activity action), so a pre-suit step should leave possession cases, emergency relief and every statutory notice and deadline untouched; the optional clause the library offers does exactly that and binds neither party to accept any proposal (see informal-dispute-resolution-or).

The jury-waiver statute, which makes a contract term waiving a jury trial unenforceable, says it does not stop parties from agreeing to arbitrate or use other forms of alternative dispute resolution (see edu-binding-arbitration-nc). Community mediation centers, also called dispute settlement centers, may take referrals and charge fees for civil mediation, and chief district court judges must encourage mediation in civil district court cases where they find it appropriate.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute on tenant portals and none that bars or requires online rent payment or limits a landlord's choice of payment methods for a long-term residential lease; payment terms are a lease matter (see acceptable-payment-methods).

The electronic transactions law, which lets leases be signed and records be delivered electronically, applies only where both parties have agreed to deal electronically, and a party who agreed may still refuse to conduct other transactions electronically, a right that cannot be waived; so a lease cannot bind a tenant to use the portal for later, separate transactions (whether a renewal, amendment or a particular record is a separate transaction is not defined in the statute and is case law, so offer paper whenever a tenant asks).

That law also does not apply at all to a notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a person's primary residence, so serve those notices the way the lease and eviction law provide, not through the portal (see edu-electronic-notices-nc).

Where a law requires information to be given to a consumer in writing, electronic delivery counts only after the tenant's affirmative consent following a clear statement of the right to paper copies and to withdraw consent, and withdrawal may not carry a fee.

The optional portal clause keeps portal notices voluntary and promises another fee-free way to pay when the portal is down (see tenant-portal-mn); vacation rentals have their own rules on processing fees (see edu-vacation-rental-scope-nc).

title: Renter's Insurance and Losses
bodyText:
North Carolina lets a lease require the tenant to carry insurance, but since July 1, 2025 the lease cannot require the tenant to buy it from a designated insurer or through a designated agent, and if the tenant does not show proof of the required coverage within three business days after you ask, you may obtain the coverage and charge the tenant only your actual cost plus an administrative fee of no more than $50 a year; a lease term contrary to those limits is void.

No North Carolina statute says whose insurance pays for which loss, requires a tenant to report a loss or claim, or governs subrogation between the landlord's and tenant's insurers; those are lease and insurance-policy matters.

By statute a tenant is not liable for damage that happens accidentally despite the tenant's reasonable diligence unless the tenant has agreed by contract to be liable, while the tenant remains responsible for damage the tenant or the tenant's guests cause deliberately or negligently (see edu-tenant-caused-damage-nc). The library's clauses state the insurance requirement and the carrier-choice and proof rules (see tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca and renters-insurance-nc).

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to register coverage with a city or county, or to tell tenants whether the landlord is insured or what the landlord's policy covers. Whether to insure, and for how much, is the landlord's own business decision and may be a condition of a mortgage or of association documents. A landlord who requires the tenant to carry renter's insurance must follow the carrier-choice and proof rules (see edu-tenant-insurance-claims-nc). Whether a city or county ordinance imposes an insurance condition, for example in a rental registration or permit program, is local and was not researched for this library (see edu-landlord-registration-nc and edu-local-preemption-nc).

title: No Statutory Absence-Notice Duty
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute requiring a tenant to tell the landlord about an extended absence, and none giving the landlord a right to enter or a remedy because of one; a lease may add an absence-notice duty with ordinary contract damages for breach, and the library offers one (see extended-absence-notice-ks).

An absence alone is not abandonment: for the procedure letting you give belongings worth $750 or less to a nonprofit, property is deemed abandoned if you find evidence clearly showing the tenant voluntarily vacated after the paid rental period ended and you have no notice of a disability that caused the vacancy, and a presumption of abandonment arises 10 or more days after you conspicuously post a notice of suspected abandonment inside and outside the home and get no response; the statute does not say whether that test also decides abandonment of the tenancy itself (see edu-abandoned-property-nc). North Carolina also has no statute on landlord entry during an absence, so entry is governed by the lease (see edu-no-entry-notice-statute-nc).

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute on landlord entry to a rented home, so there is no statutory notice period to shorten and no rule requiring a scheduled-services entry right to be written conspicuously; entry for regularly scheduled services such as filter changes or pest treatment rests on the lease (see edu-no-entry-notice-statute-nc and landlords-access). The library offers an optional clause that lists the services, the schedule and the hours, and promises advance notice and a knock before entry (see scheduled-services-entry-la).

Entry should still be reasonable: whether an unreasonable or harassing entry breaches the tenant's right to possession is case law, so enter only as the lease allows, at reasonable times and with notice, and entry may not be used to remove the tenant or the tenant's belongings outside the court process (see edu-self-help-eviction-nc). Local housing-code inspections by government inspectors are separate and are limited by state law (see edu-rental-inspection-nc).

title: Tenant Animals Left Without Care
bodyText:
North Carolina has no statute letting a landlord enter a rented home to care for, or remove, an animal left without care when the tenant is hospitalized, jailed or otherwise away, and none requiring the tenant to name a caretaker; entry for that purpose rests on the tenant's consent in the lease, and the library offers an optional animal-care clause naming a caretaker (see animal-care-access-vi).

It is a misdemeanor for an owner or possessor of an animal, or anyone with its charge or custody, to willfully abandon it without justifiable excuse, so a tenant who leaves pets behind may be reported to animal control. A landlord may charge a reasonable nonrefundable pet fee, and a pet deposit counts toward the security deposit limit (see edu-pet-fees-nc and pet-policy-nc).

The post-eviction property rules speak of personal property and do not say how they apply to a live animal left after an eviction; that is case law, so keep any animal fed and safe, contact the tenant and animal control promptly, and do not dispose of it as ordinary property (see edu-post-eviction-property-nc).

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a landlord to give a tenant who has a dog, cat or other pet any state fact sheet or notice about what happens to pets in an eviction, at signing or at any other time. The eviction notices the law does require, such as the sheriff's notice before a writ of possession is executed, are covered in the library's eviction rows (see edu-eviction-process-nc and edu-post-eviction-property-nc). For pets left without care during a tenancy, see edu-animal-care-access-nc.

title: Parking Rules and Towing Notice
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to deliver parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, to give them a prescribed heading, to limit changes during the term, or to limit the vehicle information a landlord may ask for; parking terms are a lease matter (see parking-vehicle-rules and assigned-parking-space). Notice to drivers comes from the towing law instead: in the counties and cities where the private-lot towing statute applies, an unauthorized vehicle may be towed on the owner's or lessee's written request only after signs at least 24 by 24 inches at every entrance have named the towing company and its phone number (and individually assigned spaces are marked) for 72 hours (see edu-towing-nc). Separately, at the written request of the owner or person in charge, a county or city may adopt an ordinance regulating stopping, standing or parking in specified areas of an apartment complex or condominium parking lot, and a vehicle parked in violation may be moved by law enforcement.

title: Charging Separately for Parking
bodyText: North Carolina has no statute requiring a landlord to charge for parking separately from rent, or barring a landlord from including parking in the rent or charging a separate parking fee; whether parking is included, assigned or extra is a lease matter (see parking-ks-oh-ca and assigned-parking-space). A separate parking charge is not one of the fees the fee statute regulates, but state the amount in the lease so it is clear what is rent and what is a charge (see edu-fees-as-rent-nc).

title: Housing Provided to Employees
bodyText: North Carolina has no general statute on housing a landlord provides to an employee: no required disclosure of the occupancy and vacating terms, no deadline to vacate when the job ends, and no duty to offer a rental agreement afterward. The Residential Rental Agreements Act (the fitness, repair and tenant-duty rules) does not apply to a dwelling furnished without any charge or rent, but when the employee pays rent or the housing is part of the employee's pay (wage law counts the reasonable cost of lodging an employer furnishes as wages), whether it is "without charge" and whether the occupant is a tenant are questions the statutes do not answer and case law. Whether a former employee who stays on can be removed by summary ejectment, which is written for tenants holding over, or by the expedited removal of unauthorized persons, which excludes anyone who has paid rent or any other payment for the occupancy, is likewise not stated; never lock out or remove an occupant yourself, put the occupancy terms in a signed writing, and use a court process to recover possession (see edu-self-help-eviction-nc and edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-nc). Housing for migrant agricultural workers is separately regulated (unless you regularly rent housing to the general public and rent to the workers on the same or comparable terms, or the unit is owned by an occupant and occupied solely by a family unit): the owner or controller must have it certified after a preoccupancy inspection before it is occupied, a waiver by the workers is void, and housing found uninhabitable must be fixed or replaced at the same or lower rate.

title: Drug-Free Lease Terms
bodyText: North Carolina does not require a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, prescribe its wording, or bar one. The expedited criminal-activity eviction law applies to every residential rental agreement whether or not the lease mentions drugs: the court must order eviction where criminal activity (any controlled-substance offense other than simple possession, or other crime threatening other residents' or the landlord's employees' health, safety or peaceful enjoyment) occurred in the unit, the unit was used to further it, or the tenant, a household member or a guest engaged in it on or near the premises, unless the tenant proves noninvolvement and lack of knowledge or reasonable efforts to prevent it (a defense harder to use in a later action), or the court is clearly convinced that immediate eviction would be a serious injustice whose prevention outweighs the need to protect the other tenants and residents; even when it denies complete eviction the court may remove the culpable household members (see edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-nc). A lease term still adds value: it makes the activity a lease breach supporting an ordinary eviction without a cure period, and in a nuisance case seeking forfeiture of the property, lease terms prohibiting illegal drugs together with evicting violators are among the factors showing the owner's good faith (see edu-nuisance-nc). The library's clause for this is criminal-activity-nc; collecting rent while knowing of the illegal acts does not waive the default. Federally assisted housing may have its own lease requirements, which this row does not cover.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: North Carolina follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 25-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 25-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: North Carolina's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. ch. 42 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how North Carolina's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
